companies.name: Northwind Global
companies.about:
Northwind Global designs, builds and runs technology for banks, insurers, manufacturers and public bodies in more than 40 countries. Our delivery centres in Dublin, Warsaw, Pune and Austin work as one team, so clients get the same standards whichever office picks up the work.

We invest heavily in our people. Every consultant has a funded learning path, and we partner with Walnut to certify new joiners in the cloud, data and SAP skills our clients ask for most.
benefits: Hybrid working from any Northwind office
Private health cover for you and your family

companies.name: Helix Cloud Systems
companies.about:
Helix Cloud Systems runs the compute, storage and networking platform behind thousands of digital businesses. Our regions span North America, Europe and Asia Pacific, and our engineers own their services end to end, from design reviews to on-call.

We hire for curiosity and calm under pressure. New site reliability engineers complete the Helix SRE onboarding programme, built with Walnut, before they join the rota.
benefits: Restricted stock units for every hire

companies.name: Meridian Bank Group
companies.about:
Meridian Bank Group serves 22 million retail and corporate customers across the United Kingdom, the Gulf and Asia. We are modernising a long-established bank: moving core systems to the cloud, rebuilding our mobile apps and putting data at the centre of financial crime prevention.

Our analytics teams in London, Dublin, Dubai, Singapore and Hyderabad work on the same platform. Analysts joining financial crime teams complete our Walnut-built financial crime analytics course in their first month.

companies.name: Aurora Health Technologies
companies.about:
Aurora Health Technologies builds clinical software used in more than 900 hospitals across Europe, from patient records to imaging analytics. Our products are certified medical devices, so quality and privacy are part of every engineering decision.

We hire internationally and help colleagues settle in Germany, the Netherlands, Switzerland and Sweden. Many of our international hires learn German with Walnut before and after they arrive.

companies.name: Falcon Gulf Energy
companies.about:
Falcon Gulf Energy produces and trades energy across the Gulf and beyond, with a growing portfolio of solar, hydrogen and carbon capture projects. Our digital office in Abu Dhabi supports operations in the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and our shared services centre in India.

We run one of the region's largest SAP S/4HANA estates. Finance and SAP hires complete the Falcon SAP energy finance course, designed with Walnut, during onboarding.
benefits: Annual flight tickets for the family

companies.name: Kitsune Mobility
companies.about:
Kitsune Mobility designs electric vehicles, batteries and the software that connects them. From our Yokohama headquarters and engineering hubs in Munich, Singapore and Austin, we ship over-the-air updates to more than three million vehicles.

Our software teams work in English, with Japanese language support for colleagues who want it. We value careful engineering, long-term thinking and teams that learn together.

companies.name: Lindqvist Assurance
companies.about:
Lindqvist Assurance protects homes, businesses and families in eleven European markets. We price risk with data, settle most claims digitally and are rebuilding our policy platforms on modern cloud services.

Our technology hub in Kraków and analytics teams in Stockholm and Amsterdam work closely with underwriters and claims handlers, so the people who build our tools see how they are used.

companies.name: Corvane Semiconductors
companies.about:
Corvane Semiconductors designs power and sensor chips for cars, factories and data centres. Our fabs in Malaysia and Singapore and design centres in Eindhoven, Dresden, Austin and Kyoto run around the clock.

Software and data matter as much as silicon here. Our yield analytics, test automation and manufacturing systems teams turn billions of measurements a day into better chips.

companies.name: Bellhaven Advisory
companies.about:
Bellhaven Advisory helps leadership teams make large decisions: entering new markets, restructuring finance functions and moving to modern ERP and data platforms. We work with clients in 60 countries from offices in New York, London, Paris, Dubai, Mumbai and Sydney.

Consultants build expertise through client work and structured learning. Every analyst has a sponsor partner and a funded certification plan.

companies.name: Solenne Pharma
companies.about:
Solenne Pharma discovers and manufactures medicines for oncology, immunology and rare diseases, reaching patients in more than 100 countries. Our research centres in Basel and Lyon now pair scientists with data scientists from the first day of a programme.

Our digital and data organisation, with hubs in Hyderabad and Singapore, builds platforms for clinical trials, manufacturing quality and commercial analytics.

companies.name: Pacifica Logistics Group
companies.about:
Pacifica Logistics Group moves freight by sea, air and road for manufacturers and retailers across Asia, the Middle East and Europe. We run 180 warehouses and a network of port terminals, all coordinated by our own transport management platform.

Our technology teams in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and Bengaluru build the routing, tracking and forecasting software that keeps goods moving.

companies.name: Talvik Telecom
companies.about:
Talvik Telecom connects 30 million mobile, broadband and enterprise customers in North America and Europe. We are moving our network functions to the cloud and rebuilding customer journeys around self-service.

Engineers, analysts and sales teams in Toronto, Dallas, London and Pune work on shared platforms, with clear ownership and regular rotations between teams.

companies.name: Ventora Consumer Brands
companies.about:
Ventora Consumer Brands makes personal care, home care and food brands sold in more than 120 countries. We are shifting our marketing to first-party data and direct-to-consumer channels, and rebuilding our supply chain planning on modern analytics.

Our teams in Paris, London, Dubai, Mumbai and Kuala Lumpur combine brand building with digital craft.

companies.name: Quayside Insurance
companies.about:
Quayside Insurance provides motor, home and small business cover to customers in Ireland and the United Kingdom. Most of our customers now buy and claim online, and our product and engineering teams own those journeys.

We opened our Wrocław engineering centre in 2021 and now run cross-border teams with one way of working.

companies.name: Arcwell Aviation
companies.about:
Arcwell Aviation operates a fleet of 140 aircraft from its Doha hub, linking the Gulf with Europe, Africa and Asia. Our digital teams build the booking, loyalty, crew planning and maintenance systems that keep the airline on time.

We hire internationally and provide accommodation, travel benefits and a structured welcome for colleagues relocating to Qatar.

companies.name: Najd Horizon Retail
companies.about:
Najd Horizon Retail runs 600 supermarkets, fashion and electronics stores across Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, with a fast-growing online business. We are building a customer data platform to personalise offers across stores and apps.

We offer international hires a clear path to relocation and support colleagues in learning Arabic.

companies.name: Vireo Renewables
companies.about:
Vireo Renewables develops and operates wind, solar and battery storage projects in Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States. Our 9 gigawatts of capacity are managed by a central operations platform that forecasts output and trades energy in real time.

We are a practical, mission-led team and we expect people to grow with us.

companies.name: Ledgerline Software
companies.about:
Ledgerline Software makes accounting and spend management software for mid-sized companies. Over 40,000 finance teams close their books on Ledgerline each month.

We are product-led and remote-friendly. Engineers, designers and customer teams work in small squads with clear goals and a short path to production.
benefits: Four-week paid sabbatical after four years

companies.name: Bastionworks Cyber
companies.about:
Bastionworks Cyber runs managed detection and response for banks, hospitals and governments. Our security operations centres in Manchester, Washington, Singapore and Dubai watch over 3,000 client environments around the clock.

We grow our own analysts. New SOC analysts complete a structured programme, including the Walnut SOC level 1 course, before they take live alerts.

companies.name: Akane Commerce
companies.about:
Akane Commerce runs one of Japan's largest online marketplaces and is growing fast in Southeast Asia. Millions of shoppers use our app every day for groceries, fashion and electronics.

Our Tokyo engineering organisation works mostly in English. Teams in Singapore and Kuala Lumpur build our regional marketplace and payments products.

companies.name: Kestrel Pay
companies.about:
Kestrel Pay gives online businesses a single account to accept payments, pay suppliers and manage foreign exchange. We process payments in 35 currencies and hold e-money licences in the United Kingdom and the European Union.

We are a regulated fintech with a start-up pace. Teams are small, decisions are written down and engineers talk to customers.

companies.name: Fjordlight Games
companies.about:
Fjordlight Games makes cooperative online games played by 20 million people a month. Our studios in Stockholm, Kraków and Montreal share one engine, one backend platform and one live operations team.

We care about craft, fair monetisation and healthy working hours. Crunch is not part of how we ship.

companies.name: Selasih Commerce
companies.about:
Selasih Commerce helps neighbourhood retailers in Malaysia, Singapore and India sell online, manage stock and offer same-day delivery. More than 60,000 stores run on our platform.

Our Kuala Lumpur and Bengaluru teams ship weekly and measure success by the growth of the shops we serve.

companies.name: Windmark Renewables
companies.about:
Windmark Renewables builds and operates onshore wind and solar parks in Germany, the Netherlands, Poland and France. Our digital team turns turbine and weather data into better maintenance plans and higher output.

We welcome international colleagues and pay for German or Dutch lessons for anyone who wants them.

companies.name: Orbitline Analytics
companies.about:
Orbitline Analytics builds a product analytics platform used by 3,000 software companies to understand how customers use their products. We process more than 40 billion events a day.

We hire engineers and analysts who like hard data problems and clear writing.

companies.name: Harbourstone Capital
companies.about:
Harbourstone Capital offers digital wealth management to investors in Singapore, Australia and Malaysia. Our robo-advice platform manages more than 9 billion dollars in client assets.

We combine investment discipline with product craft, and we hire people who explain complex ideas simply.

companies.name: Sablewood Insurtech
companies.about:
Sablewood Insurtech sells pet, travel and gadget insurance through partner apps and retailers. Customers buy cover in under two minutes and most claims are paid the same day.

We are a small team with large partners, so everyone works close to customers and data.
benefits: Pet insurance for your own pets

companies.name: Qanat Digital
companies.about:
Qanat Digital is a digital-first mobile operator and cloud services provider in Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar. Customers join, top up and get support entirely in our app.

We are building the region's next generation of telecoms engineers, with structured training for national talent and international hires alike.

companies.name: Neuroloop AI
companies.about:
Neuroloop AI builds assistants that help support and operations teams resolve customer requests with large language models and retrieval over company knowledge. Our customers include insurers, retailers and software companies.

We are a seed-to-Series B team in Austin and Bengaluru. Everyone ships, and everyone talks to customers.

companies.name: Paperkite Labs
companies.about:
Paperkite Labs builds workflow software for legal and compliance teams: document intake, review queues and audit trails. Our customers are mid-sized law firms and in-house legal teams.

We are small, calm and remote-friendly, with a hub in Dublin.

companies.name: Shieldnest Security
companies.about:
Shieldnest Security protects small and mid-sized businesses with a managed security service built on open tooling. Our analysts in Pune, Singapore and Dubai monitor endpoints, email and cloud accounts for more than 1,500 customers.

We hire early-career analysts and train them properly, with certifications paid for.

companies.name: Bursztyn Pay
companies.about:
Bursztyn Pay offers instant invoice financing to small businesses in Poland and Germany. Owners upload an invoice and receive funds within an hour, priced by our own risk models.

We are a compact team of engineers, risk analysts and sales people in Warsaw and Berlin.

courses.title: Python for data professionals
courses.subtitle: Write clean, reproducible Python and use pandas to turn raw files into answers a business can act on.
courses.description:
Python is the working language of data teams from London to Singapore. This course takes you from a clean installation to confident, reproducible analysis with pandas, the library behind most analyst and data scientist job descriptions.

You will learn the core language first, then load, clean, join and summarise real-world tables, chart the results and package your work so a colleague can rerun it. Every module ends with a short quiz, and the final assessment confirms the skills employers ask for.

**Who this is for**

- Analysts moving from Excel to code
- Graduates preparing for data analyst or junior data scientist roles
- Engineers and finance professionals who need to automate reporting
- Anyone applying for a role that lists Python, pandas or Git as a mandatory skill
outcomes: Set up an isolated Python environment and manage dependencies with venv and pip.
Use core Python types, functions and comprehensions to write readable data code.
Load, clean, filter, join and reshape tabular data with pandas.
Summarise data with groupby aggregations and present results as clear charts.
Track and share your work with Git using branches, commits and pull requests.
Turn an exploratory notebook into a tested, rerunnable script.

lessons.title: Setting up a reproducible environment
lessons.content:
## Why environments matter

On a shared team, "it works on my machine" is the most expensive sentence in analytics. Each project should have its own isolated Python environment with pinned dependencies, so a colleague in another country can rebuild exactly what you ran.

## Creating a virtual environment

Python ships with the **venv** module. Create one environment per project, in the project folder:

~~~bash
python -m venv .venv
# macOS and Linux
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

python -m pip install --upgrade pip
pip install pandas matplotlib jupyterlab
pip freeze > requirements.txt
~~~

Anyone can now recreate the environment with `pip install -r requirements.txt`. Add `.venv/` to your `.gitignore`; the requirements file is what you share, not the folder.

## Notebooks and scripts

- **JupyterLab** is ideal for exploration: run a cell, inspect the result, adjust.
- **Scripts** (`.py` files) are better for anything that runs on a schedule or is reviewed by others.
- A good habit is to explore in a notebook and move stable logic into functions in a module as soon as it works.

## Checklist for a new project

- Create the folder, a virtual environment and a `README.md` that says how to run the work.
- Pin versions in `requirements.txt`, and record the Python version (for example 3.12).
- Keep raw data read-only in a `data/raw` folder and write outputs to `data/processed`.
- Never commit credentials. Read them from environment variables instead.

These habits take minutes and save days when an auditor, a manager or a future you asks how a number was produced.

lessons.title: Core types, control flow and functions
lessons.content:
## The building blocks

Most data code uses a handful of built-in types:

| Type | Example | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| int, float | `42`, `3.75` | Counts and measures |
| str | `"GB"` | Codes, names, text |
| list | `[120, 95, 300]` | Ordered values |
| dict | `{"country": "DE", "rate": 0.19}` | Lookups and records |
| tuple | `("EUR", 2026)` | Fixed groups of values |
| set | `{"SQL", "Python"}` | Unique values, membership tests |

## Control flow and comprehensions

~~~python
orders = [{"id": 1, "amount": 120.0, "country": "GB"},
          {"id": 2, "amount": 80.5, "country": "IN"},
          {"id": 3, "amount": 310.0, "country": "GB"}]

uk_total = sum(o["amount"] for o in orders if o["country"] == "GB")
large_ids = [o["id"] for o in orders if o["amount"] > 100]
by_country = {}
for o in orders:
    by_country[o["country"]] = by_country.get(o["country"], 0) + o["amount"]
~~~

List and dictionary comprehensions are idiomatic, fast and easy to review. Use a plain loop when the logic needs more than one condition or a side effect.

## Writing functions

Functions make logic reusable and testable. Give them clear names, type hints and a docstring:

~~~python
def vat_inclusive(net: float, rate: float = 0.20) -> float:
    """Return the gross amount for a net amount and VAT rate."""
    if net < 0:
        raise ValueError("net must not be negative")
    return round(net * (1 + rate), 2)
~~~

## Good practice

- Follow PEP 8 naming: `snake_case` for functions and variables.
- Prefer f-strings for formatting: `f"{total:,.2f}"`.
- Raise clear exceptions early rather than returning silent wrong answers.
- Keep functions small: one job each.

lessons.title: Series, DataFrames and selecting data
lessons.content:
## Two core objects

- A **Series** is a one-dimensional labelled array: one column.
- A **DataFrame** is a table of Series that share an index.

~~~python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("data/raw/orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
df.shape          # (rows, columns)
df.dtypes         # type of each column
df.head()         # first five rows
df.info()         # types, non-null counts and memory
~~~

Always inspect `dtypes` after loading. A numeric column read as `object` usually means stray text such as "n/a" or a thousands separator.

## Selecting rows and columns

| Need | Code |
|---|---|
| One column | `df["amount"]` |
| Several columns | `df[["order_id", "amount"]]` |
| Rows by label | `df.loc[df["country"] == "DE", ["order_id", "amount"]]` |
| Rows by position | `df.iloc[0:10]` |
| Several conditions | `df[(df["amount"] > 100) & (df["country"].isin(["DE", "FR"]))]` |

Use `&` and `|` with parentheses around each condition. Python's `and`/`or` do not work element-wise.

## Creating columns

~~~python
df["amount_eur"] = df["amount"] * df["fx_rate"]
df["order_month"] = df["order_date"].dt.to_period("M")
df["is_large"] = df["amount_eur"] >= 1_000
~~~

Vectorised operations like these run in optimised C code. Avoid looping over rows with `iterrows()`: it is slow and harder to read.

## Avoiding a classic warning

If you filter a DataFrame and then assign to the result, pandas may raise a `SettingWithCopyWarning`. Take an explicit copy when you intend to modify a subset: `uk = df[df["country"] == "GB"].copy()`.

lessons.title: Cleaning and transforming data
lessons.content:
## Real data is messy

Expect missing values, duplicates, inconsistent codes and wrong types. Cleaning is usually most of the work, so make it explicit and repeatable.

## Missing values

~~~python
df.isna().sum()                              # missing per column
df["region"] = df["region"].fillna("Unknown")
df = df.dropna(subset=["customer_id"])      # rows unusable without a key
~~~

Decide case by case. Filling a missing revenue with zero changes your averages; often it is better to keep the gap and report it.

## Types and text

~~~python
df["amount"] = pd.to_numeric(df["amount"].str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")
df["signup_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["signup_date"], format="%Y-%m-%d", errors="coerce")
df["country"] = df["country"].str.strip().str.upper()
df["country"] = df["country"].replace({"UK": "GB"})   # ISO 3166-1 alpha-2
~~~

`errors="coerce"` turns unparseable values into `NaN`/`NaT` so you can count and investigate them instead of crashing.

## Duplicates

~~~python
dupes = df.duplicated(subset=["order_id"], keep=False)
print(dupes.sum(), "rows share an order_id")
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")
~~~

## Make cleaning a function

~~~python
def clean_orders(raw: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return (raw
            .rename(columns=str.lower)
            .assign(country=lambda d: d["country"].str.strip().str.upper())
            .drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])
            .query("amount >= 0"))
~~~

Method chaining keeps each step visible and easy to test. Log row counts before and after each step so that you can explain any rows you removed.

lessons.title: Grouping, joining and reshaping
lessons.content:
## Split, apply, combine

`groupby` answers most "by" questions: revenue by country, tickets by week, hires by role.

~~~python
summary = (df.groupby(["country", "order_month"], as_index=False)
             .agg(orders=("order_id", "count"),
                  revenue=("amount_eur", "sum"),
                  avg_order=("amount_eur", "mean")))
~~~

Named aggregations, as above, produce tidy column names that read well in reports.

## Joining tables

`merge` works like a SQL join:

~~~python
orders = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
~~~

- `how="left"` keeps every order even if the customer is missing.
- `validate="many_to_one"` raises an error if the customer table has duplicate keys, which would silently multiply your revenue.
- Use `indicator=True` to add a `_merge` column showing which side each row came from.

## Reshaping

| Task | Method |
|---|---|
| Long to wide (months as columns) | `pivot_table(index="country", columns="order_month", values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")` |
| Wide to long | `melt(id_vars="country", var_name="month", value_name="revenue")` |
| Stack tables with the same columns | `pd.concat([q1, q2], ignore_index=True)` |

## Window-style calculations

~~~python
df = df.sort_values(["customer_id", "order_date"])
df["order_number"] = df.groupby("customer_id").cumcount() + 1
df["revenue_3m"] = (df.set_index("order_date")
                      .groupby("customer_id")["amount_eur"]
                      .transform(lambda s: s.rolling("90D").sum())
                      .values)
~~~

`transform` returns a result aligned to the original rows, which is ideal for adding running totals or shares of a group.

lessons.title: Exploratory analysis with a purpose
lessons.content:
## Start from the question

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is not about running every chart. Write down the business question first, for example "Which markets drove the fall in repeat orders last quarter?", then explore only what helps answer it.

## A practical sequence

1. **Profile the data**: `df.describe(include="all")`, value counts for key categories, the date range covered.
2. **Check quality**: missing values, impossible values (negative quantities, dates in the future), duplicated keys.
3. **Look at distributions**: medians and percentiles are more robust than means when values are skewed, as salaries and order values usually are.
4. **Compare segments**: country, channel, product line, customer tenure.
5. **Look at change over time**: weekly or monthly trends, with seasonality in mind.

~~~python
df["amount_eur"].describe(percentiles=[0.5, 0.9, 0.99])
df["channel"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3)
(df.groupby("order_month")["customer_id"].nunique()
   .pct_change().round(3))
~~~

## Correlation is not cause

`df.corr(numeric_only=True)` is a useful scan, but a strong correlation only says that two measures move together. Before you claim a cause, look for a confounder (for example, both measures rise in December) and, where possible, a controlled comparison.

## Record what you find

Keep a short log alongside the notebook:

- What you checked and the result.
- Data issues and how you handled them.
- Open questions for the data owner.

Stakeholders trust analysis that states its limits. A sentence such as "Germany is excluded for March because the feed was incomplete" protects you and your reader.

lessons.title: Clear charts with matplotlib and pandas
lessons.content:
## Choose the chart for the message

| Message | Chart |
|---|---|
| Change over time | Line chart |
| Compare categories | Horizontal bar chart, sorted |
| Distribution | Histogram or box plot |
| Relationship between two measures | Scatter plot |
| Part of a whole (few parts) | Stacked bar; avoid pie charts with many slices |

## A clean bar chart

~~~python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

top = (df.groupby("country")["amount_eur"].sum()
         .sort_values()
         .tail(10))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
top.plot.barh(ax=ax, color="#5b3fd6")
ax.set_title("Revenue by country, last 12 months (EUR)")
ax.set_xlabel("Revenue (EUR)")
ax.set_ylabel("")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("outputs/revenue_by_country.png", dpi=200)
~~~

## Rules that make charts trustworthy

- **Title states the subject, unit and period.**
- Start bar axes at zero. Line charts may start elsewhere if you label the axis clearly.
- Sort categories by value unless they have a natural order (months, age bands).
- Use one highlight colour for the point you want people to see and neutral greys for the rest.
- Never rely on colour alone: label the series directly or add markers, which also helps colour-blind readers.
- Format large numbers: `ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter("{x:,.0f}")`.

## Small multiples

When you need to compare many groups, several small charts with a shared axis are clearer than one crowded chart:

~~~python
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6), sharey=True)
for ax, (region, part) in zip(axes.flat, monthly.groupby("region")):
    ax.plot(part["order_month"].astype(str), part["revenue"])
    ax.set_title(region)
~~~

modules.title: Professional practice: Git and production-ready code

lessons.title: Version control with Git
lessons.content:
## Why analysts use Git

Git records every change to your code with a message explaining why. It lets a team work on the same project in parallel, review each other's work and roll back safely. Most data roles list Git as a required skill.

## The everyday workflow

~~~bash
git clone https://github.com/acme/sales-analytics.git
cd sales-analytics
git switch -c feature/churn-by-region     # new branch for your change

# ...edit files...
git status
git add src/churn.py tests/test_churn.py
git commit -m "Add churn rate by region with tests"
git push -u origin feature/churn-by-region
~~~

Then open a **pull request** (GitHub) or **merge request** (GitLab). A colleague reviews it, comments, and merges it into `main` once checks pass.

## Writing good commits

- One logical change per commit.
- Imperative subject line under about 70 characters: "Fix currency conversion for JPY".
- Explain the why in the body when it is not obvious.

## What not to commit

Create a `.gitignore` at the start:

~~~bash
.venv/
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
data/raw/
.env
~~~

Never commit credentials or personal data. If a secret is committed, rotate it immediately: deleting it in a later commit does not remove it from history.

## Notebooks and Git

Notebook files store outputs and metadata, which makes diffs noisy. Clear outputs before committing, or use a tool such as `nbstripout`, and move reusable logic into `.py` modules that diff cleanly.

lessons.title: From notebook to tested script
lessons.content:
## Why move out of the notebook

Notebooks run cells in any order, hide state and are hard to schedule. Once an analysis is going to be repeated, turn it into a script with functions, a clear entry point and tests.

## A simple project layout

~~~bash
sales-analytics/
  src/sales/clean.py
  src/sales/report.py
  tests/test_clean.py
  requirements.txt
  README.md
~~~

## An entry point with arguments

~~~python
# src/sales/report.py
import argparse
import pandas as pd
from sales.clean import clean_orders

def main() -> None:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Monthly revenue report")
    parser.add_argument("--input", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--output", required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    df = clean_orders(pd.read_csv(args.input))
    report = df.groupby("order_month", as_index=False)["amount_eur"].sum()
    report.to_csv(args.output, index=False)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
~~~

## Testing with pytest

~~~python
# tests/test_clean.py
import pandas as pd
from sales.clean import clean_orders

def test_removes_duplicate_orders():
    raw = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 1], "country": [" gb", "GB"], "amount": [10, 10]})
    out = clean_orders(raw)
    assert len(out) == 1
    assert out["country"].iloc[0] == "GB"
~~~

Run `pytest -q`. Tests document what your code promises and catch regressions when someone changes it later.

## Logging, not printing

Use the `logging` module so that scheduled jobs record what happened: rows read, rows dropped and output written. Combined with Git and pinned requirements, this makes your work auditable, which regulated employers such as banks and healthcare companies expect.

courses.title: SQL for analytics and reporting
courses.subtitle: Query, join and summarise business data with standard SQL, and model tables that make reporting reliable.
courses.description:
SQL is the most requested skill in analytics job descriptions worldwide, because almost every company keeps its operational data in a relational database or a cloud warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery or Azure Synapse.

This course teaches ANSI-standard SQL that works across PostgreSQL, SQL Server, MySQL and cloud warehouses, with notes where dialects differ. You will move from simple queries to joins, common table expressions and window functions, and finish by designing a small star schema for reporting.

**Who this is for**

- Aspiring data and business analysts
- Finance, operations and marketing professionals who rely on others to pull data
- Developers who want to write better analytical queries
- Candidates whose target job lists SQL as a mandatory skill
outcomes: Explain tables, keys and relationships in a relational database.
Filter, sort and aggregate data with SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING.
Combine tables with inner, left and full outer joins without duplicating rows.
Structure complex logic with common table expressions and subqueries.
Use window functions for rankings, running totals and period-on-period change.
Design a simple star schema of fact and dimension tables for reporting.

lessons.title: How relational databases organise data
lessons.content:
## Tables, rows and columns

A relational database stores data in **tables**. Each row is one record (an order, an employee, a payment) and each column holds one attribute with a defined type such as `INTEGER`, `DECIMAL(12,2)`, `VARCHAR(100)`, `DATE` or `TIMESTAMP`.

## Keys and relationships

- A **primary key** uniquely identifies each row, for example `customer_id`.
- A **foreign key** in one table refers to the primary key of another, for example `orders.customer_id` points to `customers.customer_id`.
- Relationships are usually **one-to-many**: one customer has many orders.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  customer_id   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name          VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  country_code  CHAR(2)      NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id   INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (customer_id),
  order_date    DATE    NOT NULL,
  amount        DECIMAL(12, 2) NOT NULL
);
~~~

## Normalisation in brief

Operational systems are **normalised**: each fact is stored once. The customer's country lives in `customers`, not repeated on every order. This avoids inconsistent updates but means analysts must join tables to answer questions.

## Where you will meet SQL

| Platform | Typical use |
|---|---|
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle | Operational applications |
| Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks SQL | Cloud analytics warehouses |
| SQLite, DuckDB | Local files and quick analysis |

The core of SQL is standardised (ISO/IEC 9075), so most of what you learn transfers directly. Differences are mainly in date functions, string functions and how you limit rows.

lessons.title: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and limiting rows
lessons.content:
## The shape of a query

~~~sql
SELECT order_id, customer_id, amount
FROM   orders
WHERE  order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
  AND  amount > 500
ORDER  BY amount DESC
FETCH  FIRST 10 ROWS ONLY;   -- PostgreSQL also accepts LIMIT 10; SQL Server uses TOP (10)
~~~

SQL is written in this order but **processed** in a different one: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, then the row limit. That is why you cannot use a SELECT alias inside WHERE in most databases.

## Filtering

| Operator | Example |
|---|---|
| Comparison | `amount >= 100` |
| Range | `order_date BETWEEN DATE '2026-01-01' AND DATE '2026-03-31'` |
| List | `country_code IN ('DE', 'FR', 'NL')` |
| Pattern | `email LIKE '%@example.com'` |
| Missing | `region IS NULL` (never `= NULL`) |

Combine conditions with `AND`, `OR` and `NOT`, and use parentheses whenever you mix `AND` and `OR`.

## Calculated columns

~~~sql
SELECT order_id,
       amount,
       amount * 0.20                     AS vat,
       CASE WHEN amount >= 1000 THEN 'Large'
            WHEN amount >= 100  THEN 'Medium'
            ELSE 'Small' END             AS order_band
FROM   orders;
~~~

`CASE` is the SQL equivalent of if/else and is one of the most useful tools for analysts.

## Habits that prevent mistakes

- List columns explicitly instead of `SELECT *`: queries stay stable when tables change and scan less data in columnar warehouses.
- Use half-open date ranges (`>= start AND < next_start`) for timestamps, so the last day is not cut off at midnight.
- Format queries consistently so reviewers can follow them.

questions.explanation: A foreign key references another table's primary key and enforces that the related row exists.

questions.explanation: NULL is not equal to anything, including NULL, so you must use IS NULL.

questions.prompt: Why can't you usually reference a SELECT alias in the WHERE clause?

options.text: Aliases are only allowed in views
Aliases must be in capital letters

questions.explanation: The logical processing order evaluates WHERE before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

lessons.title: Aggregating with GROUP BY and HAVING
lessons.content:
## Aggregate functions

`COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` collapse many rows into one value per group.

~~~sql
SELECT c.country_code,
       COUNT(*)                     AS orders,
       COUNT(DISTINCT o.customer_id) AS customers,
       SUM(o.amount)                AS revenue,
       AVG(o.amount)                AS avg_order
FROM   orders o
JOIN   customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
WHERE  o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
GROUP  BY c.country_code
HAVING SUM(o.amount) > 50000
ORDER  BY revenue DESC;
~~~

## The two filters

- **WHERE** filters rows *before* grouping.
- **HAVING** filters groups *after* aggregation.

Put every condition that does not need an aggregate in WHERE. It is clearer and lets the database discard rows early.

## Rules to remember

- Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
- `COUNT(*)` counts rows; `COUNT(column)` ignores NULLs; `COUNT(DISTINCT column)` counts unique non-null values.
- `AVG` ignores NULLs, which may or may not be what the business means. If a missing value should count as zero, write `AVG(COALESCE(score, 0))`.

## Conditional aggregation

You can produce several measures in one pass by putting CASE inside an aggregate:

~~~sql
SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)               AS month,
       SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'web'   THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS web_revenue,
       SUM(CASE WHEN channel = 'store' THEN amount ELSE 0 END) AS store_revenue,
       AVG(CASE WHEN returned THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END)           AS return_rate
FROM   orders
GROUP  BY DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date);
~~~

`DATE_TRUNC` is PostgreSQL and Snowflake syntax; SQL Server 2022 offers `DATETRUNC(month, order_date)`. The pattern itself is universal.

lessons.title: Joining tables correctly
lessons.content:
## Join types

| Join | Keeps |
|---|---|
| `INNER JOIN` | Only rows with a match on both sides |
| `LEFT JOIN` | Every row from the left table, matched data or NULLs from the right |
| `FULL OUTER JOIN` | Every row from both sides |
| `CROSS JOIN` | Every combination (use deliberately, for example to build a date grid) |

~~~sql
-- Customers with no orders this year
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name
FROM   customers c
LEFT   JOIN orders o
       ON  o.customer_id = c.customer_id
       AND o.order_date >= DATE '2026-01-01'
WHERE  o.order_id IS NULL;
~~~

Notice the date filter sits in the **ON** clause. Putting it in WHERE would remove the NULL rows and turn the left join into an inner join, a very common bug.

## The fan-out trap

If you join two "many" tables to the same parent, rows multiply. For example, joining `orders` and `support_tickets` to `customers` and then summing order amounts double-counts revenue for every customer with more than one ticket.

Fix it by aggregating each child table to the parent grain first:

~~~sql
WITH order_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS revenue FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id
), ticket_totals AS (
  SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS tickets FROM support_tickets GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, o.revenue, t.tickets
FROM   customers c
LEFT   JOIN order_totals  o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
LEFT   JOIN ticket_totals t ON t.customer_id = c.customer_id;
~~~

## Check your joins

- Know the **grain** of each table: what one row represents.
- Compare row counts before and after the join.
- Check for duplicate keys with `GROUP BY key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`.

lessons.title: Common table expressions and subqueries
lessons.content:
## Breaking a problem into steps

A **common table expression** (CTE) names an intermediate result with `WITH`. Each step can be read and tested on its own, which makes long reporting queries much easier to review.

~~~sql
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT customer_id,
         DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
         SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM   orders
  GROUP  BY customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date)
),
active AS (
  SELECT month, COUNT(*) AS active_customers, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
  FROM   monthly
  GROUP  BY month
)
SELECT month,
       active_customers,
       revenue,
       revenue / NULLIF(active_customers, 0) AS revenue_per_customer
FROM   active
ORDER  BY month;
~~~

`NULLIF(x, 0)` returns NULL instead of zero, which avoids a division-by-zero error.

## Subqueries

Subqueries are still useful for short filters:

~~~sql
-- Orders above the overall average
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM   orders
WHERE  amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders);

-- Customers who bought a product in the 'Cloud' category
SELECT customer_id
FROM   customers c
WHERE  EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  JOIN   products p ON p.product_id = o.product_id
  WHERE  o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND p.category = 'Cloud'
);
~~~

`EXISTS` stops at the first match and handles NULLs safely. Be careful with `NOT IN`: if the subquery returns any NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all. Prefer `NOT EXISTS`.

## When to use which

- CTE: multi-step logic, anything you would explain in more than one sentence.
- Subquery: a single value or a simple existence test.
- Temporary table or view: an intermediate result reused by several queries.

lessons.title: Window functions for rankings and running totals
lessons.content:
## What a window function does

A window function calculates across a set of rows related to the current row **without collapsing them**, unlike GROUP BY. The window is defined with `OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ...)`.

## Ranking

~~~sql
SELECT country_code,
       product_id,
       revenue,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY country_code ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER (PARTITION BY country_code ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY country_code ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS dense_rnk
FROM   product_revenue;
~~~

| Function | Ties 100, 100, 90 |
|---|---|
| ROW_NUMBER | 1, 2, 3 |
| RANK | 1, 1, 3 |
| DENSE_RANK | 1, 1, 2 |

To keep the top three products per country, wrap the query in a CTE and filter `WHERE rn <= 3`. Snowflake, BigQuery and Databricks also support `QUALIFY rn <= 3`.

## Running totals and moving averages

~~~sql
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                          ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS ytd_revenue,
       AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                          ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)         AS avg_3m
FROM   monthly_revenue;
~~~

## Period-on-period change

~~~sql
SELECT month,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
       (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
         / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 0) AS mom_change
FROM   monthly_revenue;
~~~

`LAG` and `LEAD` read earlier and later rows. For year-on-year comparison of monthly data, use `LAG(revenue, 12)` only if every month is present; otherwise join to the same month last year.

lessons.title: Dates, NULLs and data types
lessons.content:
## Dates and time zones

Business questions are usually about calendar periods, so date handling decides whether your numbers match finance's.

| Task | PostgreSQL / Snowflake | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|
| Truncate to month | `DATE_TRUNC('month', ts)` | `DATETRUNC(month, ts)` |
| Add days | `ts + INTERVAL '7 days'` / `DATEADD(day, 7, ts)` | `DATEADD(day, 7, ts)` |
| Difference in days | `DATEDIFF('day', a, b)` (Snowflake) | `DATEDIFF(day, a, b)` |
| Extract part | `EXTRACT(YEAR FROM ts)` | `YEAR(ts)` |

Store timestamps in UTC and convert to local time for reporting, for example `ts AT TIME ZONE 'Europe/London'` in PostgreSQL. A sale at 23:30 in New York is already the next day in UTC.

## NULL behaves differently

- Any arithmetic with NULL returns NULL: `100 + NULL` is NULL.
- Comparisons with NULL are unknown, so rows drop out of WHERE filters.
- `COALESCE(a, b, c)` returns the first non-null value.

~~~sql
SELECT order_id,
       COALESCE(discount, 0)            AS discount,
       amount - COALESCE(discount, 0)   AS net_amount
FROM   orders;
~~~

## Types and precision

- Store money in `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC`, not floating point, to avoid rounding drift.
- Integer division truncates in several databases: `7 / 2` returns 3 in PostgreSQL and SQL Server. Cast first: `7 / 2.0` or `CAST(x AS DECIMAL(12,4))`.
- Compare text in a consistent case, `UPPER(country_code) = 'GB'`, or rely on a case-insensitive collation deliberately.

lessons.title: Module 3 quiz
lessons.content: Four questions on CTEs, window functions and data types.

lessons.title: Dimensional modelling: facts and dimensions
lessons.content:
## Why analytical models differ

Operational databases are normalised for fast, consistent writes. Reporting needs fast, simple reads. **Dimensional modelling**, described by Ralph Kimball, organises data into facts and dimensions that business users understand.

## Facts and dimensions

- A **fact table** records measurable events at a declared grain: one row per order line, per payment, per daily account balance. It holds numeric measures and foreign keys.
- A **dimension table** describes the context: date, customer, product, country, channel. It holds descriptive attributes used to filter and group.

~~~sql
CREATE TABLE dim_customer (
  customer_key   INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,     -- surrogate key
  customer_id    VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,    -- business key from the source
  name           VARCHAR(200),
  segment        VARCHAR(50),
  country_code   CHAR(2),
  valid_from     DATE,
  valid_to       DATE,
  is_current     BOOLEAN
);

CREATE TABLE fact_sales (
  date_key       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  customer_key   INTEGER NOT NULL,
  product_key    INTEGER NOT NULL,
  quantity       INTEGER,
  net_amount     DECIMAL(14, 2)
);
~~~

## The star schema

With the fact in the centre and dimensions around it, the model looks like a star. Every query follows the same pattern: join the fact to the dimensions you need, filter, group and sum.

## Slowly changing dimensions

When a customer moves from the SME segment to Enterprise, do you rewrite history?

| Type | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Type 1 | Overwrite the attribute; history shows the new value |
| Type 2 | Add a new row with new validity dates; history keeps the old value |

Type 2, using `valid_from`, `valid_to` and `is_current`, is standard for attributes that matter to historical reporting, such as sales region or risk rating.

## Declare the grain first

Before adding any column, write the grain in one sentence. Mixing grains in one fact table, such as order headers and order lines, is the root of many reporting errors.

lessons.title: Writing reliable reporting queries
lessons.content:
## Reports are products

A query that feeds a board pack or a regulator is a product. It needs to be correct, explainable and repeatable.

## A checklist for every reporting query

1. **State the definition.** "Active customer: at least one paid order in the last 90 days, excluding internal test accounts."
2. **Confirm the grain** of every table you touch.
3. **Reconcile** to a trusted total, such as the finance ledger for revenue, before publishing.
4. **Handle NULLs and late data explicitly.**
5. **Parameterise dates** rather than hard-coding them.

## Reconciliation example

~~~sql
WITH report AS (
  SELECT SUM(net_amount) AS revenue
  FROM   fact_sales f
  JOIN   dim_date d ON d.date_key = f.date_key
  WHERE  d.fiscal_period = '2026-P09'
), ledger AS (
  SELECT SUM(amount) AS revenue
  FROM   gl_entries
  WHERE  account_code LIKE '4%' AND fiscal_period = '2026-P09'
)
SELECT r.revenue AS report_revenue,
       l.revenue AS ledger_revenue,
       r.revenue - l.revenue AS difference
FROM   report r CROSS JOIN ledger l;
~~~

## Performance basics

- Filter early and select only the columns you need.
- In row-store databases, index columns used in joins and filters.
- In columnar warehouses, partition or cluster large fact tables by date and avoid `SELECT *`.
- Read the plan with `EXPLAIN` (PostgreSQL, Snowflake) or the actual execution plan in SQL Server.

## Views and documentation

Publish trusted logic as a **view** (`CREATE VIEW reporting.v_monthly_revenue AS ...`) so that every dashboard uses the same definition. Add comments that explain business rules, not syntax. Tools such as dbt add tests and documentation on top of this pattern, which you will meet in data engineering roles.

courses.title: Power BI analyst certification
courses.subtitle: Shape data with Power Query, model it as a star schema, write correct DAX and publish secure reports in the Power BI service.
courses.description:
Power BI is the reporting standard in thousands of organisations that run on Microsoft 365, from European banks to Gulf energy companies. Employers want analysts who can do more than drag visuals onto a canvas: they need clean models, correct measures and reports that are secure and refresh on time.

This course follows the skills measured in Microsoft's PL-300 Power BI Data Analyst exam: prepare the data, model the data, visualise and analyse the data, and deploy and maintain assets. It also shows how your Excel knowledge carries across.

**Who this is for**

- Excel power users moving to governed self-service reporting
- Analysts preparing for the PL-300 exam
- Finance and operations teams who own management reporting
- Candidates applying to roles that list Power BI and data modelling
outcomes: Connect to files, databases and SharePoint and shape data with Power Query.
Build a star-schema model with correct relationships and a dedicated date table.
Write DAX measures that respect filter context, including CALCULATE and time intelligence.
Design report pages that answer a clear question and meet accessibility basics.
Publish to the Power BI service, schedule refresh and apply row-level security.
Explain when to use Import, DirectQuery and Direct Lake storage modes.

lessons.title: Power BI in the analyst's toolkit
lessons.content:
## The parts of Power BI

| Component | What it is for |
|---|---|
| Power BI Desktop | Free Windows application for building models and reports |
| Power BI service | Cloud service (app.powerbi.com) for sharing, refresh and security |
| Power BI mobile | Viewing reports on phones and tablets |
| On-premises data gateway | Lets the service refresh data held inside the company network |
| Microsoft Fabric | The wider analytics platform that now hosts Power BI workspaces |

Sharing content generally needs a Power BI Pro or Premium Per User licence, or a workspace on Premium or Fabric capacity, where free users can view content.

## From Excel to Power BI

Much of what you know from Excel carries over:

- **Power Query** in Excel and Power BI is the same engine and uses the same M language.
- **Power Pivot** data models in Excel use DAX, exactly like Power BI.
- **Analyze in Excel** lets finance users build PivotTables on a published Power BI semantic model, so everyone uses one governed set of numbers.

The difference is scale and governance: Power BI handles millions of rows, scheduled refresh and permissions centrally, while ad hoc spreadsheets drift apart.

## The analyst workflow

1. **Get data** from sources such as SQL Server, Excel, SharePoint lists, Dataverse or Snowflake.
2. **Transform** it in Power Query.
3. **Model** it: relationships, measures, hierarchies.
4. **Visualise** it on report pages.
5. **Publish** to a workspace, configure refresh and security, and share through an app.

## Naming and structure

Agree a naming convention early: tables named for business entities (`Sales`, `Customer`, `Date`), measures in plain English (`Total revenue`, `Revenue YoY %`), and technical columns hidden from report view. Business users will see these names in every visual.

lessons.title: Shaping data with Power Query and M
lessons.content:
## Applied steps

Every transformation in Power Query becomes a recorded step written in the **M** language. Steps rerun on every refresh, so cleaning is repeatable and documented.

Common transformations:

- Remove columns you will not use (smaller models refresh faster).
- Set data types explicitly; never leave columns as "Any".
- Split, trim and clean text; replace values; fill down.
- Unpivot wide spreadsheets (months as columns) into a long table.
- Merge queries (joins) and append queries (unions).

## Reading the M behind a query

~~~
let
    Source   = Sql.Database("sql-prod.contoso.net", "Sales"),
    Orders   = Source{[Schema = "dbo", Item = "Orders"]}[Data],
    Recent   = Table.SelectRows(Orders, each [OrderDate] >= #date(2024, 1, 1)),
    Selected = Table.SelectColumns(Recent, {"OrderID", "CustomerID", "OrderDate", "NetAmount"}),
    Typed    = Table.TransformColumnTypes(Selected, {{"NetAmount", type number}, {"OrderDate", type date}})
in
    Typed
~~~

## Query folding

With databases, Power Query tries to translate steps into a single native SQL query: this is **query folding**. Folding pushes work to the source and is essential for large tables and incremental refresh.

- Right-click a step and choose **View Native Query** to confirm it folds.
- Put foldable steps (filters, column selection, joins) first.
- Steps such as adding an index column or some custom M functions can break folding for every step that follows.

## Parameters

Create parameters for server names, environments and date ranges. You can then switch a report from test to production in the service without editing queries, and incremental refresh uses the reserved parameters `RangeStart` and `RangeEnd`.

## Data profiling

Turn on **Column quality**, **Column distribution** and **Column profile** in the View ribbon, and set profiling to the entire data set, to spot errors and empty values before they reach your model.

lessons.title: Star schemas and relationships
lessons.content:
## Why the model matters most

A good model makes DAX simple and reports fast. A poor model, such as one wide flat table or a web of many-to-many relationships, produces slow reports and numbers nobody can explain.

## Star schema in Power BI

- **Fact tables** hold events and numeric columns: `Sales`, `Budget`, `Transactions`.
- **Dimension tables** hold descriptive attributes: `Date`, `Customer`, `Product`, `Region`.
- Relationships run **one-to-many** from the dimension (one side) to the fact (many side).

Filters flow from the one side to the many side. Selecting "Germany" in `Region` filters `Sales` through the relationship.

## Relationship settings

| Setting | Recommended default |
|---|---|
| Cardinality | One-to-many |
| Cross-filter direction | Single |
| Active | Yes, one active path between any two tables |

Bi-directional filtering and many-to-many relationships have legitimate uses, but they can create ambiguous filter paths and slow the model. Use them deliberately and document why.

## Role-playing dimensions

A fact often has several dates, for example order date and ship date. Power BI allows only one active relationship between two tables. Either create inactive relationships and activate them in a measure with `USERELATIONSHIP`, or load a second copy of the date table.

## Model hygiene

- Hide foreign key columns and columns used only for sorting.
- Set **Sort by column**, for example month name sorted by month number.
- Set data categories (country, city, URL) and default summarisation ("Don't summarise" for codes and years).
- Remove columns nobody uses: VertiPaq compresses columns, and high-cardinality columns such as transaction GUIDs or timestamps to the second consume the most memory.

lessons.title: Date tables and model hygiene
lessons.content:
## Every model needs a date table

Time intelligence functions in DAX require a proper date table: one row per day, no gaps, covering every date in your facts, marked as a date table.

~~~
Date =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2022, 1, 1 ), DATE ( 2027, 12, 31 ) ),
    "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "Month number", MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "mmm yyyy" ),
    "Quarter", "Q" & QUARTER ( [Date] ),
    "Fiscal year", IF ( MONTH ( [Date] ) >= 4, YEAR ( [Date] ) + 1, YEAR ( [Date] ) )
)
~~~

Then choose **Table tools, Mark as date table** and pick the `Date` column. The fiscal year example assumes an April start, as used by the UK government and many Indian and Japanese companies.

Turn off **Auto date/time** in Options for new files. It creates a hidden date table for every date column, which bloats the model and gives inconsistent results.

## Storage modes

| Mode | Use when |
|---|---|
| Import | Default; fastest queries, data refreshed on a schedule |
| DirectQuery | Data must stay at the source or be near real time; every visual queries the source |
| Composite | Mix of both, for example imported dimensions with a DirectQuery fact |
| Direct Lake | Fabric only; reads Delta tables in OneLake without import refresh |

## Incremental refresh

For large facts, configure incremental refresh with `RangeStart` and `RangeEnd` parameters, so the service reloads only recent partitions (for example the last 10 days) and keeps older history untouched. The source query must fold for this to be efficient.

## Document the model

Add descriptions to tables and measures. They appear as tooltips in the field list and make your model self-explanatory for the next analyst.

lessons.title: Measures, columns and filter context
lessons.content:
## Calculated columns and measures

| | Calculated column | Measure |
|---|---|---|
| Evaluated | At refresh, row by row | At query time, for each cell of a visual |
| Stored | Yes, adds to model size | No |
| Context | Row context | Filter context |
| Typical use | Categories to slice by | Totals, ratios, KPIs |

As a rule, if you will aggregate it, write a measure. Use calculated columns (or better, Power Query columns) for attributes you need on an axis or slicer.

## Writing basic measures

~~~
Total revenue = SUM ( Sales[NetAmount] )

Orders = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Sales[OrderID] )

Average order value = DIVIDE ( [Total revenue], [Orders] )

Gross margin % =
DIVIDE ( [Total revenue] - SUM ( Sales[Cost] ), [Total revenue] )
~~~

`DIVIDE` handles division by zero safely and returns blank by default.

## Filter context

Each cell in a visual is evaluated with its own **filter context**: the combination of filters from rows, columns, slicers, page and report filters, plus any filters you add in the measure. The same measure shows 4.2 million for Germany and 1.1 million for France because the context differs, not because the formula does.

## Iterators

Functions ending in X, such as `SUMX` and `AVERAGEX`, iterate over a table and evaluate an expression in row context for each row:

~~~
Revenue (line level) = SUMX ( Sales, Sales[Quantity] * Sales[UnitPrice] )
~~~

## Variables

Use `VAR` to name intermediate results. It makes measures readable and avoids evaluating the same expression twice:

~~~
Revenue YoY % =
VAR CurrentRevenue = [Total revenue]
VAR PriorRevenue   = CALCULATE ( [Total revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
RETURN DIVIDE ( CurrentRevenue - PriorRevenue, PriorRevenue )
~~~

lessons.title: CALCULATE and time intelligence
lessons.content:
## CALCULATE changes the context

`CALCULATE` is the most important function in DAX. It evaluates an expression in a modified filter context.

~~~
Revenue Germany = CALCULATE ( [Total revenue], Region[Country] = "Germany" )

Revenue all regions = CALCULATE ( [Total revenue], REMOVEFILTERS ( Region ) )

Share of total % = DIVIDE ( [Total revenue], [Revenue all regions] )
~~~

- A filter argument such as `Region[Country] = "Germany"` **replaces** any existing filter on that column.
- `REMOVEFILTERS` (or `ALL`) clears filters, which is how you build "share of total" measures.
- `KEEPFILTERS` intersects with the existing filter instead of replacing it.

## Time intelligence

With a marked date table, DAX offers ready-made time functions:

~~~
Revenue YTD = TOTALYTD ( [Total revenue], 'Date'[Date] )

Revenue fiscal YTD = TOTALYTD ( [Total revenue], 'Date'[Date], "03-31" )

Revenue PY = CALCULATE ( [Total revenue], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR ( 'Date'[Date] ) )

Revenue rolling 3M =
CALCULATE (
    [Total revenue],
    DATESINPERIOD ( 'Date'[Date], MAX ( 'Date'[Date] ), -3, MONTH )
)
~~~

The third argument of `TOTALYTD` sets the fiscal year end, here 31 March.

## Common mistakes

- Using time functions without a continuous, marked date table.
- Writing `FILTER ( Sales, ... )` over a whole fact table when a simple column filter would do; it is slower.
- Comparing a partial current month with a complete prior month. Consider limiting comparisons to dates with data.

## Test your measures

Put a new measure in a table visual next to known totals from the source or the finance ledger before you use it in a chart. DAX Studio and the Performance analyzer pane help you inspect queries and timing.

lessons.title: Designing report pages people use
lessons.content:
## One page, one question

Each page should answer one question for one audience, for example "Are we on track against budget this quarter?" for regional sales directors.

## Layout

- Put the headline KPIs at the top left, where readers look first.
- Follow with trend visuals, then breakdowns, then detail tables.
- Keep slicers in a consistent place on every page.
- Aim for no more than six to eight visuals per page; use drill-through pages for detail.

## Choosing visuals

| Question | Visual |
|---|---|
| Where are we against target? | Card with target and variance, or bullet-style bar |
| How is it trending? | Line chart with a clear time axis |
| Which segments drive it? | Sorted bar chart, decomposition tree |
| What is behind this number? | Drill-through page with a table |

Avoid gauges and pie charts with many slices. Reference lines and conditional formatting can show "good" and "bad" more precisely.

## Accessibility

Power BI reports must work for every colleague:

- Add **alt text** to every visual (Format pane, General, Alt text).
- Set the **tab order** in the Selection pane so keyboard users move logically.
- Never use colour alone for status; add icons, labels or data labels.
- Check contrast (a ratio of at least 4.5:1 for text, per WCAG 2.1 AA).
- Use a report theme (JSON) so fonts and colours are consistent across reports.

## Interactivity with purpose

- **Bookmarks** to switch between views, such as chart and table.
- **Tooltips** pages for extra context on hover.
- **Field parameters** so users choose the measure or dimension on an axis.

Test with a real user before you publish. Ask them to answer the page's question in under a minute.

lessons.title: Publishing, refresh and row-level security
lessons.content:
## Workspaces and apps

Publish from Desktop to a **workspace** in the Power BI service. Workspace roles control who can build content:

| Role | Can |
|---|---|
| Admin | Manage the workspace and its access |
| Member | Publish, share and manage content |
| Contributor | Publish and edit content |
| Viewer | View content only |

Distribute to wider audiences through a workspace **app** rather than individual sharing. Many organisations use separate development, test and production workspaces with **deployment pipelines**.

## Scheduled refresh

- Enter data source credentials in the semantic model settings.
- Use an on-premises data gateway for sources inside the network.
- Schedule refresh (up to 8 times a day on Pro, 48 on Premium or Fabric capacity) and add failure notification contacts.

## Row-level security (RLS)

RLS restricts which rows a user can see. Define roles in Desktop with DAX filters:

~~~
-- Role: Regional manager, on the Region table
[ManagerEmail] = USERPRINCIPALNAME ()
~~~

This **dynamic RLS** pattern uses one role for everyone: the filter reads the signed-in user's email and keeps only their regions. Test it in Desktop with **View as**, then assign users or Microsoft Entra ID security groups to the role in the service.

RLS applies to Viewers. Workspace Admins, Members and Contributors can see all data, so do not give them edit access if they should not see every row.

## Sensitivity and endorsement

- Apply **Microsoft Purview sensitivity labels** such as Confidential; they follow data exported to Excel or PDF.
- **Promote** or **Certify** trusted semantic models so analysts build on governed data.
- Monitor usage with the workspace usage metrics report and retire reports nobody opens.

Machine learning roles ask for more than library calls. Employers want people who can frame a problem, choose an honest evaluation, avoid leakage, explain a model to a risk committee and monitor it after release.

This course builds those foundations. lessons.title: Distributions, sampling and uncertainty
lessons.content:
## Why statistics comes first

Every model is fitted on a sample and used on data it has not seen. Statistics tells you how much to trust what the sample says.

## Describing data

- **Centre**: mean and median. Use the median for skewed data such as income or claim size.
- **Spread**: standard deviation, interquartile range, percentiles.
- **Shape**: skew and heavy tails. Fraud amounts and web traffic are rarely normal.

## Common distributions

| Distribution | Models | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Sums of many small effects | Measurement error |
| Binomial | Number of successes in n trials | Conversions out of visitors |
| Poisson | Counts of events in a period | Support tickets per hour |
| Log-normal | Positive, right-skewed values | Transaction amounts |

## Sampling and the central limit theorem

The mean of a large enough random sample is approximately normally distributed around the true mean, whatever the shape of the data. Its standard deviation, the **standard error**, is `s / sqrt(n)`. Quadrupling the sample halves the standard error.

## Confidence intervals

~~~python
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

sample = np.array([42.1, 39.8, 45.0, 41.2, 38.7, 44.3, 40.9, 43.6])
mean = sample.mean()
sem = stats.sem(sample)
low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(sample) - 1, loc=mean, scale=sem)
print(f"Mean {mean:.1f}, 95% CI {low:.1f} to {high:.1f}")
~~~

A 95% confidence interval means that if you repeated the sampling many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true value. It is not a 95% probability that this particular interval contains it.

## Bias in samples

A large biased sample is still wrong. Survivorship bias, selection bias and data collected only from one country or channel all distort models. Ask how the data was collected before you model it.

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and experiments
lessons.content:
## The logic of a test

1. State a **null hypothesis** (H0), for example "the new onboarding flow does not change the conversion rate".
2. Choose a significance level, usually alpha = 0.05.
3. Compute a test statistic and its **p-value**: the probability of seeing a result at least this extreme if H0 were true.
4. If p < alpha, reject H0.

A p-value is not the probability that H0 is true, and a small p-value does not mean the effect is large or useful.

## Choosing a test

| Data | Test |
|---|---|
| Two group means, roughly normal | Welch's t-test |
| Two proportions | Two-proportion z-test or chi-squared test |
| Skewed values, two groups | Mann-Whitney U test |
| Several categories | Chi-squared test of independence |

~~~python
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest

conversions = [530, 584]      # control, variant
visitors = [10_000, 10_000]
stat, p_value = proportions_ztest(conversions, visitors)
print(round(p_value, 4))
~~~

## Designing A/B experiments

- **Randomise** users, not sessions, so one person does not see both versions.
- Decide the **minimum detectable effect** and calculate sample size before starting.
- Fix the duration in advance and do not stop early when the result looks good; repeated peeking inflates false positives.
- Watch **guardrail metrics** such as refunds or complaints, not only the target metric.

## Errors and power

- **Type I error**: a false positive (rejecting a true H0), controlled by alpha.
- **Type II error**: a false negative, missing a real effect.
- **Power** = 1 minus the Type II error rate, commonly targeted at 80%.

Testing many metrics or segments raises the chance of a false positive. Apply a correction such as Bonferroni or Benjamini-Hochberg, or pre-register one primary metric.

lessons.title: Framing a machine learning problem
lessons.content:
## Start with the decision

A model is only useful if it changes a decision. Write the problem as: "We will use **prediction X** to decide **action Y**, which improves **metric Z**."

Example: "We will predict the probability that a customer cancels within 60 days, so the retention team can call the 500 highest-risk customers each week, reducing churn."

## Types of task

| Task | Target | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Binary classification | Yes/no | Will this invoice be paid late? |
| Multiclass classification | One of several labels | Which team should handle this ticket? |
| Regression | A number | What will next month's demand be? |
| Ranking | An order | Which jobs best match this candidate? |
| Clustering (unsupervised) | No target | Which customer segments exist? |

## Define the target precisely

"Churn" needs a definition: no paid activity for 60 days, measured from a specific snapshot date. Features may use only data available **before** the snapshot. This point-in-time discipline prevents the most damaging form of leakage.

## Baselines

Before training anything complex, measure simple baselines:

- Predict the majority class, or the historical average.
- A rule the business already uses ("customers with more than three complaints").
- A logistic or linear regression with a few features.

If a gradient-boosted model beats a sensible baseline only slightly, the extra complexity may not be worth it.

## Is ML the right tool?

Machine learning suits problems with many examples, stable patterns and a tolerance for some error. If the rule is known and must be applied exactly, such as a tax calculation or a regulatory threshold, write the rule in code instead.

lessons.title: Splitting data and avoiding leakage
lessons.content:
## Three sets, three jobs

- **Training set**: fit the model.
- **Validation set** (or cross-validation folds): choose features, models and hyperparameters.
- **Test set**: estimate final performance once, at the end.

If you tune against the test set, it stops being an honest estimate.

~~~python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
~~~

`stratify=y` keeps the class balance the same in both sets, which matters when positives are rare.

## Split by time or by group when needed

- **Time series and forecasting**: train on the past, test on the future. Use `TimeSeriesSplit` rather than random shuffling.
- **Repeated entities**: if a customer appears many times, keep all their rows in the same set with `GroupKFold`, otherwise the model memorises customers instead of learning patterns.

## What leakage looks like

Leakage happens when training data contains information that would not be available at prediction time.

| Leak | Example |
|---|---|
| Target leakage | Using "account closed date" to predict churn |
| Preprocessing leakage | Scaling or imputing with statistics from the full data set before splitting |
| Temporal leakage | Using next month's transactions as features |
| Duplicate leakage | The same record in both train and test |

A test score that looks too good to be true usually is. Inspect the most important features: if one perfectly predicts the target, ask how it was created.

## Reproducibility

Fix `random_state`, record the data snapshot date and library versions, and keep the split logic in code. Reviewers in regulated industries will ask to reproduce your numbers.

lessons.title: Linear and logistic regression
lessons.content:
## Linear regression

Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of features: `y = b0 + b1*x1 + ... + bn*xn`. It is fast, interpretable and a strong baseline.

~~~python
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, Ridge
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error

model = Ridge(alpha=1.0).fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = model.predict(X_test)
print(mean_absolute_error(y_test, pred))
~~~

**Regularisation** shrinks coefficients to reduce overfitting:

- **Ridge (L2)** shrinks all coefficients smoothly.
- **Lasso (L1)** can set some coefficients to exactly zero, performing feature selection.

## Logistic regression

Despite the name, logistic regression is a **classifier**. It models the log-odds of the positive class as a linear function and returns probabilities between 0 and 1.

~~~python
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, class_weight="balanced")
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
~~~

Each coefficient, once exponentiated, is an **odds ratio**: a coefficient of 0.69 roughly doubles the odds for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding others constant. This makes logistic regression popular in credit scoring, where every factor must be explainable.

## Assumptions and checks

- Relationships are roughly linear in the features (add interactions or transformations if not).
- Features on very different scales should be standardised, especially with regularisation.
- Highly correlated features make individual coefficients unstable, even if predictions are fine.
- Plot residuals for regression; patterns suggest missing structure.

## When linear models are the right answer

When data is limited, the signal is mostly linear, or the decision must be explained feature by feature, a regularised linear model often performs within a few points of complex models and is far easier to govern.

lessons.title: Decision trees and gradient-boosted ensembles
lessons.content:
## Decision trees

A tree splits the data on the feature and threshold that best separates the target, then repeats on each branch. Trees capture non-linear effects and interactions without scaling, but a single deep tree **overfits**: it memorises noise.

Control complexity with `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf` and `ccp_alpha` (cost-complexity pruning).

## Random forests

A random forest trains many trees on bootstrap samples, each considering a random subset of features at each split, and averages them. Averaging reduces variance.

~~~python
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, min_samples_leaf=5, n_jobs=-1, random_state=42)
rf.fit(X_train, y_train)
~~~

## Gradient boosting

Boosting builds trees **sequentially**, each one correcting the errors of the ensemble so far. It is the most common winner on tabular business data.

~~~python
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

gb = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
    learning_rate=0.05, max_iter=500, max_leaf_nodes=31,
    early_stopping=True, validation_fraction=0.1, random_state=42
)
gb.fit(X_train, y_train)
~~~

`HistGradientBoostingClassifier` handles missing values natively and scales to millions of rows. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are widely used alternatives with similar ideas.

## Comparing the families

| | Linear | Random forest | Gradient boosting |
|---|---|---|---|
| Non-linear effects | Manual | Yes | Yes |
| Tuning effort | Low | Low | Medium |
| Typical accuracy on tabular data | Good | Very good | Often best |
| Explainability | Direct | Needs tools | Needs tools |

## Feature importance with care

Impurity-based importances favour high-cardinality features. Prefer **permutation importance** (`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`) on validation data, and SHAP values for explaining individual predictions.

lessons.title: Pipelines and preprocessing
lessons.content:
## Why pipelines

A scikit-learn `Pipeline` chains preprocessing and the model into one object. During cross-validation, each fold fits the preprocessing on its training part only, which **prevents leakage**. The same object is then saved and used in production, so training and serving apply identical transformations.

## A complete example

~~~python
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

numeric = ["tenure_months", "monthly_spend", "support_calls"]
categorical = ["country", "plan", "channel"]

preprocess = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ]), numeric),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=20), categorical),
])

model = Pipeline([
    ("prep", preprocess),
    ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
model.fit(X_train, y_train)
~~~

`handle_unknown="ignore"` stops the model crashing when a new country appears in production. `min_frequency` groups rare categories together.

## Encoding choices

| Feature | Approach |
|---|---|
| Few categories | One-hot encoding |
| Ordered categories (small, medium, large) | `OrdinalEncoder` with an explicit order |
| Many categories (postcodes) | Target encoding with cross-fitting (`TargetEncoder`), or grouping |
| Dates | Extract day of week, month, days since an event |

## Saving the model

~~~python
import joblib
joblib.dump(model, "models/churn_v3.joblib")
~~~

Record the training data snapshot, scikit-learn version and evaluation results alongside the file. A model artefact without this context cannot be audited.
