courses.title: AWS solutions architect associate
courses.subtitle: Design secure, resilient and cost-aware architectures on AWS and prepare for the SAA-C03 exam.
courses.description:
Most global employers now run at least part of their estate on Amazon Web Services, and the solutions architect is the person who turns business requirements into a design that survives failures, passes a security review and stays within budget. This course teaches that design thinking through the services you will meet on every project: IAM, VPC, EC2, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, SQS and KMS.

Each module is built around a decision you will be asked to make at work, such as choosing between Multi-AZ and a read replica or picking a disaster recovery strategy for a stated RTO. The language and scenarios follow the AWS Certified Solutions Architect Associate (SAA-C03) exam guide, so the course doubles as structured exam preparation.

**Who this is for**

- Developers and system administrators moving into cloud architecture roles.
- Infrastructure engineers who already use AWS and want a design framework rather than a list of services.
- Candidates applying for cloud roles that list the AWS Solutions Architect Associate certification.
outcomes: Apply the AWS Well-Architected Framework to review and improve a workload design.
Design a multi-AZ VPC with public and private subnets, routing and layered network controls.
Write least-privilege IAM policies and use roles instead of long-lived access keys.
Choose the right compute, storage and database services for a stated set of requirements.
Select a disaster recovery strategy that meets a given RTO and RPO.
Reduce cost with purchasing options, storage tiering and tagging without weakening resilience.

lessons.title: Global infrastructure and the shared responsibility model
lessons.content:
## Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations

AWS is organised into **Regions**, such as eu-west-2 (London) or ap-south-1 (Mumbai). Each Region contains at least three **Availability Zones** (AZs): one or more data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected by low-latency links. **Edge locations** host CloudFront and Route 53 close to users.

Three design rules follow from this layout:

- **Spread across AZs for high availability.** A single AZ can fail; a well-designed workload keeps running when it does.
- **Choose Regions for latency, data residency and service availability.** Data protected under the GDPR or India's DPDP Act may need to stay in a particular jurisdiction.
- **Use multiple Regions only when the requirement justifies it.** Multi-Region designs add cost and operational complexity.

## The shared responsibility model

Security is split between AWS and the customer.

| AWS is responsible for | You are responsible for |
| --- | --- |
| Physical data centres and hardware | Identity and access management |
| The hypervisor and global network | Operating system patching on EC2 |
| Managed service infrastructure | Data classification and encryption choices |
| | Security group and network configuration |

The line moves with the service. On EC2 you patch the guest operating system; on RDS AWS patches the database engine; on Lambda you only own your code, its dependencies and its permissions.

## Why this matters in interviews

Hiring managers often ask who is responsible when an S3 bucket is exposed publicly. The answer is the customer: AWS provides Block Public Access and bucket policies, but configuring them correctly is your job.

lessons.title: The Well-Architected Framework
lessons.content:
## Six pillars

The AWS Well-Architected Framework gives architects a shared vocabulary for reviewing designs. It has six pillars:

1. **Operational excellence**: run and monitor systems, and improve processes. Use infrastructure as code and small, reversible changes.
2. **Security**: protect data and systems. Apply least privilege, enable traceability and encrypt data in transit and at rest.
3. **Reliability**: recover from failure and meet demand. Design for automatic recovery and test recovery procedures.
4. **Performance efficiency**: use resources efficiently as demand changes. Prefer managed and serverless services where they fit.
5. **Cost optimisation**: avoid unnecessary cost. Measure efficiency and pay only for what you use.
6. **Sustainability**: minimise environmental impact. Maximise utilisation and choose efficient instance types such as Graviton.

## Running a review

A Well-Architected review is a structured conversation, not an audit. For each pillar you answer the framework's questions, record risks as high or medium, and agree an improvement plan. The **AWS Well-Architected Tool** in the console stores reviews and tracks progress over time.

## Trade-offs are normal

Pillars pull against each other. A multi-Region active-active design improves reliability but raises cost; a single small instance is cheap but fragile. A good architect states the trade-off explicitly:

- What the business needs (for example, 99.9% availability and a four-hour RTO).
- Which design meets it at the lowest reasonable cost.
- What risk remains and who has accepted it.

## Exam tip

SAA-C03 questions usually contain one phrase that points to a pillar: "most cost-effective", "least operational overhead" or "highly available". Read for that phrase first, then eliminate options that fail it.

lessons.title: Identity and access management
lessons.content:
## The building blocks

- **Users** represent people or, rarely, legacy applications. In most organisations people sign in through **IAM Identity Center** with their corporate identity instead.
- **Groups** collect users so you attach permissions once.
- **Roles** are identities with no long-term credentials. EC2 instances, Lambda functions and users from other accounts **assume** a role and receive temporary credentials from AWS STS.
- **Policies** are JSON documents that allow or deny actions on resources.

## Reading a policy

~~~json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::invoices-prod/uploads/*",
      "Condition": { "Bool": { "aws:SecureTransport": "true" } }
    }
  ]
}
~~~

This identity-based policy lets the holder read and write objects under one prefix, and only over TLS.

## Policy evaluation

1. By default every request is **implicitly denied**.
2. An explicit **Allow** in an applicable policy permits the request.
3. An explicit **Deny** anywhere overrides every Allow.

Service control policies (SCPs) in AWS Organizations and permissions boundaries set the maximum permissions; they never grant access on their own.

## Good practice

- Enable MFA for every human, and lock away the root user.
- Give workloads roles, never access keys stored in code.
- Start from AWS managed policies, then tighten with IAM Access Analyzer's policy generation.
- Review unused permissions regularly with the last-accessed data.

Attach an IAM role through an instance profile

lessons.title: Designing a VPC
lessons.content:
## The standard three-tier layout

A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is your isolated network in a Region. A common production layout uses a /16 CIDR block, such as 10.0.0.0/16, and creates subnets in at least two AZs:

- **Public subnets** for load balancers and NAT gateways. Their route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an **internet gateway**.
- **Private application subnets** for EC2 or containers. Outbound traffic goes through a **NAT gateway** in the same AZ.
- **Private data subnets** for RDS and ElastiCache, with no route to the internet at all.

~~~bash
aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.0.0.0/16
aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id vpc-0abc --cidr-block 10.0.1.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id rtb-0pub --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id igw-0abc
~~~

## Security groups and network ACLs

| | Security group | Network ACL |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Applies to | Network interfaces | Subnets |
| State | Stateful | Stateless |
| Rules | Allow only | Allow and deny |
| Evaluation | All rules together | In number order |

Use security groups as your main control and reference other security groups instead of IP ranges, for example "the app tier accepts port 8080 only from the load balancer's security group". Use NACLs for coarse subnet-wide blocks.

## Private connectivity

- **Gateway endpoints** give private subnets free access to S3 and DynamoDB without a NAT gateway.
- **Interface endpoints** (AWS PrivateLink) expose other services through private IP addresses.
- **VPC peering** connects two VPCs; **Transit Gateway** connects many VPCs and on-premises networks in a hub-and-spoke model.

lessons.title: Compute choices: EC2, Auto Scaling and Lambda
lessons.content:
## EC2 instance families

Instance names encode their purpose: **m7g.large** is a general-purpose (m), seventh-generation, Graviton (g) instance of size large.

- **General purpose (m, t)**: balanced workloads; t-family instances are burstable and suit low, spiky load.
- **Compute optimised (c)**: batch processing, video encoding, high-traffic web servers.
- **Memory optimised (r, x)**: in-memory caches and large databases.
- **Storage optimised (i, d)**: high local disk throughput.

## Auto Scaling behind a load balancer

An **Auto Scaling group** keeps a desired number of instances across AZs, replaces unhealthy ones and scales with demand. A **target tracking** policy is the simplest to reason about:

~~~bash
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name web-asg \
  --policy-name cpu-50 \
  --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling \
  --target-tracking-configuration '{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}'
~~~

Put an **Application Load Balancer** (layer 7, path and host routing) in front of HTTP services, or a **Network Load Balancer** (layer 4, static IPs, very high throughput) in front of TCP or UDP services.

## Serverless with Lambda

Lambda runs code in response to events with no servers to manage. It suits event-driven and spiky workloads. Remember its limits:

- Maximum run time of 15 minutes per invocation.
- Memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, with CPU allocated in proportion.
- Cold starts add latency; provisioned concurrency removes them at a cost.

## Choosing

If a scenario says "least operational overhead" and the work is short and event-driven, Lambda is usually right. Long-running, stateful or licensed software usually belongs on EC2 or containers (ECS or EKS, often on Fargate).

lessons.title: Storage: S3, EBS and EFS
lessons.content:
## Three kinds of storage

| Service | Type | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amazon S3 | Object | Data lakes, backups, static assets, logs |
| Amazon EBS | Block, one instance per volume (mostly) | Boot volumes and databases on EC2 |
| Amazon EFS | Shared file system (NFS) | Content shared by many Linux instances |

## S3 storage classes

- **S3 Standard**: frequent access, lowest latency.
- **S3 Intelligent-Tiering**: moves objects between tiers automatically; ideal when access patterns are unknown.
- **S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA**: infrequent access with a retrieval fee; One Zone stores data in a single AZ.
- **S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive**: archives, from milliseconds to hours to retrieve.

S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability. Durability is not availability: plan for a Region being unreachable even though the data is safe.

## Lifecycle rules

~~~json
{
  "Rules": [{
    "ID": "archive-logs",
    "Filter": { "Prefix": "logs/" },
    "Status": "Enabled",
    "Transitions": [
      { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "STANDARD_IA" },
      { "Days": 180, "StorageClass": "GLACIER" }
    ],
    "Expiration": { "Days": 730 }
  }]
}
~~~

## Protecting data

- Keep **Block Public Access** on at the account level.
- Enable **versioning** and consider **Object Lock** for ransomware-resistant backups.
- Use **gp3** EBS volumes by default: you set IOPS and throughput independently of size.
- Take EBS snapshots with **AWS Backup** so retention is managed centrally.

lessons.title: Module 2 quiz
lessons.content: Test your design choices for networking, compute and storage.

questions.prompt: Instances in a private subnet need to download operating system patches from the internet without accepting inbound connections. What should you add?

options.text: An internet gateway route in the private subnet
A NAT gateway in a public subnet and a route to it
An Elastic IP on each instance

questions.explanation: A NAT gateway allows outbound connections from private subnets while blocking unsolicited inbound traffic.

questions.prompt: Which statement about security groups is correct?

options.text: They are stateless and evaluate rules in number order
They are stateful and support allow rules only

questions.explanation: Security groups are stateful, attach to network interfaces and only contain allow rules. Network ACLs are the stateless, subnet-level control.

questions.prompt: Several Linux web servers in different AZs need to read and write the same set of files. Which service fits best?
questions.explanation: EFS is a regional, shared NFS file system that many instances across AZs can mount at once.

questions.prompt: Access patterns for a large dataset in S3 are unpredictable. Which storage class reduces cost with no retrieval fees or manual rules?
questions.explanation: Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically and does not charge retrieval fees.

lessons.title: Relational and NoSQL databases
lessons.content:
## Amazon RDS and Aurora

RDS runs MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server as a managed service. Two features are often confused:

| | Multi-AZ deployment | Read replica |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | High availability | Read scaling |
| Replication | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
| Serves reads | No (standby only, for the classic option) | Yes |
| Failover | Automatic, usually 60 to 120 seconds | Manual promotion |

**Aurora** is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine. It stores six copies of data across three AZs, supports up to 15 low-lag replicas and offers **Aurora Global Database** for cross-Region recovery measured in seconds.

## DynamoDB

DynamoDB is a serverless key-value and document database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.

- Choose a **partition key** with high cardinality, such as customerId, so traffic spreads evenly.
- Add a **sort key** to model one-to-many relationships, such as orderDate.
- Use **on-demand** capacity for unpredictable traffic and **provisioned** capacity with auto scaling for steady traffic.
- **DAX** adds a microsecond in-memory cache; **global tables** give multi-Region, multi-active replication.

~~~bash
aws dynamodb query \
  --table-name Orders \
  --key-condition-expression "customerId = :c AND orderDate >= :d" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":c":{"S":"C-1042"},":d":{"S":"2026-01-01"}}'
~~~

## Choosing

Relational data with joins and complex transactions suits RDS or Aurora. Known access patterns at very high scale suit DynamoDB. Caching hot reads in **ElastiCache** (Redis OSS or Valkey) often removes the need for a bigger database.

lessons.title: Decoupling with SQS, SNS and EventBridge
lessons.content:
## Why decouple

Tightly coupled systems fail together. If an order service calls an email service synchronously and the email service slows down, checkout slows down too. Placing a queue or event bus between them lets each side scale and fail independently.

## Amazon SQS

- **Standard queues** offer nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering.
- **FIFO queues** guarantee ordering within a message group and exactly-once processing.
- The **visibility timeout** hides a message while a consumer works on it; set it longer than processing time.
- A **dead-letter queue** collects messages that fail repeatedly so they can be inspected.

## Amazon SNS and fan-out

SNS is publish/subscribe. One message published to a topic is delivered to every subscriber: SQS queues, Lambda functions, HTTPS endpoints, email or SMS. The **fan-out pattern** (SNS topic to several SQS queues) lets billing, analytics and notifications each process the same order event at their own pace.

## Amazon EventBridge

EventBridge routes events using content-based rules and integrates with SaaS partners and AWS services.

~~~json
{
  "source": ["com.shop.orders"],
  "detail-type": ["OrderPlaced"],
  "detail": { "total": [{ "numeric": [">", 1000] }] }
}
~~~

This rule matches only high-value orders, which could trigger a fraud check.

## Picking the right tool

- Work queue with retries: **SQS**.
- Same message to many consumers: **SNS** fan-out.
- Routing by event content, schedules or SaaS events: **EventBridge**.
- Multi-step workflows with branching and human approval: **Step Functions**.

lessons.title: Disaster recovery strategies
lessons.content:
## RTO and RPO

- **Recovery time objective (RTO)**: how long the business can tolerate the workload being unavailable.
- **Recovery point objective (RPO)**: how much data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose.

Both are business decisions. The architect's job is to meet them at the lowest reasonable cost.

## Four strategies

| Strategy | Typical RTO / RPO | What runs in the recovery Region |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backup and restore | Hours | Nothing; data is backed up and restored on demand |
| Pilot light | Tens of minutes | Core data stores replicated; compute switched off |
| Warm standby | Minutes | A scaled-down but working copy of the full stack |
| Multi-site active/active | Near zero | Full capacity serving live traffic |

Cost rises as you move down the table.

## Building blocks

- **AWS Backup** with cross-Region and cross-account copy for the backup and restore strategy.
- **Aurora Global Database**, **DynamoDB global tables** and **S3 Cross-Region Replication** for data.
- **Infrastructure as code** (CloudFormation or Terraform) so the stack can be recreated quickly.
- **Route 53 failover routing** with health checks to move traffic.
- **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery** for continuous block-level replication of servers.

## Test it

A recovery plan that has never been exercised is an assumption. Schedule game days, restore backups into an isolated account, and measure the real RTO. Record the results and update the runbook each time.

lessons.title: Module 3 quiz
lessons.content: Check your grasp of database choices, decoupling and disaster recovery.

questions.prompt: A reporting workload is slowing down the primary RDS PostgreSQL database. What is the simplest fix?

options.text: Move the reports to a read replica

questions.explanation: Read replicas serve read traffic asynchronously and take load off the primary. Multi-AZ improves availability, not read capacity.

questions.prompt: An order event must be processed independently by billing, analytics and email services. Which pattern fits?

options.text: One SQS queue read by all three services
Synchronous HTTPS calls from the order service
SNS topic fanning out to three SQS queues
A single Lambda function that calls all three

questions.explanation: SNS delivers a copy of each message to every subscribed queue, so each consumer scales and retries independently.

questions.prompt: The business accepts up to four hours of downtime but wants the lowest possible cost. Which DR strategy fits?

options.text: Pilot light with full-size compute running

questions.explanation: A four-hour RTO is achievable with tested backup and restore, which is the cheapest strategy.

lessons.title: Encryption, secrets and detection
lessons.content:
## Encryption with AWS KMS

AWS Key Management Service (KMS) creates and controls encryption keys. Most services use **envelope encryption**: KMS protects a data key, and the data key encrypts your data.

- **AWS managed keys** are created for you per service and are simple to use.
- **Customer managed keys** let you write the key policy, rotate yearly, audit use in CloudTrail and share across accounts.
- **CloudHSM** gives you dedicated, single-tenant hardware security modules validated to FIPS 140-3 level 3, when regulation requires it.

Encrypt in transit with TLS: ACM issues and renews public certificates for load balancers and CloudFront at no extra charge.

## Secrets

Never put passwords in code, AMIs or plain environment variables.

- **AWS Secrets Manager** stores secrets and rotates database credentials automatically.
- **SSM Parameter Store** SecureString parameters are a cheaper option for configuration that does not need rotation.

~~~bash
aws secretsmanager get-secret-value --secret-id prod/orders/db --query SecretString --output text
~~~

## Detection and audit

| Service | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| AWS CloudTrail | Records API calls for audit and investigation |
| Amazon GuardDuty | Detects threats from logs, DNS and runtime signals |
| AWS Config | Records resource configuration and checks rules |
| AWS Security Hub | Aggregates findings and scores against standards |
| Amazon Inspector | Scans EC2, containers and Lambda for vulnerabilities |
| AWS WAF and Shield | Protect web applications and absorb DDoS attacks |

Turn on an organisation-wide CloudTrail trail to a locked-down log archive account. It is the first thing investigators will ask for.

lessons.title: Cost optimisation in practice
lessons.content:
## Pay for what you need

Cost optimisation is not about the cheapest option; it is about removing waste while meeting requirements.

## Purchasing options for compute

| Option | Discount versus On-Demand | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-Demand | None | Short-term, unpredictable work |
| Savings Plans | Up to about 72% | Steady usage, flexible across instance families and Lambda |
| Reserved Instances | Up to about 72% | Steady usage of a specific instance type, and RDS |
| Spot Instances | Up to about 90% | Fault-tolerant batch, CI runners, stateless workers |

Spot capacity can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning, so design workloads to checkpoint or retry.

## Right-sizing and scheduling

- Use **AWS Compute Optimizer** to find over-provisioned instances.
- Move to **Graviton** instances for better price-performance on supported software.
- Stop development environments outside working hours with **Instance Scheduler** or simple EventBridge rules.

## Storage and data transfer

- Apply S3 lifecycle rules and Intelligent-Tiering.
- Delete unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots.
- Use gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB instead of paying NAT gateway processing charges.
- Serve static content through CloudFront to cut data transfer out.

## Visibility and accountability

Activate **cost allocation tags** such as team, environment and cost-centre, then use **Cost Explorer** and **AWS Budgets** to alert owners before they overspend. Teams that see their own bill make better decisions than a central team chasing them afterwards.

lessons.title: Approaching scenario questions
lessons.content:
## How SAA-C03 questions work

The exam has 65 questions in 130 minutes, scored from 100 to 1,000 with 720 to pass. Most questions are scenarios with four options, two of which are plausible. The domains are:

- Design secure architectures (30%).
- Design resilient architectures (26%).
- Design high-performing architectures (24%).
- Design cost-optimised architectures (20%).

## A repeatable method

1. **Find the constraint.** Look for "least operational overhead", "most cost-effective", "minimal downtime" or "without changing application code".
2. **Note the hard facts.** RTO, RPO, data size, access frequency, compliance requirements.
3. **Eliminate the impossible.** Options that break a hard limit (for example, a Lambda job running for two hours) go first.
4. **Prefer managed services** when the scenario values low operational effort.
5. **Choose the simplest option that satisfies every requirement.** Over-engineered answers are usually wrong.

## Common pairings

| Phrase in the scenario | Likely answer |
| --- | --- |
| "Decouple" or "buffer spikes" | SQS |
| "Unknown access pattern" | S3 Intelligent-Tiering |
| "Shared file system for Linux" | EFS |
| "Rotate database credentials" | Secrets Manager |
| "Millisecond latency at any scale" | DynamoDB |
| "Static IP for a load balancer" | Network Load Balancer or Global Accelerator |

## At work

The same method works in design reviews. Write the constraints at the top of every design document, and let them decide between options rather than personal preference.

lessons.title: Final assessment
lessons.content: Eight scenario questions covering the whole course. You need 70% to pass and earn your certificate.

questions.prompt: A web application must remain available if one Availability Zone fails. Which design meets this with the least change?

options.text: Run two instances in the same AZ behind an ALB
Run an Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB

questions.explanation: Spreading instances across at least two AZs behind a load balancer survives the loss of a single AZ.

questions.prompt: Which service should store database credentials that must rotate automatically every 30 days?
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager has built-in rotation for RDS, Aurora and other databases.

questions.prompt: A nightly batch job is fault tolerant, restarts from checkpoints and runs for three hours. Which purchasing option is cheapest?
questions.explanation: Spot gives the largest discount and suits interruptible, checkpointed work. Lambda cannot run for three hours.

questions.prompt: Private subnet instances transfer terabytes to S3 each month and NAT gateway charges are high. What reduces cost most simply?

options.text: Move the instances to a public subnet
Add an S3 gateway endpoint to the route tables

questions.explanation: Gateway endpoints route S3 traffic privately with no data processing charge.

questions.prompt: Which statements about RDS Multi-AZ (classic, one standby) are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Replication to the standby is synchronous
It replaces the need for backups

questions.explanation: Multi-AZ synchronously replicates to a standby and fails over automatically. The classic standby does not serve reads, and backups are still needed against corruption or deletion.

questions.prompt: The business needs an RTO of 10 minutes for a critical system in a second Region at moderate cost. Which strategy fits best?
questions.explanation: A warm standby already runs a scaled-down working stack and can scale up within minutes, at less cost than active/active.

questions.prompt: Which service records who called which AWS API and when?
questions.explanation: CloudTrail logs API activity. GuardDuty analyses such logs for threats, and Config records resource configuration.

questions.prompt: A DynamoDB table uses country code as its partition key and suffers throttling. What is the best fix?

options.text: Add a global secondary index on country
Choose a high-cardinality partition key such as customerId

questions.explanation: Few distinct country codes create hot partitions. A high-cardinality key spreads traffic evenly.

courses.title: Azure cloud administrator
courses.subtitle: Run identities, storage, compute, networking and monitoring on Microsoft Azure to the AZ-104 standard.
courses.description:
Microsoft Azure is the default cloud for many enterprises that already run Microsoft 365, Windows Server and SQL Server, which makes Azure administrators some of the most requested cloud professionals in Europe, the Gulf and India. This course covers the day-to-day work of the role: managing identities in Microsoft Entra ID, governing subscriptions, configuring storage and virtual networks, running Windows and Linux virtual machines, and keeping everything monitored and backed up.

Every lesson uses the Azure CLI alongside the portal, so you learn tasks you can script and repeat. The structure follows the Microsoft Certified: Azure Administrator Associate (AZ-104) skills outline.

**Who this is for**

- System administrators moving on-premises skills to Azure.
- Support and operations engineers who want to own an Azure estate.
- Candidates preparing for the AZ-104 exam or applying for cloud administrator roles.
outcomes: Manage users, groups and role-based access control across management groups, subscriptions and resource groups.
Enforce standards with Azure Policy, tags and resource locks.
Configure storage accounts with the right redundancy, access tier and secure access method.
Deploy and maintain Windows and Linux virtual machines with availability zones and scale sets.
Build virtual networks with subnets, network security groups, peering and load balancing.
Monitor resources with Azure Monitor and KQL, and protect them with Azure Backup.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra ID essentials
lessons.content:
## What Entra ID is

Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure Active Directory) is the cloud identity service behind Azure, Microsoft 365 and thousands of SaaS applications. Every Azure subscription trusts exactly one Entra tenant.

Key objects:

- **Users**: members of your organisation or **guest users** invited through B2B collaboration.
- **Groups**: security groups for access, Microsoft 365 groups for collaboration. Membership can be **assigned** or **dynamic**, based on rules such as user.department -eq "Finance".
- **Service principals and managed identities**: identities for applications. A **managed identity** lets an Azure resource authenticate to other services with no secret to store.

## Creating identities with the CLI

~~~bash
az ad user create --display-name "Priya Nair" \
  --user-principal-name priya.nair@contoso.onmicrosoft.com \
  --password "<temporary-password>" --force-change-password-next-sign-in true

az ad group create --display-name "Ops Engineers" --mail-nickname ops-engineers
az ad group member add --group "Ops Engineers" --member-id <user-object-id>
~~~

## Securing sign-in

- Turn on **multifactor authentication** for everyone, using Conditional Access policies or security defaults.
- Use **Conditional Access** to require compliant devices or block sign-ins from unexpected countries.
- Enable **self-service password reset** to cut helpdesk tickets.
- Use **Privileged Identity Management** (PIM) so administrators activate high-privilege roles just in time, with approval and an audit trail.

## Licensing

Conditional Access and PIM require Entra ID P1 and P2 licences respectively. Check licensing before promising a feature to a client.

lessons.title: Role-based access control and scopes
lessons.content:
## How RBAC works

Azure role-based access control answers three questions: **who** (a security principal), **what** (a role definition) and **where** (a scope). A **role assignment** joins all three.

## The scope hierarchy

1. Management group
2. Subscription
3. Resource group
4. Resource

Assignments are **inherited** downwards. Giving a team Contributor on a resource group gives them Contributor on every resource inside it.

## Built-in roles to know

| Role | Can do |
| --- | --- |
| Owner | Everything, including assigning access |
| Contributor | Create and manage resources, but not grant access |
| Reader | View resources only |
| User Access Administrator | Manage access only |
| Virtual Machine Contributor | Manage VMs, but not their network or storage |

~~~bash
az role assignment create \
  --assignee "ops-engineers-group-object-id" \
  --role "Virtual Machine Contributor" \
  --scope "/subscriptions/<sub-id>/resourceGroups/rg-app-prod"
~~~

## Entra roles versus Azure roles

They are separate systems. **Entra roles** (Global Administrator, User Administrator) control the directory. **Azure roles** control resources. A Global Administrator does not automatically manage virtual machines, although they can elevate themselves to User Access Administrator at the root scope in an emergency.

## Good practice

- Assign roles to **groups**, not individuals.
- Use the **narrowest scope** that lets people do their work.
- Create **custom roles** only when no built-in role fits, and keep their actions list short.
- Review assignments quarterly with **access reviews**.

lessons.title: Azure Policy, tags and locks
lessons.content:
## Governance at scale

Large organisations use **management groups** to apply rules to many subscriptions at once, for example one management group for production and one for sandboxes.

## Azure Policy

Azure Policy evaluates resources against rules and can **deny**, **audit**, **append**, **modify** or **deployIfNotExists**. Common examples:

- Allow only approved Regions, such as UK South and UK West.
- Require a cost-centre tag on every resource group.
- Deny public IP addresses on network interfaces in production.

Group related policies into an **initiative**, such as the built-in Microsoft cloud security benchmark, and assign it at a management group.

~~~bash
az policy assignment create \
  --name allowed-locations \
  --policy "e56962a6-4747-49cd-b67b-bf8b01975c4c" \
  --scope "/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/mg-prod" \
  --params '{"listOfAllowedLocations":{"value":["uksouth","ukwest"]}}'
~~~

## Tags

Tags are name-value pairs such as environment=prod and owner=payments-team. They drive cost reports and automation. Tags are **not inherited** by default, so use a policy with the modify effect to copy tags from resource groups to resources.

## Resource locks

- **CanNotDelete**: users can change but not delete the resource.
- **ReadOnly**: users can read but not change or delete.

Locks apply to everyone, including Owners, until removed. Put a CanNotDelete lock on production resource groups and shared networking.

## Cost management

Use **Cost Management** budgets with alerts at 80% and 100%, and review **Azure Advisor** cost recommendations each month.

lessons.title: Module 1 quiz
lessons.content: Check your knowledge of identity, RBAC and governance.

questions.prompt: A team needs to manage virtual machines in one resource group but must not grant access to others. Which assignment is most appropriate?

options.text: Virtual Machine Contributor at the resource group

questions.explanation: Virtual Machine Contributor at the resource group gives the needed rights at the narrowest scope and does not allow granting access.

questions.prompt: Which feature stops anyone, including Owners, from deleting a production resource group by mistake?
questions.explanation: A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletion for every user until the lock is removed.

questions.prompt: Which service lets administrators activate the Global Administrator role only when needed, with approval?
questions.explanation: PIM provides just-in-time, time-bound and approved role activation with auditing.

lessons.title: Storage accounts and redundancy
lessons.content:
## Storage account basics

A **storage account** is the container for Azure Blob, Files, Queue and Table storage. Its name must be globally unique, 3 to 24 lowercase letters and numbers, because it forms the endpoint URL, for example https://contosologs.blob.core.windows.net.

Use **Standard general-purpose v2** for most work, and **Premium** block blob or file shares when you need consistently low latency.

## Redundancy options

| Option | Copies | Protects against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LRS | 3 in one data centre | Disk and rack failure |
| ZRS | 3 across availability zones | Loss of a zone |
| GRS | LRS plus 3 in the paired Region | Loss of a Region |
| GZRS | ZRS plus 3 in the paired Region | Zone and Region loss |

Add **RA-** (RA-GRS, RA-GZRS) to read from the secondary Region at any time. Without it, the secondary is readable only after failover.

~~~bash
az storage account create \
  --name contosologs2026 \
  --resource-group rg-shared \
  --location uksouth \
  --sku Standard_ZRS \
  --kind StorageV2 \
  --min-tls-version TLS1_2 \
  --allow-blob-public-access false
~~~

## Choosing

- Development and easily recreated data: **LRS**.
- Production data inside one Region that must survive a zone outage: **ZRS**.
- Business-critical data with a regional disaster requirement: **GZRS** or **RA-GZRS**.

## Data protection features

Turn on **soft delete** for blobs and containers, **versioning** for important containers, and **immutability policies** for records that must not change, such as financial audit logs.

lessons.title: Blob tiers, secure access and AzCopy
lessons.content:
## Access tiers

| Tier | Use | Minimum retention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hot | Frequently accessed data | None |
| Cool | Infrequent access | 30 days |
| Cold | Rarely accessed, needs quick retrieval | 90 days |
| Archive | Offline, hours to rehydrate | 180 days |

Deleting or moving a blob before the minimum period incurs an early deletion charge. Use **lifecycle management** rules to move blobs automatically, for example to Cool after 30 days without modification.

## Granting access

From most to least preferred:

1. **Entra ID with RBAC**, using roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader. Works with managed identities, so applications hold no secrets.
2. **User delegation SAS**: a shared access signature signed with Entra credentials, time-limited and scoped.
3. **Service or account SAS** signed with the account key.
4. **Account keys**: full access to everything. Rotate them, store them in Key Vault, and consider disabling shared key access altogether.

Restrict network access with the storage **firewall** and **private endpoints**, so the account is reachable only from your virtual network.

## Moving data with AzCopy

~~~bash
azcopy login
azcopy copy "/data/exports/*" \
  "https://contosologs2026.blob.core.windows.net/exports" --recursive
azcopy sync "/data/reports" "https://contosologs2026.blob.core.windows.net/reports"
~~~

For large offline transfers, use **Azure Data Box**. For hybrid file servers, **Azure File Sync** caches an Azure file share on Windows Server and tiers cold files to the cloud.

lessons.title: Module 2 quiz
lessons.content: Test your storage design decisions.

questions.prompt: Production data must survive the loss of an entire availability zone but does not need cross-Region copies. Which redundancy option is the best fit?
questions.explanation: ZRS keeps three copies across availability zones in one Region.

questions.prompt: An application on an Azure VM must read blobs without storing any secret. What should you use?

options.text: The storage account key in app settings
A managed identity with the Storage Blob Data Reader role
An account SAS valid for one year

questions.explanation: A managed identity authenticates through Entra ID, and RBAC grants only the needed data permission.

questions.prompt: Compliance backups are read perhaps once a year and can wait hours to be retrieved. Which tier is cheapest to store them?
questions.explanation: Archive has the lowest storage cost but requires rehydration that can take hours.

lessons.title: Virtual machines and availability
lessons.content:
## Deploying a VM

~~~bash
az vm create \
  --resource-group rg-app-prod \
  --name vm-web-01 \
  --image Ubuntu2404 \
  --size Standard_D2s_v5 \
  --zone 1 \
  --admin-username azureops \
  --ssh-key-values ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub \
  --public-ip-address ""
~~~

Setting an empty public IP keeps the VM private. Administrators then connect through **Azure Bastion** instead of exposing SSH or RDP to the internet.

## Availability options

| Option | Protects against | SLA (two or more VMs) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Availability set | Rack and host failure, planned maintenance | 99.95% |
| Availability zones | Data centre failure | 99.99% |
| Single VM with Premium SSD | Nothing beyond the VM itself | 99.9% |

An availability set spreads VMs across **fault domains** (separate power and network) and **update domains** (rebooted at different times).

## Scale sets

**Virtual Machine Scale Sets** manage a group of identical VMs, scale on metrics such as CPU, and spread instances across zones. Pair them with a load balancer and an image built with **Azure Compute Gallery**.

## Disks

- **Premium SSD v2** and **Ultra Disk** for databases needing tuned IOPS.
- **Standard SSD** for web servers and light workloads.
- Encrypt with platform-managed keys by default, or customer-managed keys in Key Vault when required.

## Resizing and maintenance

Resizing a VM usually restarts it. Use **Update Manager** to schedule operating system patching across Windows and Linux machines, and check the VM's boot diagnostics when it fails to start.

lessons.title: Linux administration on Azure
lessons.content:
## First boot with cloud-init

Most Azure Linux images support cloud-init, which configures the VM on first boot.

~~~yaml
#cloud-config
package_update: true
packages:
  - nginx
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now nginx
~~~

Pass it with az vm create --custom-data cloud-init.yaml.

## Everyday commands

~~~bash
sudo systemctl status nginx          # service health
journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago"
df -h && free -m                      # disk and memory
sudo ss -tulpn                        # listening ports
lsblk                                 # attached disks
~~~

## Adding a data disk

~~~bash
az vm disk attach -g rg-app-prod --vm-name vm-web-01 --name data01 --new --size-gb 128 --sku Premium_LRS
# on the VM
sudo parted /dev/sdc --script mklabel gpt mkpart primary ext4 0% 100%
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdc1
sudo mkdir /data && echo "UUID=$(sudo blkid -s UUID -o value /dev/sdc1) /data ext4 defaults,nofail 0 2" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab
sudo mount -a
~~~

Always mount by UUID with nofail: device names can change after a reboot, and a missing disk should not stop the VM from booting.

## Access and troubleshooting

- Sign in with Entra ID using the **AADSSHLoginForLinux** extension, so access follows RBAC.
- Use **Run Command** to execute scripts when SSH is broken.
- Use the **serial console** to fix a bad fstab entry or network configuration.

## Platform services

Not everything needs a VM. **App Service** hosts web apps without operating system management, **Azure Container Apps** runs containers with scale to zero, and **AKS** runs managed Kubernetes.

lessons.title: Module 3 quiz
lessons.content: Check your compute knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which option protects a two-VM web tier against the failure of a whole data centre within a Region?
questions.explanation: Availability zones place VMs in physically separate data centres. Availability sets protect only against rack and host failures.

questions.prompt: Why should a data disk be mounted by UUID with the nofail option in /etc/fstab?

options.text: Device names can change and a missing disk should not block boot

questions.explanation: Device names such as /dev/sdc are not stable. Using UUID and nofail keeps boots predictable.

questions.prompt: SSH to a Linux VM fails after a firewall change. Which tool lets you run a fix without network access?
questions.explanation: Run Command and the serial console reach the VM through the Azure platform, not the network.

lessons.title: VNets, subnets and network security groups
lessons.content:
## Virtual networks

A **virtual network** (VNet) is a private address space in a Region, such as 10.20.0.0/16, divided into subnets. Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet: the network address, the broadcast address and three for Azure services.

~~~bash
az network vnet create -g rg-net -n vnet-prod-uks \
  --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/16 \
  --subnet-name snet-web --subnet-prefixes 10.20.1.0/24
az network vnet subnet create -g rg-net --vnet-name vnet-prod-uks \
  -n snet-data --address-prefixes 10.20.2.0/24
~~~

Plan address space carefully: overlapping ranges cannot be peered or connected to on-premises networks.

## Network security groups

An NSG holds inbound and outbound rules, each with a **priority** from 100 to 4096. Lower numbers are evaluated first and the first match wins. Default rules allow traffic within the VNet and from the load balancer, and deny all other inbound traffic.

~~~bash
az network nsg rule create -g rg-net --nsg-name nsg-web -n allow-https \
  --priority 100 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --destination-port-ranges 443
~~~

Associate NSGs with **subnets** for consistency. Use **application security groups** to write rules such as "web servers may reach database servers on 1433" without listing IP addresses.

## Diagnosing traffic

- **IP flow verify** in Network Watcher tells you which rule allowed or denied a packet.
- **Effective security rules** show the combined result of subnet and NIC NSGs.
- **Next hop** shows where a route table sends traffic, which helps with user-defined routes and firewalls.

lessons.title: Connectivity and load balancing
lessons.content:
## Connecting networks

- **VNet peering** links two VNets over the Microsoft backbone with low latency. Peering is **not transitive**: if A peers with B and B with C, A cannot reach C unless you peer them or route through a hub.
- **Hub-and-spoke**: a hub VNet holds shared services such as Azure Firewall and VPN gateways; spokes peer to the hub. **Azure Virtual WAN** manages this at scale.
- **VPN Gateway** connects on-premises sites over IPsec across the internet.
- **ExpressRoute** provides a private, dedicated connection through a connectivity provider, with more predictable latency.

## Name resolution

**Azure DNS** hosts public zones. **Private DNS zones** resolve names inside VNets, and are essential for **private endpoints**, for example privatelink.blob.core.windows.net.

## Load balancing options

| Service | Layer | Scope | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Azure Load Balancer | 4 (TCP/UDP) | Regional | VMs, scale sets, non-HTTP traffic |
| Application Gateway | 7 (HTTP) | Regional | Path routing, TLS termination, WAF |
| Azure Front Door | 7 (HTTP) | Global | Global web apps, CDN, WAF at the edge |
| Traffic Manager | DNS | Global | DNS-based failover for any protocol |

A common pattern for a global web application is Front Door in front of Application Gateways in two Regions.

## Health probes

Every load balancer uses health probes. Point HTTP probes at a lightweight endpoint such as /healthz that checks the application is ready, not merely that the web server process is running.

lessons.title: Module 4 quiz
lessons.content: Test your networking knowledge.

questions.prompt: VNet A is peered with VNet B, and VNet B is peered with VNet C. Can VMs in A reach VMs in C by default?

options.text: Only if both use the same NSG

questions.explanation: Peering is non-transitive. You need a direct peering or a hub with routing such as Azure Firewall.

questions.prompt: An NSG has an allow rule at priority 200 and a deny rule for the same traffic at priority 100. What happens?

options.text: The rule with the newer timestamp wins

questions.explanation: Lower numbers are processed first and the first match wins, so the deny at 100 applies.

questions.prompt: Which service gives HTTP path-based routing and a web application firewall within one Region?
questions.explanation: Application Gateway is a regional layer 7 load balancer with optional WAF.

lessons.title: Azure Monitor and KQL
lessons.content:
## The data platform

Azure Monitor collects two kinds of data:

- **Metrics**: numeric time series such as CPU percentage, kept for 93 days and ideal for fast alerts.
- **Logs**: records in a **Log Analytics workspace**, queried with the Kusto Query Language (KQL).

Send platform logs to a workspace with **diagnostic settings**, and collect guest operating system data with the **Azure Monitor Agent** and data collection rules.

## Writing KQL

~~~sql
// VMs with average CPU above 80% in the last hour
Perf
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where ObjectName == "Processor" and CounterName == "% Processor Time"
| summarize AvgCPU = avg(CounterValue) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where AvgCPU > 80
| order by AvgCPU desc
~~~

~~~sql
// Who deleted resources yesterday
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(2d) .. ago(1d))
| where OperationNameValue endswith "DELETE" and ActivityStatusValue == "Success"
| project TimeGenerated, Caller, ResourceGroup, _ResourceId
~~~

## Alerts

An alert rule has a **scope**, a **condition** (metric, log query or activity log event) and an **action group** that sends email or SMS, calls a webhook or starts an automation runbook. Use **dynamic thresholds** for metrics with daily patterns, and keep alert counts low: every alert should demand action.

## Insights

**VM insights**, **Container insights** and **Application Insights** give ready-made dashboards. **Azure Service Health** tells you when Microsoft has an incident in your Regions, which is the first thing to check during an unexplained outage.

lessons.title: Azure Backup and Site Recovery
lessons.content:
## Two different jobs

- **Azure Backup** protects data so you can restore a file, disk, database or whole VM to a point in time.
- **Azure Site Recovery** replicates running workloads to another Region so you can fail over during a disaster.

## Recovery Services vaults and policies

A **Recovery Services vault** stores backups and replication settings. A **backup policy** sets frequency and retention, for example a daily backup at 22:00 kept for 30 days, weekly for 12 weeks and monthly for 12 months.

~~~bash
az backup vault create -g rg-backup -n rsv-prod-uks -l uksouth
az backup protection enable-for-vm \
  -g rg-backup --vault-name rsv-prod-uks \
  --vm vm-web-01 --policy-name DefaultPolicy
az backup protection backup-now -g rg-backup --vault-name rsv-prod-uks \
  --container-name vm-web-01 --item-name vm-web-01 --backup-management-type AzureIaasVM
~~~

Vault storage can be LRS, ZRS or GRS; choose before protecting the first item. Enable **soft delete** and **immutable vaults** so an attacker with stolen credentials cannot erase backups.

## Restoring

You can restore a whole VM, replace its disks, or recover individual files by mounting a recovery point. Practise restores into an isolated resource group and record how long they take.

## Site Recovery

Site Recovery continuously replicates VMs to a target Region. A **recovery plan** orders failover, for example databases first, then application servers, then web servers, with scripts between groups. Run a **test failover** into an isolated VNet at least twice a year; it does not affect production.

## Matching objectives

Backup typically gives an RPO of up to 24 hours for daily VM backups. Site Recovery can give an RPO of seconds to minutes and an RTO measured in minutes to hours.

lessons.title: Final assessment
lessons.content: Eight questions across the whole course. You need 70% to pass and earn your certificate.

questions.prompt: Where should you assign a role so that it applies to every subscription in the production estate?
questions.explanation: Assignments at a management group are inherited by all subscriptions beneath it.

questions.prompt: Which Azure Policy effect blocks creation of a non-compliant resource?
questions.explanation: Deny prevents the request. Audit only records non-compliance.

questions.prompt: Which redundancy option lets an application read data from the secondary Region at any time?
questions.explanation: The read-access (RA-) variants expose a readable secondary endpoint.

questions.prompt: A VM needs to be reachable by administrators without a public IP address. What should you deploy?
questions.explanation: Bastion provides browser-based RDP and SSH over TLS without exposing the VM.

questions.prompt: Which KQL operator groups rows and calculates aggregates such as averages?
questions.explanation: summarize aggregates rows, optionally grouped with by and bin().

questions.prompt: What does an action group define?

options.text: Who or what is notified when an alert fires
Which VMs belong to an availability set

questions.explanation: An action group lists notifications and automated actions an alert triggers.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Azure Site Recovery are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It replicates running VMs to another Region
Recovery plans can order the failover of tiers
It replaces the need for backups

questions.explanation: Site Recovery replicates workloads and supports ordered recovery plans. Test failovers are isolated, and backups are still needed for point-in-time recovery.

questions.prompt: A user is given Contributor on a resource group. What can they not do?

options.text: Delete a storage account in it

questions.explanation: Contributor manages resources but cannot grant access; that needs Owner or User Access Administrator.

courses.title: DevOps with Docker, Kubernetes and Terraform
courses.subtitle: Package, provision and ship software with Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and automated pipelines.
courses.description:
Platform and DevOps engineers are hired to make delivery fast and boring: every change built the same way, tested automatically, deployed with no drama and rolled back in minutes. This course builds that capability end to end, from writing a small, secure container image to running it on Kubernetes, provisioning the cloud underneath with Terraform, and wiring everything together in a CI/CD pipeline.

The course is hands-on and vendor-neutral. Examples use Docker, kubectl, Helm, Terraform and GitHub Actions, and the patterns transfer directly to GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, EKS, AKS and GKE.

**Who this is for**

- Developers who want to own how their services are built and deployed.
- System administrators moving into platform engineering or site reliability roles.
- Engineers applying for DevOps roles that ask for Kubernetes, Terraform and CI/CD experience.
outcomes: Write small, secure, multi-stage Dockerfiles and publish versioned images to a registry.
Deploy and operate applications on Kubernetes with Deployments, Services, probes and resource limits.
Provision cloud infrastructure with Terraform using remote state, modules and reviewed plans.
Build a CI/CD pipeline that tests, scans, builds and deploys on every merge.
Choose between rolling, blue-green and canary releases and roll back safely.
Apply GitOps so the cluster's state is declared and audited in Git.

lessons.title: Images, layers and the container model
lessons.content:
## What a container is

A container is an ordinary Linux process isolated with **namespaces** (its own view of processes, network and file system) and limited with **cgroups** (CPU and memory caps). It shares the host kernel, which is why containers start in milliseconds and are much lighter than virtual machines.

An **image** is a read-only stack of layers plus metadata such as the default command. Each Dockerfile instruction that changes the file system adds a layer. Layers are cached and shared, so ordering instructions well makes builds faster.

## Everyday commands

~~~bash
docker build -t orders-api:1.4.2 .
docker run -d --name orders -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env orders-api:1.4.2
docker ps
docker logs -f orders
docker exec -it orders sh
docker image ls
docker system df            # disk used by images, containers and cache
~~~

## Tags and digests

A tag such as 1.4.2 is a movable label; a **digest** such as sha256:9f86d0... identifies exact content. Deploy by immutable version tag or digest, never by latest, so you always know what is running and can roll back.

## Registries

Push images to a registry such as Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry, GitHub Container Registry or Docker Hub:

~~~bash
docker tag orders-api:1.4.2 ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.4.2
docker push ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.4.2
~~~

## Compose for local development

Docker Compose describes multi-container setups, such as an API with PostgreSQL and Redis, in one compose.yaml file. It is ideal on a laptop and in CI integration tests, but production orchestration belongs to Kubernetes or a managed container service.

lessons.title: Writing production-grade Dockerfiles
lessons.content:
## A multi-stage build

Multi-stage builds compile in one image and copy only the result into a small runtime image.

~~~dockerfile
# build stage
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build && npm prune --omit=dev

# runtime stage
FROM node:22-alpine
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=build /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
EXPOSE 8080
HEALTHCHECK CMD wget -qO- http://[::1]:8080/healthz || exit 1
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]
~~~

## Why each choice matters

- **Copy dependency manifests first.** The npm ci layer is reused until package files change.
- **Small base images** (alpine, distroless, slim) reduce download time and attack surface.
- **USER node** runs as a non-root user, limiting damage if the app is compromised.
- **Exec form CMD** (a JSON array) makes the app PID 1 so it receives SIGTERM and can shut down gracefully.
- **.dockerignore** keeps .git, node_modules and secrets out of the build context.

## Security scanning and supply chain

~~~bash
trivy image ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.4.2 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1
~~~

Fail the pipeline on critical vulnerabilities, rebuild images regularly to pick up base image patches, generate a **software bill of materials** (SBOM) and sign images with **cosign** so the cluster can verify their origin.

## Configuration

Follow the twelve-factor approach: one image for every environment, with configuration supplied through environment variables or mounted files at run time. Never bake secrets into an image layer; they remain in the history even if a later layer deletes them.

lessons.title: Module 1 quiz
lessons.content: Check your understanding of images and Dockerfiles.

questions.prompt: Why should package.json and the lock file be copied before the rest of the source code?

options.text: So the dependency install layer is cached until dependencies change
To run as a non-root user

questions.explanation: Layer caching reuses the expensive install step when only application code changes.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a multi-stage build?

options.text: It builds images for several CPU types
It runs several containers at once
Only the runtime artefacts reach the final, smaller image

questions.explanation: Build tools and source stay in the build stage; the final image carries only what runs.

questions.prompt: A secret was added in one layer and deleted in the next. Is it safe?

options.text: No, it remains in the earlier layer and image history
Yes, deleted files are removed from the image
Yes, if the image is pushed to a private registry
Only if the image uses alpine

questions.explanation: Layers are immutable, so the secret can still be extracted. Use build secrets or run-time injection instead.

lessons.title: Kubernetes architecture and core objects
lessons.content:
## The control plane and nodes

- **kube-apiserver**: the front door; every change goes through it.
- **etcd**: the consistent key-value store holding cluster state.
- **kube-scheduler**: assigns Pods to nodes based on resources and constraints.
- **kube-controller-manager**: runs control loops that move actual state towards desired state.
- On every node, the **kubelet** runs Pods through a container runtime such as containerd, and **kube-proxy** or an eBPF data plane such as Cilium handles Service networking.

Managed services (EKS, AKS, GKE) run the control plane for you.

## Core objects

| Object | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Pod | One or more containers sharing network and storage |
| Deployment | Declares replicas and rolls out new versions of stateless Pods |
| Service | Stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of matching Pods |
| Ingress or Gateway | HTTP routing from outside the cluster |
| ConfigMap and Secret | Configuration and sensitive values injected into Pods |
| StatefulSet | Stable identity and storage for databases and queues |
| Namespace | Logical partition for teams, quotas and policies |

## Working with kubectl

~~~bash
kubectl apply -f deploy/
kubectl get pods -n orders -o wide
kubectl describe pod orders-api-7d9c8b-x2kqp -n orders
kubectl logs deploy/orders-api -n orders --since=15m
kubectl rollout status deploy/orders-api -n orders
kubectl rollout undo deploy/orders-api -n orders
~~~

## Declarative thinking

You do not tell Kubernetes to start three containers; you declare that three replicas should exist, and controllers keep it true. If a node dies, the Deployment's ReplicaSet notices the shortfall and schedules replacements elsewhere. Store manifests in Git and apply them, rather than editing live objects by hand.

lessons.title: A production-ready Deployment
lessons.content:
## The manifest

~~~yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: orders-api
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: orders-api }
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxUnavailable: 0, maxSurge: 1 }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: orders-api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:1.4.2
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: orders-config }
            - secretRef: { name: orders-secrets }
          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
~~~

## What each part does

- **Requests** reserve capacity and drive scheduling; **limits** cap usage. Exceeding a memory limit gets the container OOMKilled.
- **Readiness probes** remove a Pod from Service endpoints until it can serve. **Liveness probes** restart a stuck container. Do not point liveness at dependencies such as the database, or one outage will restart every Pod.
- **maxUnavailable: 0** keeps full capacity during rollouts.

## Scaling and resilience

~~~bash
kubectl autoscale deploy orders-api -n orders --cpu-percent=70 --min=3 --max=12
~~~

Add a **PodDisruptionBudget** so node upgrades never evict too many replicas at once, and use **topologySpreadConstraints** to spread Pods across zones.

## Packaging with Helm

Helm templates manifests into a versioned chart with values per environment:

~~~bash
helm upgrade --install orders ./charts/orders -n orders -f values-prod.yaml --atomic
~~~

--atomic rolls back automatically if the release fails.

lessons.title: Module 2 quiz
lessons.content: Test your Kubernetes knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which component stores the desired and actual state of a Kubernetes cluster?
questions.explanation: etcd is the cluster's consistent key-value store; the API server reads and writes it.

questions.prompt: A Pod should stop receiving traffic while it warms its cache, but should not be restarted. Which probe handles this?
questions.explanation: A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints without restarting it.

questions.prompt: A container repeatedly exceeds its memory limit. What will you see?

options.text: The container is OOMKilled and restarted

questions.explanation: Exceeding a memory limit causes the kernel to kill the container, shown as OOMKilled.

questions.prompt: Which command reverts a Deployment to its previous revision?
questions.explanation: rollout undo returns the Deployment to its previous ReplicaSet template.

lessons.title: Terraform fundamentals and state
lessons.content:
## The workflow

Terraform describes infrastructure in HashiCorp Configuration Language (HCL). The core loop is:

~~~bash
terraform init       # download providers, configure the backend
terraform fmt -check # consistent formatting
terraform validate   # syntax and type checks
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
~~~

Always apply a **saved plan** that someone has reviewed, so what you approved is exactly what runs.

## A small configuration

~~~hcl
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6"
  required_providers {
    aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws", version = "~> 5.0" }
  }
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-tf-state"
    key            = "network/prod.tfstate"
    region         = "eu-west-2"
    dynamodb_table = "tf-locks"
    encrypt        = true
  }
}

provider "aws" { region = var.region }

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "artefacts" {
  bucket = "acme-artefacts-prod"
  tags   = { team = "platform", environment = "prod" }
}
~~~

## State

Terraform records what it manages in **state**, mapping resource addresses to real IDs. State matters because:

- It is the basis for every plan, so it must be shared by the team: use a **remote backend** (S3, Azure Storage, GCS or HCP Terraform).
- Concurrent applies corrupt it, so enable **locking**. Recent Terraform versions also support S3-native locking with use_lockfile.
- It can contain secrets, so encrypt it and restrict access.

## Drift

When someone changes infrastructure by hand, terraform plan shows **drift**. Decide whether to update the code or let Terraform revert the change, and remove console access that causes repeated drift. Use terraform import or import blocks to bring existing resources under management.

lessons.title: Modules, environments and safe change
lessons.content:
## Modules

A module is a folder of Terraform files with inputs (variables) and outputs. Good modules wrap a meaningful unit, such as "a VPC with standard subnets", not a single resource.

~~~hcl
module "network" {
  source          = "git::https://github.com/acme/tf-modules.git//vpc?ref=v2.3.0"
  name            = "prod"
  cidr            = "10.0.0.0/16"
  azs             = ["eu-west-2a", "eu-west-2b", "eu-west-2c"]
  private_subnets = ["10.0.1.0/24", "10.0.2.0/24", "10.0.3.0/24"]
}

output "vpc_id" { value = module.network.vpc_id }
~~~

Pin module sources to a tag and provider versions with a constraint, and commit the **.terraform.lock.hcl** file.

## Separating environments

| Approach | How it works | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Directory per environment | envs/dev, envs/prod each with their own state | Clear and explicit; most common |
| Workspaces | One configuration, several states | Simple, but easy to apply to the wrong one |
| Separate accounts or subscriptions | Each environment in its own cloud account | Strongest blast-radius isolation |

## Making change safe

- Run fmt, validate, **tflint** and a policy check such as **Checkov** or OPA in CI on every pull request.
- Post the plan output to the pull request so reviewers see exactly what will change.
- Watch for **"must be replaced"** in plans: replacing a database destroys data. Use lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } on critical resources.
- Use **moved** blocks when renaming resources so Terraform does not destroy and recreate them.

## Secrets

Never hard-code secrets in .tf files. Read them from a secrets manager with a data source, mark variables sensitive = true, and remember that values may still be written to state.

lessons.title: Module 3 quiz
lessons.content: Check your Terraform knowledge.

questions.prompt: Why should Terraform state be stored in a remote backend with locking?

options.text: It is required for the fmt command
It hides resources from the cloud console
So the team shares one state and concurrent applies cannot corrupt it

questions.explanation: A shared backend gives everyone the same view, and locking prevents two applies writing at once.

questions.prompt: A plan shows that a production database 'must be replaced'. What is the right response?

options.text: Apply quickly before anything else changes
Stop and find which argument forces replacement before applying

questions.explanation: Replacement destroys and recreates the resource. Investigate first, and protect critical resources with prevent_destroy.

questions.prompt: Which block lets you rename a resource address without destroying the real resource?
questions.explanation: A moved block tells Terraform the old address and new address refer to the same object.

lessons.title: Building a pipeline with GitHub Actions
lessons.content:
## What a good pipeline does

1. **Builds** the same way every time from a clean environment.
2. **Tests** with unit, integration and contract tests.
3. **Scans** code, dependencies and images for vulnerabilities and secrets.
4. **Publishes** an immutable, versioned artefact.
5. **Deploys** to staging automatically and to production with an approval or automated checks.

## An example workflow

~~~yaml
name: orders-api
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  id-token: write

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test -- --coverage

  image:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/acme/orders-api:${{ github.sha }}
~~~

## Practices that matter

- **Least-privilege tokens**: set permissions explicitly and use **OIDC federation** (id-token: write) to get short-lived cloud credentials instead of storing access keys.
- **Fast feedback**: keep the pull request pipeline under ten minutes with caching and parallel jobs.
- **Environments with protection rules** for production approvals.
- **Trunk-based development** with short-lived branches keeps merges small and pipelines meaningful.

## DORA metrics

Measure delivery with deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. They tell you whether pipeline improvements are working.

lessons.title: Deployment strategies and GitOps
lessons.content:
## Strategies compared

| Strategy | How it works | Rollback | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rolling | Replace Pods a few at a time | Roll forward or undo | Lowest |
| Blue-green | Run the new version beside the old, switch traffic at once | Switch back instantly | Double capacity briefly |
| Canary | Send a small share of traffic (say 5%) to the new version, increase while metrics are healthy | Shift traffic back | Moderate |
| Feature flags | Deploy code dark, enable for users separately | Turn the flag off | Low, but adds code complexity |

Canary releases need good metrics: compare error rate and latency of the canary against the stable version before promoting. Tools such as **Argo Rollouts** and **Flagger** automate the analysis.

## GitOps

In GitOps, Git is the source of truth for what runs in the cluster. An agent inside the cluster, such as **Argo CD** or **Flux**, pulls the desired state from a repository and reconciles continuously.

~~~yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: orders-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/acme/deploy-config.git
    path: orders/overlays/prod
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: orders
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
~~~

Benefits:

- Every change to production is a reviewed pull request with an audit trail.
- **selfHeal** reverts manual changes, eliminating drift.
- Rollback is a git revert.
- The CI system no longer needs cluster credentials, which shrinks the attack surface.

## Putting it together

CI builds and tests the image, then opens a pull request that bumps the image tag in the deploy repository. Merging it triggers Argo CD to roll out, and Argo Rollouts manages the canary.
