lessons.title: Pod failures and how to read them
lessons.content:
## Start with the status

~~~bash
kubectl get pods -n volume-attach -o wide
kubectl describe pod volume-attach-6c9f7d-kq2lm -n volume-attach
kubectl logs volume-attach-6c9f7d-kq2lm -n volume-attach --previous
kubectl get events -n volume-attach --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail -20
~~~

--previous shows the logs of the last crashed container, which is usually what you need for a crash loop.

## Common states

| Status | Typical cause | First checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pending | No node fits the requests, unbound PVC, taints | describe pod events, node allocatable, PVC status |
| ImagePullBackOff | Wrong tag, registry auth, rate limits | Image name, imagePullSecrets, registry status |
| CrashLoopBackOff | App exits on start: bad config, missing secret, failed dependency | logs --previous, env, mounted config |
| OOMKilled | Memory limit exceeded | Last state in describe, memory metrics, limit size |
| Running but not Ready | Readiness probe failing | Probe path, dependency health, start-up time |
| CreateContainerConfigError | Missing ConfigMap or Secret key | describe pod, the referenced objects |

## Exit codes

An exit code of **137** means the container received SIGKILL, often from the OOM killer. **143** means SIGTERM, usually a normal shutdown. **1** is a generic application error, so read the logs.

## Debugging inside the Pod

Helix images are distroless and have no shell. Use an ephemeral debug container that shares the Pod's process namespace:

~~~bash
kubectl debug -it volume-attach-6c9f7d-kq2lm -n volume-attach \
  --image=busybox:1.36 --target=api -- sh
~~~

## Do no harm

On a production incident, collect evidence before deleting a Pod: its describe output and previous logs disappear with it. Prefer scaling out or rolling back over editing live objects, and record every command you run in the incident channel.

lessons.title: Nodes, networking and DNS
lessons.content:
## Node problems

~~~bash
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node ip-10-42-7-19.us-east-2.compute.internal
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -A --sort-by=memory | head
~~~

Look at **Conditions**: MemoryPressure, DiskPressure and PIDPressure cause the kubelet to evict Pods. NotReady usually means the kubelet has stopped reporting, because of a crashed kubelet, a broken container runtime, or a network partition.

To take a node out of service safely:

~~~bash
kubectl cordon <node>
kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --timeout=10m
~~~

Drains respect PodDisruptionBudgets. If a drain hangs, a PDB is usually blocking it; check which one before overriding anything.

On the node itself (through Helix's break-glass access only):

~~~bash
journalctl -u kubelet --since "30 min ago"
crictl ps -a
df -h /var/lib/containerd
~~~

## Service networking

When a service cannot reach another:

1. Does the Service have **endpoints**? kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>. No endpoints means the selector does not match ready Pods.
2. Does **DNS** resolve? From a debug container: nslookup billing.billing.svc.cluster.local.
3. Is a **NetworkPolicy** blocking it? Helix namespaces default-deny ingress, so each allowed flow must be declared.
4. Is the target port right? Service port and targetPort are often confused.

## DNS at scale

CoreDNS is a frequent hidden bottleneck. Watch coredns_dns_requests_total and the error rate, and remember that the default ndots:5 setting causes several lookups for external names. Use fully qualified names ending in a dot for hot external calls, or tune dnsConfig.

lessons.title: Module 3 quiz
lessons.content: Check your troubleshooting knowledge.

questions.prompt: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Which command most directly shows why the last container exited?
questions.explanation: --previous shows output from the crashed container instance rather than the new one.

questions.prompt: A container's last state shows exit code 137 and reason OOMKilled. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The image tag does not exist
The readiness probe path is wrong
The container exceeded its memory limit

questions.explanation: 137 is SIGKILL; with OOMKilled it means the kernel killed the process for exceeding its memory limit.

questions.prompt: A Service returns connection refused and kubectl shows it has no endpoints. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the Service selector matches labels of ready Pods

questions.explanation: No endpoints means no ready Pods match the selector, often a label mismatch or failing readiness.

questions.prompt: A node drain hangs. What is the most common reason?

options.text: Too many Services in the namespace

questions.explanation: Drains respect PDBs, so if evicting another Pod would breach a budget the drain waits.

lessons.title: On-call and incident command
lessons.content:
## On-call at Helix

- Primary and secondary on-call rotate weekly, with handover on Tuesdays at 16:00 UTC so no handover lands on a weekend.
- Follow-the-sun coverage across Austin, Dublin and Bengaluru keeps night pages rare.
- Acknowledge a page within **5 minutes**; if you cannot, the secondary is paged automatically.
- Every page links to a **runbook**. A page with no useful runbook is itself a bug: file it.

## Severity levels

| Severity | Definition | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SEV1 | Major customer impact, data at risk or a region-wide outage | Incident commander assigned, status page within 15 minutes, executives informed |
| SEV2 | Significant impact on a subset of customers or a key feature | Incident commander assigned, status page if customer-visible |
| SEV3 | Minor impact or degraded redundancy | Owning team handles in hours |

When in doubt, declare a higher severity; downgrading is cheap.

## Roles

Helix follows the incident command model used by many large operators:

- **Incident commander (IC)**: owns coordination and decisions, not the keyboard. Sets priorities and keeps time.
- **Operations lead**: directs the technical investigation and mitigation.
- **Communications lead**: updates the status page and customer-facing teams at a fixed cadence, every 30 minutes for SEV1.
- **Scribe**: keeps the timeline of findings, decisions and actions.

## Mitigate first

The first goal is to stop customer impact, not to find the root cause. Typical mitigations: roll back the last deployment, shift traffic away from a region, scale out, disable a feature flag. Root cause analysis happens after service is restored.

## Communication pattern

~~~text
[14:32 UTC] SEV2 update 3. Impact: volume attach failures for ~8% of us-east-2 requests.
Current action: rolled back volume-attach v2.41 at 14:27; error ratio falling (4.1% -> 0.6%).
Next update: 15:00 UTC or sooner if status changes. IC: M. Alvarez.
~~~

lessons.title: Blameless postmortems
lessons.content:
## Why blameless

Incidents emerge from systems: deployment tooling, alert design, documentation, time pressure. If people fear blame, they hide information and the organisation stops learning. A blameless postmortem assumes everyone acted reasonably given what they knew at the time, and asks how the system allowed the failure.

## When Helix requires one

- Every SEV1 and SEV2.
- Any incident consuming more than 20% of a service's monthly error budget.
- Any data loss, security exposure or missed customer SLA, whatever the severity.

Drafts are due within **five working days** and reviewed in the weekly reliability review.

## Structure

1. **Summary**: two or three sentences a customer-facing manager can understand.
2. **Impact**: duration, customers and regions affected, SLO budget consumed, SLA credits owed.
3. **Timeline** in UTC: detection, escalation, key decisions, mitigation, resolution.
4. **Contributing factors**: usually several. Avoid a single "root cause" and avoid "human error" as an explanation; ask why the system made the error easy.
5. **What went well** and **where we got lucky**.
6. **Action items**.

## Good action items

| Weak | Strong |
| --- | --- |
| Be more careful with config changes | Add schema validation for attach-service config in CI (owner: storage-platform, due 15 Nov) |
| Improve monitoring | Add a burn-rate alert on attach latency SLO with runbook link (owner: storage-sre, due 8 Nov) |
| Train the team | Run a game day on regional failover for block storage before end of quarter (owner: SRE lead) |

Each action has one owner, a due date and a way to verify it is done. Actions are tracked in Jira with the postmortem label and reviewed until closed.

## Sharing

Postmortems are published internally to all of engineering. Reading other teams' postmortems is one of the fastest ways for a new SRE to learn how Helix's platform really fails.

lessons.title: Final assessment
lessons.content: Eight questions covering the Helix SRE onboarding course. You need 70% to pass and earn your certificate.

questions.prompt: Helix's tier-1 API has a 99.95% SLO. Roughly how much full downtime does that allow in 30 days?
questions.explanation: 0.05% of 43,200 minutes is 21.6 minutes.

questions.prompt: Under the Helix error budget policy, what happens when a service exhausts its budget?

options.text: Feature releases pause for that service while engineering focuses on reliability

questions.explanation: An exhausted budget shifts priority from features to reliability until the SLO is met again.

questions.prompt: Which PromQL expression gives the 5xx error ratio for a service?
questions.explanation: Divide the rate of 5xx requests by the rate of all requests, applying rate() before sum().

questions.prompt: Which signal is best for finding which downstream service made one request slow?
questions.explanation: Traces show the time spent in each span across services for a single request.

questions.prompt: A Pod is Pending with the event '0/12 nodes are available: insufficient memory'. What is the most direct fix?

options.text: Add capacity or reduce the Pod's memory request

questions.explanation: The scheduler cannot place the Pod because no node has enough allocatable memory for its request.

questions.prompt: During a SEV1, what is the incident commander's main responsibility?

options.text: Coordinating the response and making decisions, rather than debugging hands-on
Writing the postmortem during the incident

questions.explanation: The IC coordinates, prioritises and decides, while others investigate and communicate.

questions.prompt: Which are good postmortem action items? Select all that apply.

options.text: Add CI validation for the attach-service config, owned by storage-platform, due 15 November
Add a burn-rate alert with a runbook link, owned by storage-sre, due 8 November
Run a regional failover game day before quarter end, owned by the SRE lead

questions.explanation: Strong actions are specific, owned, dated and verifiable. 'Be more careful' changes nothing in the system.

questions.prompt: What is the first priority once an incident is declared?

options.text: Mitigate customer impact, for example by rolling back

questions.explanation: Restoring service comes first; root cause analysis follows once customers are no longer affected.

courses.title: SAP S/4HANA Finance (FICO) consultant
courses.subtitle: Configure and run financial accounting and controlling in SAP S/4HANA, from the Universal Journal to the period-end close.
courses.description:
SAP S/4HANA Finance is the ledger behind thousands of multinational groups. This course takes you through the way finance actually works in S/4HANA: one Universal Journal, the business partner model, new asset accounting, controlling, and a disciplined period-end close.

Every module pairs configuration concepts with the day-to-day transactions and Fiori apps that consultants and key users rely on. You will learn the vocabulary that project teams use in workshops, so you can contribute from your first week on an implementation or support team.

**Who this is for**

- Accountants and finance analysts moving into SAP roles
- ECC FICO consultants preparing for S/4HANA projects
- Graduates targeting SAP consulting firms and shared service centres
- Finance key users who want to understand what happens behind the screens
outcomes: Explain how the Universal Journal (table ACDOCA) unifies financial accounting and controlling postings.
Design an enterprise structure with company codes, a controlling area, ledgers and fiscal year variants.
Process procure-to-pay and order-to-cash postings, including the automatic payment run and dunning.
Set up and run new asset accounting, from acquisition through depreciation to retirement.
Use cost centres, internal orders and margin analysis to report profitability.
Plan and execute a month-end close using standard transactions and Fiori apps.

lessons.title: The Universal Journal and ACDOCA
lessons.content:
## One table for every posting

In SAP ECC, a single business transaction could write to a dozen tables: BKPF and BSEG for the accounting document, GLT0 for totals, COEP for controlling line items, ANEP for assets and many index tables such as BSIS and BSAS. Reconciling those tables was a project in itself.

S/4HANA replaces that design with the **Universal Journal**, stored in table **ACDOCA**. Every financial line item, whether it comes from the general ledger, asset accounting, controlling or material ledger, is written once to ACDOCA. Totals tables are no longer needed because the in-memory database aggregates line items on the fly.

## Key fields you will meet

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| RLDNR | Ledger, for example 0L for the leading ledger |
| RBUKRS | Company code |
| GJAHR / POPER | Fiscal year and posting period |
| BELNR / DOCLN | Document number and line item |
| RACCT | G/L account |
| HSL / KSL / TSL | Amounts in company code, group and transaction currency |
| RCNTR / PRCTR | Cost centre and profit centre |

## Why it matters to consultants

- **No FI–CO reconciliation**: cost elements are now G/L accounts (maintained in FS00), so primary costs post once.
- **Real-time reporting**: trial balances and margin reports read ACDOCA directly.
- **Extensibility**: customer fields added through the coding block appear in ACDOCA and in Fiori reports.

A key user can query the Universal Journal for analysis, for example in a sandbox through SQL tools connected to the HANA database:

~~~sql
SELECT rbukrs, racct, SUM(hsl) AS balance
FROM acdoca
WHERE rldnr = '0L' AND gjahr = '2026' AND poper <= '006'
GROUP BY rbukrs, racct
ORDER BY rbukrs, racct;
~~~

In production you would normally use the Fiori app **Trial Balance** or CDS views such as I_JournalEntryItem rather than querying the table directly.

lessons.title: Enterprise structure: company codes, controlling areas and ledgers
lessons.content:
## The organisational backbone

Before a single posting is made, an S/4HANA project agrees the **enterprise structure**. Getting it wrong is expensive, because most elements cannot be changed once transactional data exists.

- **Company**: the consolidation unit, usually a legal group entity.
- **Company code**: the smallest unit with a complete, self-contained balance sheet. Each legal entity normally gets one company code with its own local currency, for example AED for a UAE entity or EUR for a German GmbH.
- **Controlling area**: the unit for cost accounting. In S/4HANA, company codes assigned to one controlling area must share the same operating chart of accounts and fiscal year variant.
- **Chart of accounts**: the operating chart holds the G/L accounts used for daily postings. A country chart can be added where local statutory reporting requires different account numbers, such as the French PCG.

## Ledgers and accounting principles

S/4HANA uses the **ledger approach** for parallel accounting. The leading ledger **0L** usually follows IFRS or the group's primary GAAP. Non-leading ledgers, such as a local GAAP ledger, receive postings that differ only where the accounting principles differ.

| Element | Typical choice for a multinational |
| --- | --- |
| Leading ledger | 0L, IFRS |
| Non-leading ledger | 2L, local GAAP such as HGB |
| Group currency | USD or EUR |
| Fiscal year variant | K4 (calendar year, four special periods) |

## Posting periods

Each company code is linked to a **posting period variant**, opened and closed in transaction **OB52**. During close, finance usually keeps only the current period open for most account types while allowing special periods 13 to 16 for audit adjustments.

## Practical advice

Document every structural decision in the design workshop minutes, including the reason. Auditors and future support teams will ask why a company code shares, or does not share, a controlling area.

lessons.title: Check your understanding: foundations
lessons.content: Answer these questions to confirm you understand the Universal Journal and the enterprise structure.

questions.prompt: Which table stores line items from G/L, asset accounting and controlling in S/4HANA?
questions.explanation: ACDOCA is the Universal Journal. BSEG still exists for compatibility, but ACDOCA holds the complete line item.

questions.prompt: What is the smallest organisational unit with its own complete balance sheet?
questions.explanation: A company code represents an independent accounting unit, normally a legal entity, with a full balance sheet and profit and loss statement.

questions.prompt: Which transaction opens and closes posting periods?
questions.explanation: OB52 maintains the posting period variant. FS00 maintains G/L accounts, F110 is the payment run and KS01 creates cost centres.

questions.prompt: In the ledger approach, what does the leading ledger 0L typically represent?

options.text: The group's primary accounting principle, often IFRS

questions.explanation: The leading ledger carries the primary accounting principle and is integrated with controlling.

lessons.title: G/L accounts, document types and posting keys
lessons.content:
## G/L accounts in S/4HANA

G/L accounts are created centrally in **FS00**. Each account has a chart of accounts section (description, account group, account type) and a company code section (currency, tax category, open item management, line item display, field status group).

In S/4HANA the **G/L account type** decides behaviour:

- **Balance sheet account**
- **Nonoperating expense or income**
- **Primary costs or revenue**, which replaces the old primary cost element
- **Secondary costs**, used for allocations and settlements inside controlling
- **Cash account**, used for bank reconciliation reporting

## Document types and number ranges

Every journal entry has a **document type** that controls the number range and which account types can be posted.

| Document type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| SA | G/L account document |
| KR | Vendor invoice |
| KZ | Vendor payment |
| DR | Customer invoice |
| DZ | Customer payment |
| AA | Asset posting |

## Posting keys

Posting keys define debit or credit and the account type. Common pairs are **40/50** for G/L debit and credit, **31/21** for vendor credit and debit, and **01/11** for customer debit and credit.

## Entering a journal

Users post simple journals with the Fiori app **Post General Journal Entries** or transaction **FB50**. Recurring entries, such as monthly rent accruals, are set up as recurring documents (FBD1) and executed with F.14.

## Good practice

- Use **open item management** for clearing accounts such as GR/IR and bank clearing.
- Keep a small set of document types with clear meaning, so auditors can filter quickly.
- Never post directly to reconciliation accounts; the system blocks it because they are fed by vendor and customer sub-ledgers.

lessons.title: Procure-to-pay and the three-way match
lessons.content:
## The flow

Procure-to-pay (P2P) links materials management and finance. The standard flow is:

1. **Purchase order** created in ME21N or the Fiori app Manage Purchase Orders.
2. **Goods receipt** in MIGO. The system posts *Dr Inventory or expense, Cr GR/IR clearing*.
3. **Supplier invoice** in MIRO. The system posts *Dr GR/IR clearing, Dr input tax, Cr vendor*.
4. **Payment** through the automatic payment program **F110**, posting *Dr vendor, Cr bank clearing*.

## The three-way match

MIRO compares the purchase order price, the goods receipt quantity and the invoice. Differences above tolerance (configured in OMR6) block the invoice for payment. Blocked invoices are released in **MRBR** once the buyer resolves the variance.

## Suppliers as business partners

In S/4HANA, vendors and customers are maintained as **business partners** in transaction **BP**. Customer–vendor integration (CVI) synchronises the BP with the classic vendor and customer tables. A single business partner can hold both a supplier role (FLVN01) and a customer role (FLCU01), which is useful for intercompany partners and joint venture partners.

## Running F110

The payment run has a clear sequence:

- Enter run date and identification, then **parameters**: company codes, payment methods, next posting date and vendor range.
- Run the **proposal** and review exceptions in the log.
- Edit the proposal to block or reassign items if needed.
- Run the **payment** and generate the medium, usually an ISO 20022 pain.001 XML file for the bank.

## Watch the GR/IR account

The GR/IR clearing account should net to zero over time. Old open items mean either goods received but not invoiced, or invoiced but not received. At month end, the GR/IR regrouping program (FAGL_GR_IR or the Fiori app) reclassifies the balances for the balance sheet.

lessons.title: Order-to-cash, dunning and customer clearing
lessons.content:
## From sales order to cash

Order-to-cash (O2C) integrates sales and distribution with receivables:

1. **Sales order** (VA01)
2. **Outbound delivery and goods issue** (VL01N): *Dr cost of goods sold, Cr inventory*
3. **Billing document** (VF01): *Dr customer, Cr revenue, Cr output tax*
4. **Incoming payment**: *Dr bank, Cr customer*, cleared automatically from the bank statement or manually in F-28

## Revenue account determination

Billing finds revenue accounts through **VKOA**, using the chart of accounts, sales organisation, customer account assignment group, material account assignment group and account key (ERL for revenue, ERS for sales deductions). Most posting errors in O2C come from a missing VKOA entry.

## Credit management

S/4HANA uses **SAP Credit Management** (FIN-FSCM-CR). Credit limits are kept on the business partner in credit segment data, and sales orders are blocked when exposure exceeds the limit.

## Dunning

Dunning reminds customers about overdue items. A **dunning procedure** defines the number of levels, days in arrears, charges and form texts. The dunning run (**F150**) follows the same parameter, proposal and print pattern as F110.

## Bank statements and clearing

Electronic bank statements in camt.053 or MT940 format are imported with the Fiori app **Manage Bank Statements** (or FF_5). Search strings and interpretation algorithms match payment references to open invoices, so most receipts clear without manual work.

## Measures to track

- **Days sales outstanding (DSO)**
- Percentage of incoming payments cleared automatically
- Overdue receivables by ageing bucket, available in the app **Aging Analysis**

lessons.title: Check your understanding: GL, AP and AR
lessons.content: Confirm the core postings and transactions in procure-to-pay and order-to-cash.

questions.prompt: Which transaction posts a supplier invoice with reference to a purchase order?
questions.explanation: MIRO performs logistics invoice verification against the purchase order and goods receipt.

questions.prompt: What is the accounting entry when a goods receipt is posted for stock material?

options.text: Dr cost of goods sold, Cr inventory

questions.explanation: The goods receipt debits inventory and credits the GR/IR clearing account; the invoice later clears GR/IR.

questions.prompt: Where are customers and suppliers maintained in S/4HANA?

options.text: As business partners in transaction BP

questions.explanation: S/4HANA uses the business partner model; customer–vendor integration keeps the classic tables in sync.

questions.prompt: Which configuration transaction determines revenue G/L accounts for billing?
questions.explanation: VKOA is revenue account determination. OBYC covers materials management account determination.

lessons.title: New asset accounting in S/4HANA
lessons.content:
## What changed

S/4HANA uses **new asset accounting** by default. Asset postings are written in real time to every depreciation area and ledger in the Universal Journal. The old periodic APC posting program (RAPERB2000) is gone; only depreciation is posted periodically.

## Key configuration

- **Chart of depreciation**: a country-specific set of depreciation areas, assigned to the company code.
- **Depreciation areas**: area 01 for book depreciation (IFRS), area 15 for tax, area 32 for local GAAP, each linked to an accounting principle and ledger group.
- **Asset classes**: such as buildings, plant and machinery, vehicles and IT equipment. Each class proposes account determination, screen layout and default useful life.
- **Depreciation keys**: for example LINR for straight-line over useful life.

## The asset life cycle

| Step | Transaction or app |
| --- | --- |
| Create asset master | AS01 / Manage Fixed Assets |
| Acquisition from supplier | F-90 or MIRO with asset account assignment |
| Acquisition without supplier | ABZON |
| Transfer within company code | ABUMN |
| Depreciation run | AFAB |
| Retirement with revenue | F-92 |
| Asset explorer | AW01N |
| Year-end close | AJAB, then fiscal year change with AJRW |

## The depreciation run

AFAB posts planned depreciation for a period. It runs in test mode first, then in update mode, usually as a background job. In S/4HANA you can repeat the run for a period at any time, and the system posts only the difference.

## Practical checks

- Reconcile the asset sub-ledger with the balance sheet accounts through the Fiori app **Asset Balances** before close.
- Make sure assets under construction (AuC) are settled to final assets when they are ready for use, otherwise depreciation never starts.
- Keep useful lives aligned with your accounting policy and IAS 16 componentisation for significant parts.

lessons.title: Cost centres, internal orders and margin analysis
lessons.content:
## Controlling in one ledger

Because primary costs are G/L accounts, every expense posting with a cost object updates controlling at the same moment. Controlling then moves costs internally with secondary cost accounts.

## Cost centre accounting

- **Standard hierarchy**: every cost centre belongs to a node in the controlling area's standard hierarchy, maintained in OKEON.
- **Cost centres** (KS01) represent places where cost is incurred, such as Finance Dubai or Plant maintenance Ruwais.
- **Allocations**: assessments (KSU5) move costs with a secondary cost account; distributions (KSV5) keep the original primary account.
- **Activity types** and planned rates allow internal charging, for example engineering hours charged to projects.

## Internal orders

Internal orders (KO01) collect costs for a limited activity, such as a trade fair or a plant shutdown. They carry a **settlement rule** that sends the costs at period end to a cost centre, a fixed asset or a WBS element. Settlement runs in **KO88** for one order or KO8G for a batch.

## Profitability: margin analysis

S/4HANA recommends **margin analysis** (account-based CO-PA). Revenue and cost of goods sold post directly with market segment attributes such as customer, product, region and sales organisation. Because it is account-based, profitability always reconciles with the general ledger.

## Profit centres

Profit centres support management reporting by business unit and, with **document splitting**, can produce a full balance sheet per profit centre or segment, which helps with IFRS 8 segment reporting.

## Reporting tools

- Fiori app **Cost Centres – Actuals** for plan and actual comparison
- **Product Profitability** and **Market Segment – Actuals** for margin analysis
- Classic report KSB1 for cost centre line items

lessons.title: Check your understanding: assets and controlling
lessons.content: Check your knowledge of asset accounting and controlling objects.

questions.prompt: Which transaction executes the periodic depreciation run?
questions.explanation: AFAB posts planned depreciation. AJAB closes the asset fiscal year and AS01 creates an asset master.

questions.prompt: Why is there no FI–CO reconciliation in S/4HANA for primary costs?

options.text: Cost elements are G/L accounts and post once to ACDOCA
Costs are only posted at period end

questions.explanation: Primary cost elements became G/L accounts, so a single posting updates both views of the same line item.

questions.prompt: What determines where the costs of an internal order go at period end?
questions.explanation: Each internal order carries a settlement rule that names the receivers and percentages.

modules.title: Close, reporting and working on projects

lessons.title: Running the period-end close
lessons.content:
## A predictable sequence

A strong close follows a calendar that everyone knows. A typical S/4HANA month-end close runs over three to five working days:

| Day | Activities |
| --- | --- |
| Day minus 1 | Cut-off reminders, GR/IR review, open period checks |
| Day 1 | Final invoices, accruals, depreciation run (AFAB), recurring entries (F.14) |
| Day 2 | Foreign currency valuation (FAGL_FCV), GR/IR regrouping, internal order settlement |
| Day 3 | Cost allocations, intercompany reconciliation, balance sheet reconciliations |
| Day 4 | Review of trial balance, management pack, close the period in OB52 |

## Foreign currency valuation

**FAGL_FCV** revalues open items and balances in foreign currency at the period-end rate. It posts unrealised gains or losses and can reverse them on the first day of the next period. Exchange rates are maintained with rate type M in OB08 or loaded automatically.

## Intercompany reconciliation

Multinationals use the **Intercompany Matching and Reconciliation** apps to match receivables and payables across company codes before consolidation. Differences are usually timing, currency or missing invoices.

## Orchestrating the close

The **SAP S/4HANA Financial Closing cockpit** (or Advanced Financial Closing) lets you build a task list template with dependencies, owners and background jobs. Each close then becomes a task list instance, giving a full audit trail of who ran what, and when.

## Controls auditors expect

- Evidence of balance sheet reconciliations with sign-off
- Restricted access to OB52 and to posting in closed periods
- Review of manual journals above a threshold
- Segregation of duties between creating and approving vendors and payments

lessons.title: Fiori apps and finance reporting
lessons.content:
## The Fiori launchpad

SAP Fiori is the user experience layer of S/4HANA. Users open apps from tiles on the **Fiori launchpad**, grouped into spaces and pages assigned through business roles such as General Ledger Accountant or Accounts Payable Accountant.

There are three app types:

- **Transactional apps**: create or change data, such as Post General Journal Entries or Manage Supplier Line Items.
- **Analytical apps**: KPIs and drill-down on live data, such as Trial Balance or Journal Entry Analyzer.
- **Fact sheets**: a 360-degree view of an object, such as a supplier or fixed asset.

## Apps finance teams use every day

| Area | App |
| --- | --- |
| General ledger | Manage Journal Entries, Display Line Items in General Ledger, Trial Balance |
| Payables | Manage Supplier Line Items, Manage Automatic Payments |
| Receivables | Manage Customer Line Items, Process Receivables |
| Assets | Manage Fixed Assets, Asset Balances |
| Close | Manage Bank Statements, Financial Statement Versions |

## Classic transactions still work

Most SAP GUI transactions remain available and many are also exposed as Fiori tiles through SAP GUI for HTML. Consultants should be fluent in both, because support tickets often reference transaction codes.

## Finding the right app

The **SAP Fiori apps reference library** lists every app with its technical name, required business role and the release it belongs to. Use it during fit-to-standard workshops to show users the standard app before anyone suggests a custom report.

## Embedded analytics

Analytical apps run on **CDS views**, for example I_GLAccountLineItem. Key users can build their own queries with the Custom Analytical Queries app without writing code, which reduces demand for custom ABAP reports.

lessons.title: Working as a FICO consultant
lessons.content:
## How projects run: SAP Activate

Most S/4HANA projects follow **SAP Activate**, which has six phases: Discover, Prepare, Explore, Realise, Deploy and Run.

- **Explore** is where FICO consultants lead **fit-to-standard workshops**, demonstrating standard processes and recording gaps in a backlog.
- **Realise** delivers configuration in sprints, with unit testing and integration testing of end-to-end scenarios.
- **Deploy** covers data migration, user acceptance testing, cutover and go-live.

## Greenfield, brownfield and selective

| Approach | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Greenfield | New implementation with fresh configuration and data migration |
| Brownfield | System conversion of an existing ECC system to S/4HANA |
| Selective data transition | A mix, moving selected organisations or history |

Mainstream maintenance for SAP ECC 6.0 ends in 2027, which is why demand for S/4HANA finance consultants is strong across Europe, the Middle East and Asia.

## Documents you will write

- **Business process design** documents per process area
- **Functional specifications** for reports, interfaces, conversions, enhancements and forms (RICEF)
- **Test scripts** with expected postings
- **Cutover plans** with open item and balance migration steps

## Skills that set you apart

- Explaining postings in debit and credit terms to accountants, and in table and field terms to developers
- Reading an ABAP debugger trace well enough to find which user exit changed a field
- Clear written English for international teams spread across time zones
- Knowing local requirements: VAT returns, e-invoicing mandates and statutory reports in your target countries

lessons.title: Final assessment
lessons.content: This final assessment covers the whole course. You need 70 percent to earn your certificate.

questions.explanation: ACDOCA holds a single line item for financial accounting and controlling.

options.text: The AuC has not been settled to a final asset
OB52 is closed for special periods
The customer has no credit limit

questions.explanation: Assets under construction must be settled to final assets when ready for use so depreciation can begin.

courses.title: Salesforce administrator
courses.subtitle: Configure, secure and automate Salesforce so sales and service teams trust their CRM.
courses.description:
Salesforce is the most widely used CRM in the world, and every organisation that runs it needs administrators who can shape the platform to the business. This course covers the work an administrator does in the first year: the data model, security, automation with Flow, data quality, reports and release management.

Lessons follow the way a real org is built, from objects and fields to the sharing model and dashboards that leadership reviews every Monday. You will finish ready to work towards the Salesforce Certified Platform Administrator credential and to contribute to an admin team straight away.

**Who this is for**

- Sales and service operations staff who already use Salesforce
- Career changers looking for a first role in the Salesforce ecosystem
- Business analysts who need to configure CRM processes without code
outcomes: Design custom objects, fields and relationships that model a business process.
Configure the sharing model with organisation-wide defaults, roles, sharing rules and permission sets.
Automate processes with record-triggered and screen flows.
Protect data quality with validation rules, duplicate rules and controlled imports.
Build reports and dashboards that answer sales and service questions.
Manage changes safely with sandboxes, change sets and the three-release cycle.

lessons.title: Salesforce orgs, editions and Setup
lessons.content:
## What an org is

A Salesforce **org** is a single tenant's instance of the platform: its data, metadata, users and configuration. Most companies have one production org plus several sandboxes for building and testing.

## Editions

Features and limits depend on the edition. Enterprise Edition is the most common for mid-sized and large companies because it includes the full API, workflow automation and sandboxes. Unlimited Edition adds higher limits and more sandboxes, while Professional Edition suits smaller teams with lighter needs.

## Finding your way around Setup

Everything an administrator configures lives in **Setup**, opened from the gear icon. The most used areas are:

- **Object Manager**: objects, fields, page layouts, record types, validation rules
- **Users**: users, profiles, permission sets, roles
- **Process Automation**: Flows and approval processes
- **Security**: sharing settings, session settings, Health Check
- **Company Settings**: fiscal year, currencies, business hours

Use **Quick Find** at the top of Setup instead of browsing menus. Typing "sharing" takes you straight to Sharing Settings.

## Lightning Experience

Lightning Experience is the modern user interface. Admins use the **Lightning App Builder** to design record pages, home pages and app pages from standard and custom components. Dynamic Forms let you place fields directly on the page and show them conditionally, for example showing the Loss reason field only when Stage equals Closed Lost.

## Your weekly routine

- Review the **Setup Audit Trail** to see who changed what in the last 180 days.
- Check **System Overview** for limits on data storage, API calls and custom objects.
- Read the release notes for the next seasonal release well before it arrives in your sandboxes.

lessons.title: Objects, fields and relationships
lessons.content:
## Standard and custom objects

Salesforce stores data in **objects**, which behave like database tables. Standard objects include Account, Contact, Lead, Opportunity and Case. When the business needs something new, such as a Job Application or Course Enrolment, you create a **custom object**; its API name ends in __c, for example Job_Application__c.

## Field types

Choose the type carefully, because changing it later can lose data.

| Type | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Text, Text Area | Free text |
| Picklist, Multi-select picklist | Controlled values for reporting |
| Number, Currency, Percent | Calculations |
| Date, Date/Time | Deadlines and timestamps |
| Formula | Read-only calculated values |
| Roll-up summary | Count, sum, min or max of child records |
| Lookup, Master-detail | Relationships |

## Relationships

- **Lookup relationship**: a loose link. The child can exist without the parent, and each record keeps its own owner and sharing.
- **Master-detail relationship**: a tight link. The detail record has no owner of its own, inherits sharing from the master and is deleted with it. Only master-detail supports roll-up summary fields.
- **Many-to-many**: built with a **junction object** that has two master-detail relationships, for example Candidate and Job joined by Job Application.

## Schema Builder

Schema Builder shows objects and relationships as a diagram. Use it to explain the data model to stakeholders, but create fields through Object Manager so you can set help text, descriptions and field-level security properly.

## Naming habits that save time

- Write a description on every custom field explaining why it exists.
- Add help text that users see on hover.
- Avoid creating a field that duplicates a standard one; check the standard object first.

questions.explanation: Custom objects and fields end in __c. The __r suffix is used for relationship names in queries.

lessons.title: The sharing model: defaults, roles and sharing rules
lessons.content:
## Layers of access

Salesforce decides what a user can see in layers. Start restrictive, then open access where needed.

1. **Organisation-wide defaults (OWD)** set the baseline for each object: Private, Public Read Only or Public Read/Write.
2. **Role hierarchy** opens access upwards: managers see records owned by people below them.
3. **Sharing rules** open access sideways, based on record owner or criteria. For example, share all Opportunities in region EMEA with the EMEA Finance group, read only.
4. **Teams** (account teams and opportunity teams) and **manual sharing** give access record by record.
5. **Restriction rules** can narrow visibility for specific users, for example contractors seeing only active records.

## Object and field permissions

Record access is only half the picture. A user also needs **object permissions** (create, read, edit, delete) and **field-level security** to see a field. If a user cannot see a field, check field-level security before anything else.

## Designing the model

| Question | Typical answer |
| --- | --- |
| Should sales reps see each other's opportunities? | OWD Private, open with roles and rules |
| Should everyone see all accounts? | OWD Public Read Only |
| Who can see cases? | Service team via sharing rule by queue or record type |

## Testing access

Use **Login As** (when enabled by the user or by admin policy) to see the org through a user's eyes, and the **Sharing** button on a record to see why someone has access. Document the design in a simple matrix of profiles, permission sets, roles and objects so auditors and new admins can follow it.

lessons.title: Profiles, permission sets and permission set groups
lessons.content:
## Profiles

Every user has exactly one **profile**. Historically profiles held almost everything: object permissions, field permissions, app access, page layout assignments and login hours. That made them large and hard to maintain.

## Permission sets first

Salesforce now recommends a **permission-set-led** model. Keep profiles minimal, for example one Standard User profile per licence type, and grant real access through **permission sets**:

- A permission set adds permissions; it never removes them.
- A user can have many permission sets.
- **Permission set groups** bundle several sets for a persona, such as Sales Manager EMEA.
- **Muting permission sets** inside a group can remove specific permissions from that group only.

## A worked example

A recruiting operations team needs to manage job applications:

| Component | Grants |
| --- | --- |
| Profile: Minimum Access | Login, licence type |
| Permission set: Recruiting Core | Read and edit Job Application, Candidate |
| Permission set: Recruiting Reports | Create and customise reports |
| Group: Recruiter | Both sets above |

Assigning the Recruiter group to new joiners gives them everything in one step, and removing it on leaving is just as simple.

## Licences and security hygiene

- Check that each user has the right **user licence**, because licences are the main Salesforce cost.
- Enforce **multi-factor authentication**, which Salesforce requires for direct logins to its products.
- Freeze users who are leaving before deactivation if they own important records, then reassign ownership.
- Run **Health Check** to compare password, session and network settings with the Salesforce baseline.

lessons.title: Check your understanding: security
lessons.content: Confirm how Salesforce controls who sees what.

questions.prompt: Which setting defines the most restrictive baseline access to records of an object?
questions.explanation: Organisation-wide defaults set the baseline; the other mechanisms open access from there.

questions.prompt: A user can open a record but a field is missing. What should you check first?
questions.explanation: Field visibility is controlled by field-level security in profiles and permission sets.

questions.prompt: Which statement about permission sets is true?

options.text: A user can have only one
They remove permissions granted by the profile
They add permissions and a user can have many

lessons.title: Flow Builder: record-triggered and screen flows
lessons.content:
## Flow is the automation tool

Salesforce has retired Workflow Rules and Process Builder for new automation; **Flow** is the declarative tool for all of it. Flows are built in **Flow Builder** and come in several types:

- **Record-triggered flow**: runs when a record is created, updated or deleted.
- **Screen flow**: guides a user through screens, for example a returns wizard on a Case page.
- **Schedule-triggered flow**: runs at a set time for a batch of records.
- **Autolaunched flow**: called from other flows, Apex or the API.

## Before-save and after-save

Record-triggered flows can run **before save** (fast field updates on the same record, no extra DML) or **after save** (create related records, send emails, call subflows). Choose before-save when you only need to set fields on the triggering record.

## Example: create an onboarding task

When an Opportunity moves to Closed Won, create a Task for the account manager:

1. Trigger: Opportunity, when a record is updated, condition StageName equals Closed Won, only when the record is updated to meet the condition.
2. Optimise for: Actions and Related Records.
3. Element: Create Records, Task, with Subject "Plan onboarding call", WhatId = Opportunity Id and OwnerId = Opportunity Owner.

## Good flow habits

- One record-triggered flow per object and timing is easier to manage; use **entry conditions** to keep it fast.
- Never put Get Records or Create Records inside a loop; collect records in a collection variable and write once, to stay within governor limits.
- Add a **fault path** to elements that write data, and send the error to an admin.
- Test with the **Debug** button and with real users in a sandbox before activation.

lessons.title: Validation rules and formulas
lessons.content:
## Why validation rules matter

Validation rules stop bad data at the point of entry. A rule contains a formula that returns true when the data is **invalid**, and an error message shown to the user.

## Examples

Require a contract start date when an opportunity is won:

~~~text
AND(
  ISPICKVAL(StageName, "Closed Won"),
  ISBLANK(Contract_Start_Date__c)
)
~~~

Block discounts above 20 percent unless the user has a custom permission:

~~~text
AND(
  Discount__c > 0.20,
  NOT($Permission.Approve_Large_Discount)
)
~~~

Make sure a phone number for UK contacts follows E.164 format:

~~~text
AND(
  MailingCountry = "United Kingdom",
  NOT(ISBLANK(Phone)),
  NOT(REGEX(Phone, "\\+44[0-9]{9,10}"))
)
~~~

## Useful functions

| Function | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| ISPICKVAL | Compare a picklist value |
| ISCHANGED, PRIORVALUE | Detect edits |
| ISNEW | Only on creation |
| $User, $Profile, $Permission | Context about the current user |
| REGEX | Pattern matching |
| TEXT | Convert a picklist to text |

## Writing good error messages

State what is wrong and how to fix it, and show the message next to the relevant field: "Add a contract start date before closing this opportunity as won." Avoid messages such as "Invalid data", which generate support tickets.

## Bypass for integrations

Data migrations sometimes need to bypass rules. Use a custom permission assigned only to the integration user rather than switching rules off in production.

lessons.title: Imports, duplicates and data quality
lessons.content:
## Choosing an import tool

| Tool | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| Data Import Wizard | Up to 50,000 records for accounts, contacts, leads, campaign members and custom objects, run from Setup |
| Data Loader | Up to 5 million records, all objects, insert, update, upsert, delete and export |
| Integration tools and APIs | Ongoing feeds from ERP, HR or marketing systems |

## Prepare the file

- Use **external IDs** so updates and upserts match existing records reliably, for example an ERP customer number.
- Convert picklist values to the exact labels or API names used in the org.
- Format dates as YYYY-MM-DD and keep the file in UTF-8 so names such as Müller or Ødegaard survive.
- Run a small test batch of ten records in a sandbox first.

## Duplicate management

Salesforce uses two components:

- **Matching rules** define what counts as a duplicate, using exact or fuzzy matching on fields such as name, email and phone.
- **Duplicate rules** define what happens: block the save, or allow it with an alert and report on it.

Standard rules exist for accounts, contacts and leads. Duplicate record sets can be reviewed and merged by data stewards.

## Measuring data quality

Build a simple dashboard with:

- Percentage of contacts with an email address
- Accounts missing industry or country
- Opportunities past close date and still open

Share it with sales leadership monthly. Data quality improves fastest when owners can see their own gaps.

lessons.title: Leads, opportunities and the sales process
lessons.content:
## Lead to cash in Salesforce

- **Leads** are unqualified prospects. Web-to-lead forms, events and marketing tools create them.
- **Lead conversion** turns a qualified lead into an Account, a Contact and optionally an Opportunity.
- **Opportunities** track deals through stages to Closed Won or Closed Lost.

## Configuring the sales process

1. Define **opportunity stages** in the Stage picklist, each with a probability and forecast category.
2. Create a **sales process** that selects which stages apply, for example New Business and Renewal.
3. Assign each sales process to a **record type**, then give users access to record types through permission sets.
4. Add a **Path** component with guidance for success at each stage, such as "Confirm budget owner and timeline before moving to Proposal".

## Lead assignment and scoring

Lead assignment rules route leads by country, product or company size. Many international teams route by region: EMEA, APAC and Americas queues, with round-robin assignment handled in Flow.

## Products and price books

Opportunities can carry **products** priced from **price books**. With multiple currencies enabled, each price book entry has a price per active currency, so a deal for a German customer can be quoted in EUR while the corporate currency stays USD.

## Service basics

Cases track customer issues. Key features are **queues**, **assignment rules**, **escalation rules**, **entitlements** for service-level agreements and **email-to-case**. Omni-Channel routes work to agents based on capacity and skills.

lessons.title: Reports and dashboards
lessons.content:
## Report types

Every report is built on a **report type**, which defines the primary object and related objects. Standard report types cover common combinations; custom report types let you include, for example, Accounts with or without Opportunities.

## Report formats

| Format | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Tabular | Simple lists and exports |
| Summary | Grouped by rows with subtotals |
| Matrix | Grouped by rows and columns |
| Joined | Several report blocks side by side |

## Building useful reports

- Start with the question: "What is our pipeline by region and stage for this quarter?"
- Use **filters** with relative dates such as THIS FISCAL QUARTER so the report never goes stale.
- Add **summary formulas**, for example win rate as won count divided by closed count.
- Use **bucket fields** to group values without changing data, such as deal size bands.
- Use **row-level formulas** for simple per-record calculations such as days since last activity.

## Dashboards

Dashboards display up to 20 components from source reports. Each dashboard has a **running user**: either a fixed user, so everyone sees the same data, or the **dynamic** viewer, so each person sees their own data according to sharing.

## Making dashboards trusted

- Show a small number of measures that leaders discuss every week.
- Label every component with the time period.
- Subscribe stakeholders so dashboards arrive by email on Monday morning.
- Retire unused reports; the Reports tab has a "last run" column to help.

lessons.title: Sandboxes, change sets and release management
lessons.content:
## Never build in production

Changes are built and tested in **sandboxes**, which are copies of production metadata and, depending on type, data.

| Sandbox | Data | Typical use | Refresh interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Developer | Metadata only, small storage | Building and unit testing | 1 day |
| Developer Pro | Metadata only, more storage | Larger builds, integration tests | 1 day |
| Partial Copy | Metadata and a sample of data | User acceptance testing | 5 days |
| Full | Full copy of data | Performance tests, staging | 29 days |

## Moving changes

- **Change sets** move metadata between connected orgs. Create an outbound change set in the sandbox, upload it, then validate and deploy the inbound change set in production.
- **DevOps Center** and the **Salesforce CLI** add version control with Git for teams that want a proper pipeline. For example:

~~~bash
sf project retrieve start --metadata CustomObject:Job_Application__c --target-org uat
sf project deploy start --source-dir force-app --target-org production --test-level RunLocalTests
~~~

## Seasonal releases

Salesforce ships three major releases a year: **Spring, Summer and Winter**. Sandboxes on preview instances receive the release about a month before production. Use that window to run regression tests on critical flows and integrations.

## A release checklist

- Read release notes and the list of release updates with enforcement dates.
- Test critical processes in a preview sandbox.
- Communicate visible changes to users with screenshots.
- Record every production deployment in a change log.

lessons.content: This final assessment covers the whole course. You need 70 percent to earn your certificate.

courses.title: Product management professional
courses.subtitle: Discover the right problems, prioritise with evidence and ship outcomes with agile teams.
courses.description:
Product managers decide what a team builds and why. This course teaches the practical craft used by product teams at global technology companies and banks: continuous discovery, clear strategy, evidence-based prioritisation, agile delivery in Jira and the metrics that show whether a release mattered.

You will work through realistic artefacts such as opportunity solution trees, RICE scores, user stories with acceptance criteria, JQL filters and experiment designs. The final module covers stakeholder management across countries and time zones, which is where many product managers succeed or struggle.

**Who this is for**

- Business analysts, engineers and designers moving into product roles
- Associate product managers who want a structured foundation
- Founders and project managers who need product discipline
outcomes: Run discovery interviews and map opportunities before committing to solutions.
Write a product strategy linked to measurable objectives and key results.
Prioritise a backlog with RICE, Kano and cost of delay, and explain the trade-offs.
Write user stories with testable acceptance criteria and manage them in Jira.
Choose product metrics and design A/B tests that produce trustworthy decisions.
Manage stakeholders across functions and countries with clear communication.

lessons.title: What product managers own
lessons.content:
## Outcomes, not output

A product manager is accountable for **outcomes**: changes in customer behaviour that create business value. Output, such as features shipped, matters only when it moves an outcome. Marty Cagan summarises the job as managing four risks:

- **Value risk**: will customers buy or choose to use it?
- **Usability risk**: can users figure out how to use it?
- **Feasibility risk**: can engineers build it with the time, skills and technology available?
- **Business viability risk**: does it work for legal, finance, sales and the rest of the business?

## The product trio

Strong teams make decisions as a **trio**: product manager, product designer and tech lead. The product manager brings customer, market and business context; the designer owns the experience; the tech lead owns feasibility and architecture.

## What the role is not

| Common myth | Reality |
| --- | --- |
| The PM is the CEO of the product | The PM has little formal authority and leads through influence |
| The PM writes all the requirements | The trio shapes solutions together |
| The PM is a project manager | Delivery tracking is part of the job, not the job |

## Titles around the world

Titles vary: Product Owner is common in European enterprises using Scrum, Product Manager in US technology firms, and Product Lead or Group Product Manager for people managing other PMs. Read the job description rather than the title, and look for words such as discovery, metrics and roadmap ownership.

## A week in the life

- Two or three customer conversations
- Backlog refinement and sprint review with the team
- A metrics review of the last release
- A stakeholder update to sales, support and leadership

lessons.title: Discovery: problems before solutions
lessons.content:
## Continuous discovery

Teresa Torres describes **continuous discovery** as weekly touchpoints with customers by the team building the product. Small, regular conversations beat a big research project every six months.

## Interviewing well

- Ask about specific past behaviour: "Tell me about the last time you shortlisted a candidate for a role abroad."
- Avoid leading questions such as "Would you use a feature that…?" because people are poor predictors of their own future behaviour.
- Capture quotes, then summarise the **opportunity**: an unmet need, pain point or desire.

## The opportunity solution tree

The tree links a **desired outcome** at the top to the **opportunities** you discovered, then to candidate **solutions**, then to **assumption tests**.

~~~text
Outcome: increase completed applications per active candidate
├── Opportunity: candidates do not know which skills they lack
│   ├── Solution: skill gap summary on each job page
│   └── Solution: weekly gap digest by email
└── Opportunity: candidates abandon long forms
    └── Solution: one-click apply with saved profile
~~~

## Jobs to be done

Jobs-to-be-done framing asks what progress a customer is trying to make: "When I move to a new country, I want to prove my skills quickly so that employers take my application seriously." Framing needs as jobs helps teams see competitors they would otherwise miss, such as a recruiter's spreadsheet.

## Testing assumptions cheaply

Before building, test the riskiest assumption with the smallest possible experiment: a prototype test with five users, a fake door button that measures interest, or a concierge test where the team delivers the service by hand.

lessons.title: Check your understanding: role and discovery
lessons.content: Check your grasp of the product role and discovery techniques.

questions.prompt: Which risk asks whether customers will buy or choose to use the product?
questions.explanation: Value risk is about whether the product is worth it to customers.

questions.prompt: Which interview question produces the most reliable evidence?

options.text: Would you pay for this feature?
Do you like our new design?
Tell me about the last time you did this task.
How much would you use this every week?

questions.explanation: Questions about specific past behaviour give more reliable evidence than predictions or opinions.

questions.prompt: In an opportunity solution tree, what sits directly below the desired outcome?
questions.explanation: The outcome branches into opportunities; solutions and assumption tests sit below them.

lessons.title: Vision, strategy and OKRs
lessons.content:
## Three levels

- **Vision** describes the future you want to create, usually three to five years out: "Every skilled person can prove their skills and get hired anywhere."
- **Strategy** explains where you will play and how you will win: which customers, which problems, and what you will deliberately not do.
- **Roadmap** shows the sequence of problems the team will tackle, not a promise of dated features.

## Writing a strategy

Richard Rumelt's kernel of good strategy has three parts:

1. **Diagnosis**: what is going on and what is the critical challenge?
2. **Guiding policy**: the overall approach to the challenge.
3. **Coherent actions**: a small set of steps that reinforce each other.

## OKRs

Objectives and key results connect strategy to measurable outcomes.

~~~text
Objective: make international applicants ready faster
  KR1: median days from sign-up to first application falls from 21 to 10
  KR2: 40 percent of candidates with a skill gap start a recommended course
  KR3: application-to-interview rate for certified candidates reaches 18 percent
~~~

Good key results are **outcomes** you can measure, not tasks. "Launch skill gap page" is an initiative; the change in behaviour it causes is the key result.

## Outcome-based roadmaps

A popular format uses three columns: **Now, Next, Later**. Items are problems or opportunities, each linked to an objective. Dates appear only where there is a real external commitment, such as a regulatory deadline or a contract.

## Saying no

Every strategy implies trade-offs. Keep a visible "not now" list so stakeholders see their request was considered, and explain which objective it would compete with.

lessons.title: Prioritisation frameworks: RICE, Kano and cost of delay
lessons.content:
## RICE

RICE, created at Intercom, scores an initiative as:

~~~text
RICE score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort
~~~

- **Reach**: people affected per period, for example 4,000 candidates per quarter
- **Impact**: 3 massive, 2 high, 1 medium, 0.5 low, 0.25 minimal
- **Confidence**: 100, 80 or 50 percent
- **Effort**: person-months

| Initiative | Reach | Impact | Confidence | Effort | Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Skill gap summary | 4,000 | 2 | 80% | 2 | 3,200 |
| Saved searches | 2,500 | 1 | 100% | 1 | 2,500 |
| Video CV | 1,000 | 2 | 50% | 4 | 250 |

The score is a conversation starter, not an answer. Challenge inputs, especially confidence.

## Kano model

The Kano model groups features by how they affect satisfaction:

- **Basic** (must-be): expected; absence causes frustration, presence goes unnoticed. Secure login is an example.
- **Performance**: more is better, such as faster search.
- **Delighters**: unexpected features that create delight, such as automatic CV translation.

Delighters become basics over time, so revisit the classification yearly.

## Cost of delay and WSJF

**Cost of delay** asks how much value you lose each week an item is not delivered. Dividing cost of delay by duration gives **CD3** (cost of delay divided by duration). SAFe's **weighted shortest job first** (WSJF) uses a similar idea with relative scores. These methods favour small, valuable, time-critical items.

## Choosing a method

Use one method consistently for a quarter, combine it with judgement about strategy, and publish the reasoning so stakeholders understand the order.

lessons.content: Confirm you can link strategy, OKRs and prioritisation.

options.text: Increase weekly active recruiters from 1,200 to 1,800

questions.explanation: Key results measure outcomes; launching or hiring are initiatives or tasks.

options.text: The sequence of problems and opportunities

questions.explanation: Outcome-based roadmaps communicate order and intent without false date precision.

lessons.title: Scrum and Kanban in practice
lessons.content:
## Scrum in one page

The **Scrum Guide** (2020 edition) defines three accountabilities, five events and three artefacts.

| Accountabilities | Events | Artefacts and commitments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Product Owner | Sprint | Product backlog and product goal |
| Scrum Master | Sprint planning | Sprint backlog and sprint goal |
| Developers | Daily scrum | Increment and definition of done |
| | Sprint review | |
| | Sprint retrospective | |

Sprints last one month or less; two weeks is common. The product owner orders the backlog, and developers decide how much they can take into a sprint.

## Kanban

Kanban visualises work on a board, **limits work in progress (WIP)** and manages flow. There are no fixed sprints. Key measures are:

- **Cycle time**: from start to finish for an item
- **Throughput**: items finished per week
- **Work item age**: how long current items have been in progress

Kanban suits support and platform teams with unpredictable demand, while Scrum suits teams building towards a product goal.

## Backlog refinement

Refinement is an ongoing activity where the team clarifies, splits and estimates upcoming items. Aim to keep about two sprints of refined work ready. A widely used checklist is **INVEST**: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable.

## Estimation

Many teams use **story points** with planning poker, using a Fibonacci-like scale. Others count items and forecast with throughput, which avoids debates about point values. Whatever you choose, use it to forecast, never to compare teams.

lessons.title: User stories and acceptance criteria
lessons.content:
## The user story format

A user story describes a need from the user's point of view:

~~~text
As a candidate relocating to Germany,
I want to see which mandatory skills I am missing for a job,
so that I can close the gap before I apply.
~~~

The story is a placeholder for a conversation. Details live in **acceptance criteria**, designs and notes added during refinement.

## Acceptance criteria with Gherkin

Gherkin's Given–When–Then format makes criteria testable and easy to automate:

~~~text
Scenario: candidate lacks a mandatory skill
  Given a job requires "SAP FICO" at level 4
  And my profile shows "SAP FICO" at level 2
  When I open the job page
  Then I see "SAP FICO" listed as a mandatory gap
  And I see the course that closes the gap
  And the Apply now button is disabled

Scenario: candidate meets all mandatory skills
  Given my profile meets every mandatory skill
  When I open the job page
  Then the Apply now button is enabled
~~~

## Splitting large stories

Large stories, often called epics, should be split vertically so each slice delivers user value end to end. Useful patterns:

- By workflow step: search, then filter, then save
- By business rule: one country first, then all countries
- By data variation: one currency, then multiple currencies
- Simple case first, edge cases later

## Definition of ready and done

A **definition of done** is shared by the whole team: code reviewed, tests pass, accessibility checked, released behind a feature flag and analytics events firing. Some teams also use a lightweight definition of ready, but avoid turning it into a gate that slows collaboration.

lessons.title: Running Jira well
lessons.content:
## Structure

Jira organises work into **projects** containing **issues**. The common hierarchy is Epic, then Story, Task or Bug, then Sub-task. Teams choose a **Scrum** board with sprints or a **Kanban** board with continuous flow.

## Workflows

A workflow defines statuses and transitions, such as To Do, In Progress, In Review and Done. Keep workflows short. Every extra status creates handoffs and slows flow. Map each status to a status category (To Do, In Progress, Done) so reports stay meaningful.

## JQL: Jira Query Language

JQL lets you build precise filters for boards, dashboards and reports.

~~~sql
project = JOBS AND sprint in openSprints() AND statusCategory != Done ORDER BY priority DESC

project = JOBS AND type = Bug AND priority in (Highest, High) AND created >= -14d

project = JOBS AND "Epic Link" = JOBS-120 AND assignee is EMPTY

project = JOBS AND labels = gdpr AND resolution = Unresolved
~~~

In newer Jira Cloud projects, use parent = JOBS-120 instead of "Epic Link".

## Reports that help

- **Burndown chart**: remaining work in the sprint
- **Velocity chart**: completed work per sprint, used for forecasting
- **Cumulative flow diagram**: work in each status over time; widening bands reveal bottlenecks
- **Control chart**: cycle time distribution

## Hygiene rules

- Each issue has one owner and a clear summary starting with a verb: "Show skill gaps on job page".
- Close or archive stale issues every quarter.
- Link issues to the product goal or OKR so the backlog tells a story.

lessons.title: Product metrics: north star, funnels and retention
lessons.content:
## A north star metric

A **north star metric** captures the value customers get from your product and predicts long-term revenue. Examples:

| Product | North star |
| --- | --- |
| Job portal | Qualified applications submitted per week |
| Learning platform | Learners completing a course per week |
| Collaboration tool | Weekly active teams |

Support the north star with **input metrics** that teams can influence directly, such as profile completion rate or course start rate.

## Funnels

A funnel tracks conversion between steps:

~~~text
Visited job page      10,000
Clicked Apply now      2,400   (24%)
Completed form         1,500   (62.5% of clicks)
Submitted              1,350   (90% of forms)
~~~

Find the biggest drop and investigate with session recordings, interviews and segment analysis, for example by country or device.

## Retention

Retention is the strongest signal of product value. Use **cohort analysis**: group users by sign-up week and track the share active in later weeks. A curve that flattens shows a core of retained users; a curve that keeps falling shows weak product–market fit.

## Frameworks to structure metrics

- **AARRR** (pirate metrics): acquisition, activation, retention, referral, revenue.
- **HEART** from Google: happiness, engagement, adoption, retention, task success, each with goals, signals and metrics.

## Guardrail metrics

Every change can harm something else. Define guardrails such as page load time, unsubscribe rate or support contacts, and check them alongside the primary metric.

lessons.title: Experiments and A/B testing
lessons.content:
## Why experiment

An A/B test randomly splits users between a control and a variant, so differences in outcomes can be attributed to the change rather than to seasonality or marketing campaigns.

## Designing a test

1. **Hypothesis**: "Showing skill gaps on the job page will increase course starts among candidates with gaps, because they will see a clear next step."
2. **Primary metric**: course starts per candidate with a gap.
3. **Guardrails**: application rate and page load time.
4. **Minimum detectable effect** and **sample size**: decide the smallest lift worth detecting, then calculate the sample needed for 80 percent power at a 5 percent significance level.
5. **Duration**: run for whole weeks to cover weekday patterns, and do not stop early because the result looks good.

## Reading results

- The **p-value** is the probability of seeing a difference at least this large if there were truly no effect. A p-value below 0.05 is the usual threshold, not proof.
- Report the **confidence interval** of the effect, for example +3.1 percent (95 percent CI +0.8 to +5.4).
- Beware **peeking** and testing many metrics at once; both increase false positives.
- Check for **sample ratio mismatch**: if a 50/50 test shows 52/48, the assignment may be broken.

## When not to A/B test

Low-traffic B2B products, legal changes and major strategic bets often cannot be tested cleanly. Use qualitative research, staged rollouts with feature flags and before-and-after analysis with care.

lessons.title: Stakeholder management across countries
lessons.content:
## Map your stakeholders

Use a **power–interest grid** to plan engagement:

| | Low interest | High interest |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **High power** | Keep satisfied | Manage closely |
| **Low power** | Monitor | Keep informed |

A regional sales director with strong views on your roadmap is "manage closely". A finance controller who needs only release dates is "keep informed".

## Communication rhythm

- **Weekly**: short written update with progress on outcomes, decisions needed and risks.
- **Monthly**: roadmap review with sales, support and marketing.
- **Quarterly**: OKR planning and retrospective with leadership.

Write updates so they make sense to someone reading on a phone in another time zone: lead with the decision or result, then details.

## Working across cultures

Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map* shows that countries differ in how they give feedback, make decisions and build trust. Teams in Germany or the Netherlands may expect direct negative feedback, while colleagues in Japan or India may signal disagreement indirectly. Decision-making may be consensual (Sweden, Japan) or top-down (many US and Gulf organisations).

Practical habits:

- Rotate meeting times so the same region is not always on a late call.
- Send pre-reads 24 hours ahead so non-native speakers can prepare.
- Confirm decisions in writing after every meeting.

## Handling conflicting requests

Bring conflicting stakeholders together with the data: the objective, the options and the trade-offs. Ask them to agree the criteria first, then the choice. When you cannot agree, escalate early with a clear recommendation.

courses.description:
Performance marketing is accountable marketing: every pound, euro or rupee spent should be traceable to a result. This course teaches the full loop used by in-house growth teams and agencies, from unit economics and tracking through Google Ads, Meta Ads and SEO to attribution and reporting.

You will learn the platforms as they work today, including Google Analytics 4, Performance Max, Advantage+ campaigns, the Conversions API and consent requirements in the European Economic Area. Each lesson focuses on decisions you will make in a real account.

**Who this is for**

- Marketing executives moving into paid media or growth roles
- Founders and small business owners running their own campaigns
- Analysts who want to understand how marketing data is generated
outcomes: Calculate CAC, ROAS, CPA and customer lifetime value, and set targets from unit economics.
Set up GA4 events, UTM conventions and consent-aware tracking.
Build Google Search and Performance Max campaigns with the right bidding strategy.
Structure Meta campaigns, audiences and creative tests that scale.
Improve organic visibility with technical, on-page and international SEO.
Report results with sensible attribution and clear recommendations.

lessons.title: The funnel and unit economics
lessons.content:
## Start with the numbers that pay the bills

Before opening an ad account, agree how much you can afford to pay for a customer. Four measures do most of the work:

| Measure | Formula |
| --- | --- |
| Cost per acquisition (CPA) | Spend ÷ conversions |
| Return on ad spend (ROAS) | Revenue from ads ÷ ad spend |
| Customer acquisition cost (CAC) | All sales and marketing cost ÷ new customers |
| Customer lifetime value (LTV) | Average order value × purchase frequency × lifetime × gross margin |

## A worked example

A subscription course platform sells at USD 40 per month with an 80 percent gross margin, and customers stay seven months on average.

~~~text
LTV = 40 × 0.80 × 7 = 224 USD
Target LTV:CAC ratio = 3:1
Maximum CAC ≈ 224 ÷ 3 ≈ 75 USD
~~~

If paid media is about 70 percent of total acquisition cost, your target paid CPA is roughly USD 52.

## Break-even ROAS

For e-commerce, break-even ROAS equals 1 ÷ gross margin. With a 40 percent margin, break-even ROAS is 2.5. A campaign at ROAS 2.0 loses money on the first order, though it may still be profitable if customers buy again.

## The funnel

Map campaigns to stages:

- **Awareness**: video, display, reach campaigns. Measure reach and cost per thousand impressions (CPM).
- **Consideration**: search, retargeting, content. Measure click-through rate (CTR) and cost per click (CPC).
- **Conversion**: high-intent search, shopping, retargeting. Measure CPA and ROAS.

## Incrementality

The real question is not "who clicked an ad" but "who bought **because** of the ad". Keep this in mind when brand search campaigns report high ROAS: many of those buyers would have arrived anyway.

lessons.title: Tracking with UTMs, GA4 and consent
lessons.content:
## UTM parameters

UTM parameters tell analytics where a visit came from. Agree a naming convention and keep it in a shared sheet.

~~~text
https://example.com/courses/sap?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=paid_social&utm_campaign=2026q4_sap_uae&utm_content=carousel_v2
~~~

- Use lower case only, because GA4 treats "LinkedIn" and "linkedin" as different values.
- Google Ads auto-tagging (gclid) should stay on; do not add manual UTMs that conflict.

## Google Analytics 4

GA4 is **event-based**. Every interaction is an event with parameters. Recommended events include page_view, sign_up, generate_lead, begin_checkout and purchase. Mark the events that matter as **key events** and import them into Google Ads as conversions.

With Google Tag Manager, a purchase event sent from the data layer looks like this:

~~~tsx
window.dataLayer = window.dataLayer || [];
window.dataLayer.push({
  event: "purchase",
  ecommerce: {
    transaction_id: "T-10482",
    value: 149.0,
    currency: "USD",
    items: [{ item_id: "german-a1-b1", item_name: "German for professionals", price: 149.0 }],
  },
});
~~~

## Consent

Under the GDPR and the ePrivacy rules, users in the EEA and the UK must consent before non-essential cookies are set. Google requires **Consent Mode v2** for advertisers using EEA data, with the signals ad_storage, analytics_storage, ad_user_data and ad_personalization. A certified consent management platform passes these signals to Google tags.

## Server-side and first-party data

Browser restrictions and ad blockers reduce tracked conversions. **Server-side tagging**, **enhanced conversions** in Google Ads and the **Conversions API** for Meta send hashed first-party data from your server, improving match rates while respecting consent.
