lessons.title: Search campaigns, keywords and Quality Score
lessons.content:
## Account structure

A Google Ads account contains **campaigns** (budget, bidding, location, language), **ad groups** (themed sets of keywords) and **ads**. Keep ad groups tightly themed so ads match the search.

## Match types

| Match type | Syntax | Matches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broad | sap course | Related searches, guided by signals |
| Phrase | "sap course" | Searches that include the meaning of the phrase |
| Exact | [sap fico course] | Searches with the same meaning |

Broad match works best with smart bidding and strong conversion data. Use **negative keywords** to exclude irrelevant searches, such as "free", "jobs" or "download" for a paid course.

## Responsive search ads

Responsive search ads take up to **15 headlines** (30 characters each) and **4 descriptions** (90 characters each). Google combines them per search. Write headlines that cover the keyword, the benefit, proof and the call to action, and pin only when legally required.

## Quality Score

Quality Score (1 to 10) is a keyword-level diagnostic based on:

- **Expected click-through rate**
- **Ad relevance**
- **Landing page experience**

Higher quality lowers cost per click because ad rank combines your bid with quality and expected impact of assets.

## The search terms report

Review the **search terms report** weekly. Add winning terms as keywords and irrelevant ones as negatives. In international accounts, check for wrong-language searches when targeting multilingual countries such as Switzerland, Belgium or the UAE.

## Location settings

Choose "Presence: people in or regularly in your targeted locations" for local services. The default "presence or interest" can spend budget on people elsewhere who merely search about a place.

lessons.title: Performance Max and bidding strategies
lessons.content:
## Smart bidding

Google's automated bidding sets a bid for every auction using signals such as device, location, time, audience and query.

| Strategy | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| Maximise clicks | New account, building traffic |
| Maximise conversions | Enough budget, want volume |
| Target CPA | You know an acceptable cost per conversion |
| Maximise conversion value | You track revenue |
| Target ROAS | You have reliable revenue data and a return target |

Give smart bidding enough data: a useful rule of thumb is at least 30 conversions in 30 days per campaign. After changing a target, allow a **learning period** of one to two weeks before judging.

## Performance Max

Performance Max (PMax) runs one campaign across Search, Shopping, YouTube, Display, Discover, Gmail and Maps. You supply:

- **Asset groups**: headlines, descriptions, images, logos and videos
- **Audience signals**: customer lists, website visitors and custom segments that guide the system
- **Conversion goals** and a budget

PMax is strong for e-commerce with a product feed in Google Merchant Center. For lead generation, feed back offline conversion data, such as qualified leads from your CRM, so the system optimises for quality rather than form fills.

## Keeping control

- Add **account-level negative keywords** and brand exclusions where appropriate.
- Use the **insights** and **channel performance** reports to see where spend goes.
- Run a separate brand search campaign so PMax does not take credit for brand demand.

## Budget pacing

Google can spend up to twice the average daily budget on a given day, but no more than the daily budget multiplied by about 30.4 over a month. Watch pacing at month end when budgets are fixed.

lessons.title: Campaign structure, objectives and audiences
lessons.content:
## Three levels

Meta Ads Manager has three levels:

1. **Campaign**: the objective and, optionally, Advantage campaign budget.
2. **Ad set**: audience, placements, schedule, optimisation event and budget if not set at campaign level.
3. **Ad**: creative, copy, call to action and tracking.

## Objectives

Meta simplified objectives to six: **Awareness, Traffic, Engagement, Leads, App promotion and Sales**. Choose the objective that matches the business result. If you want course purchases, use Sales with the Purchase event, not Traffic.

## Audiences

- **Broad targeting**: country, age and language only, letting the algorithm find buyers. This often works best with strong creative and good conversion data.
- **Custom audiences**: website visitors from the Meta Pixel, customer lists, video viewers, lead form openers.
- **Lookalike audiences**: people similar to a seed audience, from 1 percent (closest) to 10 percent of a country's population.
- **Advantage+ audience**: you provide suggestions and Meta can expand beyond them when it predicts better results.

## Advantage+ sales campaigns

Advantage+ sales campaigns (formerly Advantage+ shopping) automate audience and placement choices for sales objectives. They need a healthy volume of purchase events and a range of creatives.

## Placements

Advantage+ placements let Meta deliver across Facebook, Instagram, Messenger, Audience Network and Threads. Manual placements are useful for brand safety or when a creative only suits one format, such as 9:16 Reels.

## Special ad categories

Ads about **employment**, housing, credit and social issues must declare a special ad category. Targeting options are restricted to prevent discrimination, so a job advert cannot target by age or gender. Recruitment marketers must plan for this from the start.

lessons.title: Creative testing and the Conversions API
lessons.content:
## Creative is the targeting

On Meta, the creative decides who stops scrolling. Strong performance accounts test creative constantly.

A practical testing framework:

- Test **concepts** first (different messages or angles), then **formats** (static, carousel, video, Reels), then **iterations** (hooks, headlines, colours).
- Use **A/B test** in Ads Manager when you need a clean, statistically valid comparison.
- Judge on the optimisation event, such as cost per purchase, not on likes.

## Creative checklist

| Element | Guideline |
| --- | --- |
| Hook | Show the outcome in the first two seconds |
| Format | 9:16 for Stories and Reels, 4:5 for feed |
| Text | Keep key text inside safe zones |
| Captions | Always add captions; most video is watched muted |
| Proof | Reviews, results, recognisable employer logos used with permission |

## Creative fatigue

Rising frequency, falling CTR and rising CPA together signal fatigue. Refresh creative before performance drops sharply, and keep a pipeline of new concepts.

## The Conversions API

The **Meta Pixel** tracks events in the browser; the **Conversions API (CAPI)** sends the same events from your server. Use both, with the same **event_id** so Meta deduplicates them.

~~~python
import hashlib, time, requests

email_hash = hashlib.sha256("ana@example.com".strip().lower().encode()).hexdigest()
payload = {"data": [{
    "event_name": "Purchase",
    "event_time": int(time.time()),
    "event_id": "order-10482",
    "action_source": "website",
    "user_data": {"em": [email_hash]},
    "custom_data": {"currency": "EUR", "value": 149.00},
}]}
requests.post(f"https://graph.facebook.com/v21.0/{PIXEL_ID}/events",
              params={"access_token": TOKEN}, json=payload, timeout=10)
~~~

Check the **Event Match Quality** score in Events Manager and send only data covered by consent.

lessons.title: Technical, on-page and international SEO
lessons.content:
## How search engines work

Search engines **crawl** pages, **index** them and **rank** them for queries. SEO removes obstacles at each stage and makes your pages the best answer.

## Technical SEO checklist

- A clean **XML sitemap** submitted in Google Search Console
- A **robots.txt** that does not block important sections
- One **canonical URL** per page to avoid duplicate content
- Fast pages that pass **Core Web Vitals**:

| Metric | Measures | Good threshold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) | Loading | 2.5 seconds or less |
| Interaction to Next Paint (INP) | Responsiveness | 200 milliseconds or less |
| Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) | Visual stability | 0.1 or less |

- Structured data where relevant, for example JobPosting or Course schema in JSON-LD

## On-page SEO

- Match **search intent**: informational, navigational, commercial or transactional.
- Use one clear H1 and descriptive H2s.
- Write a unique **title tag** (around 50 to 60 characters) and meta description.
- Link internally from strong pages to new ones with descriptive anchor text.
- Demonstrate experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust (**E-E-A-T**): named authors, sources and up-to-date facts.

## International SEO

Use **hreflang** to tell search engines which language and region each page targets:

~~~text
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en-gb" href="https://example.com/uk/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="de-de" href="https://example.com/de/" />
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="x-default" href="https://example.com/" />
~~~

Every page in the set must reference all the others, including itself. Translate properly rather than machine-translate key landing pages, and research keywords in each market; Germans search for "Weiterbildung", not a translation of your English keyword.

lessons.title: Attribution, incrementality and reporting
lessons.content:
## Attribution models

Attribution assigns credit for a conversion to touchpoints.

| Model | How credit is assigned |
| --- | --- |
| Last click | All credit to the final click |
| Data-driven | Credit shared by machine learning based on observed paths |
| Platform self-reported | Each ad platform claims conversions within its own window |

GA4 and Google Ads now use **data-driven attribution** as the default; most rule-based models such as linear and time decay were removed in 2023. Platforms each claim conversions within their own windows, so the totals across Google, Meta and LinkedIn usually exceed real sales.

## Measuring incrementality

- **Conversion lift studies** on Meta and Google compare exposed and holdout groups.
- **Geo experiments** switch spend off in matched regions to measure the drop.
- **Marketing mix modelling (MMM)** estimates channel impact from aggregated data over time; open-source tools such as Meridian and Robyn make it accessible.

## Querying the GA4 BigQuery export

The free GA4 export to BigQuery allows custom analysis:

~~~sql
SELECT
  traffic_source.source AS source,
  traffic_source.medium AS medium,
  COUNTIF(event_name = 'purchase') AS purchases,
  SUM(IF(event_name = 'purchase', ecommerce.purchase_revenue, 0)) AS revenue
FROM `analytics_123456.events_*`
WHERE _TABLE_SUFFIX BETWEEN '20260901' AND '20260930'
GROUP BY source, medium
ORDER BY revenue DESC;
~~~

## A weekly report that gets read

1. One line on performance against target: spend, CPA or ROAS, conversions.
2. What changed and why.
3. What you will do next week, with expected impact.

Leaders want decisions, not screenshots of dashboards.

courses.title: Financial modelling and IFRS reporting
courses.subtitle: Build three-statement models, apply key IFRS standards and turn forecasts into valuation and decisions.
courses.description:
Financial modelling and IFRS are the two languages of corporate finance in most of the world. This course teaches both together: how to build a clean, auditable three-statement model in Excel, and how the main IFRS standards change the numbers that go into it.

You will apply modelling standards used by banks and Big Four firms, practise the Excel functions that analysts rely on, and work through IFRS 15 revenue, IFRS 16 leases and IFRS 9 expected credit losses with numerical examples. The course closes with discounted cash flow valuation, budgeting and scenario analysis.

**Who this is for**

- Finance analysts, FP&A professionals and accountants preparing for international roles
- ACCA, CIMA and CFA candidates who want applied practice
- Consultants and founders who build business cases
outcomes: Structure a financial model with separate inputs, calculations and outputs that others can audit.
Use XLOOKUP, SUMIFS, INDEX, EOMONTH, XNPV and XIRR confidently in models.
Build a linked income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement that balances.
Apply IFRS 15, IFRS 16 and IFRS 9 to forecast figures correctly.
Value a business with a discounted cash flow model, WACC and terminal value.
Prepare budgets, rolling forecasts and scenario analysis for management.

lessons.title: Model structure and best practice
lessons.content:
## Why structure matters

A model is a decision tool. If reviewers cannot follow it, they will not trust it. Errors in spreadsheets are common, and most come from poor layout rather than poor maths.

## Separate inputs, calculations and outputs

- **Inputs**: assumptions such as growth rates, prices, FX rates and tax rates, held in one place and clearly formatted.
- **Calculations**: the engine, built in consistent time-based blocks.
- **Outputs**: financial statements, charts and key metrics for decision-makers.

## Conventions used by professional modellers

The **FAST Standard** (flexible, appropriate, structured, transparent) and similar bank standards share common rules:

| Rule | Example |
| --- | --- |
| One formula per row | The same formula runs across all periods |
| Consistent timeline | Months or years in the same columns on every sheet |
| Colour coding | Blue font for hard-coded inputs, black for formulas, green for links to other sheets |
| No hard-coded numbers in formulas | Write =Revenue × Tax_Rate, not =Revenue × 0.25 |
| Short formulas | Split long formulas into helper rows |
| Flags for timing | 1 or 0 flags for operating periods, construction, debt repayment |

## Checks

Build a **checks** sheet that turns red when something is wrong:

- Balance sheet balances (assets minus liabilities minus equity equals zero)
- Cash in the cash flow statement equals cash on the balance sheet
- Sources equal uses in a transaction model

Sum all checks into one master check shown on every sheet.

## Version control

Name files with a date and version, such as Model_v12_2026-10-20.xlsx, keep a change log sheet and lock input cells with sheet protection before sending the model to others.

lessons.title: Excel functions modellers use
lessons.content:
## Lookups

**XLOOKUP** replaces VLOOKUP and HLOOKUP. It searches any direction and returns a value or a whole row.

~~~text
=XLOOKUP(B5, Rates[Currency], Rates[USD_rate], "Missing")
~~~

**INDEX with MATCH** still appears in older models and works in every Excel version:

~~~text
=INDEX(Rates[USD_rate], MATCH(B5, Rates[Currency], 0))
~~~

## Conditional sums

**SUMIFS** aggregates by several criteria, for example revenue for one region in one year:

~~~text
=SUMIFS(Data[Revenue], Data[Region], "EMEA", Data[Year], 2027)
~~~

## Dates

- **EOMONTH(start, n)** returns the last day of the month n months later, ideal for monthly timelines.
- **EDATE(start, n)** shifts a date by n months.
- **YEARFRAC** measures part-year periods for interest and depreciation.

## Valuation functions

- **NPV(rate, values)** assumes cash flows at the end of each equal period.
- **XNPV(rate, values, dates)** uses actual dates, which is more accurate for irregular flows.
- **XIRR(values, dates)** returns the internal rate of return for dated cash flows.
- **PMT(rate, nper, pv)** calculates a loan or lease payment.

## Modern Excel

- **LET** names intermediate values inside a formula, making it readable.
- **Dynamic arrays** such as FILTER, UNIQUE and SORT spill results into neighbouring cells.

~~~text
=LET(rev, C10, cogs, C11, gm, (rev - cogs) / rev, IF(rev = 0, 0, gm))
~~~

## What to avoid

- OFFSET and INDIRECT, which are volatile and hard to audit
- Merged cells in calculation areas
- Circular references, except a deliberate, switchable interest circularity

lessons.title: Building the income statement and balance sheet
lessons.content:
## Revenue drivers

Forecast revenue from drivers rather than a single growth rate:

~~~text
Subscription revenue = (opening subscribers + new subscribers − churned subscribers)
                       × average monthly price × months
Project revenue      = billable consultants × utilisation × hours × day rate
~~~

Drivers let management test what actually moves the business.

## Costs

- **Cost of sales**: variable with volume, often as a percentage of revenue or cost per unit.
- **Operating expenses**: headcount × fully loaded cost, plus fixed costs such as rent and software.
- **Depreciation and amortisation**: from a fixed asset schedule.

## Supporting schedules

The balance sheet is built from schedules, each following the same **corkscrew** pattern:

| Line | Fixed asset schedule |
| --- | --- |
| Opening balance | Prior period closing |
| Plus additions | Capital expenditure forecast |
| Less depreciation | From useful life assumptions |
| Less disposals | Net book value of assets sold |
| Closing balance | Feeds the balance sheet |

Use the same pattern for debt, equity, provisions and retained earnings.

## Working capital

Forecast working capital with day ratios:

~~~text
Trade receivables = revenue × DSO ÷ 365
Inventory         = cost of sales × DIO ÷ 365
Trade payables    = cost of sales × DPO ÷ 365
~~~

A business with 60 days DSO and 30 days DPO needs cash to fund growth even when it is profitable.

## Tax

Calculate income tax on profit before tax, using the statutory rate of each jurisdiction. Track losses carried forward separately. For groups, remember global minimum tax (Pillar Two) at 15 percent for groups with revenue of at least EUR 750 million.

lessons.title: The cash flow statement and balancing the model
lessons.content:
## Indirect method

IAS 7 allows the direct or indirect method for operating cash flows. Models usually use the **indirect method**, starting from profit:

~~~text
Profit after tax
+ depreciation and amortisation
+/− changes in working capital (increase in receivables is an outflow)
+/− non-cash items such as provisions
= Cash flow from operating activities
− capital expenditure
+ proceeds from disposals
= Cash flow from investing activities
+ debt drawdowns − repayments − dividends + equity issued
= Cash flow from financing activities
~~~

Net cash flow plus opening cash equals closing cash, which links to the balance sheet.

## Why models do not balance

If the balance sheet check fails, look for these common causes:

- A balance sheet item changes but its movement is missing from the cash flow statement.
- A sign error in a working capital movement.
- Profit not linked to retained earnings.
- An item in the cash flow statement with no matching balance sheet line.

Find the first period where the imbalance appears and compare the difference with individual movements in that period.

## Interest and circularity

Interest depends on average debt, which depends on cash, which depends on interest. This creates a **circular reference**. Options:

- Calculate interest on **opening** balances to avoid circularity.
- Use average balances with iterative calculation enabled, plus a **circuit breaker** switch that sets interest to zero if the model breaks.

## Revolving credit facility

A revolver draws automatically when cash would fall below a minimum balance and repays when cash is available:

~~~text
Revolver draw/(repay) = MAX(−opening revolver, minimum cash − cash before revolver)
~~~

This keeps the model solvent and shows management the funding need.

lessons.title: Check your understanding: three statements
lessons.content: Confirm how the three statements link together.

In the indirect method, an increase in trade receivables is treated as…
questions.explanation: When receivables rise, revenue has been booked but cash has not yet been received, so it reduces operating cash flow.

questions.prompt: Which approach avoids circular interest calculations?
questions.explanation: Interest on opening balances does not depend on the current period's cash, so no circularity arises.

options.text: Find the first period where the difference appears

questions.explanation: Isolating the first period with an imbalance narrows the search to that period's movements.

lessons.title: IFRS 15: revenue from contracts with customers
lessons.content:
## The five-step model

IFRS 15 sets out five steps for recognising revenue:

1. **Identify the contract** with a customer.
2. **Identify the performance obligations**: distinct goods or services promised.
3. **Determine the transaction price**, including variable consideration such as discounts, rebates and penalties, constrained so that a significant reversal is highly unlikely.
4. **Allocate the transaction price** to obligations based on relative **standalone selling prices**.
5. **Recognise revenue** when, or as, each obligation is satisfied: at a point in time or over time.

## A worked example

A software company signs a 12-month contract for USD 120,000 covering a licence, implementation and support.

| Obligation | Standalone price | Allocation | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Software licence (right to use) | 60,000 | 51,429 | Point in time, at go-live |
| Implementation | 40,000 | 34,286 | Over time, by progress |
| Support for 12 months | 40,000 | 34,285 | Over time, evenly |
| **Total** | **140,000** | **120,000** | |

The discount of 20,000 is allocated proportionally (120,000 ÷ 140,000 ≈ 85.7 percent of each standalone price).

## Over time or point in time

Revenue is recognised over time if any of these is true: the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefit; the work enhances an asset the customer controls; or the asset has no alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for work to date.

## Contract balances

- **Contract asset**: revenue recognised before the right to invoice is unconditional.
- **Contract liability** (deferred revenue): cash received or due before revenue is recognised.

## Modelling tip

Forecast billings and revenue separately and let the contract liability balance absorb the difference. That keeps cash flow realistic for annual-in-advance subscriptions.

lessons.title: IFRS 16 leases
lessons.content:
## One model for lessees

Under IFRS 16, a lessee recognises almost every lease on the balance sheet:

- A **right-of-use (ROU) asset**
- A **lease liability** equal to the present value of lease payments

Two optional exemptions apply: **short-term leases** of 12 months or less, and leases of **low-value assets**, such as laptops (the IASB had in mind assets worth around USD 5,000 or less when new).

## Measuring the liability

Discount payments at the **interest rate implicit in the lease** or, if that is not readily determinable, the lessee's **incremental borrowing rate**.

Example: five annual payments of 100,000 in arrears at 6 percent.

~~~text
Lease liability = 100,000 × (1 − 1.06^−5) ÷ 0.06 = 421,236
Year 1 interest = 421,236 × 6% = 25,274
Year 1 closing liability = 421,236 + 25,274 − 100,000 = 346,510
ROU depreciation (straight line) = 421,236 ÷ 5 = 84,247
~~~

In Excel: =PV(6%, 5, -100000) returns 421,236.

## Effect on the statements

| Item | Before IFRS 16 (operating lease) | After IFRS 16 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Income statement | Rent expense in operating costs | Depreciation plus interest |
| EBITDA | Lower | Higher |
| Net debt | Lower | Higher, includes lease liabilities |
| Operating cash flow | Lower | Higher; principal repayments move to financing |

## Why modellers care

Lenders, analysts and acquirers adjust EBITDA and net debt for leases. When comparing companies, make sure all figures are on the same basis. US GAAP (ASC 842) still classifies leases as operating or finance for lessees, so US peers can look different.

lessons.title: IFRS 9 expected credit losses
lessons.content:
## From incurred to expected loss

IFRS 9 requires entities to recognise **expected credit losses (ECL)** on financial assets measured at amortised cost, such as trade receivables, loans and contract assets. Losses are provided for before a default happens.

## The general approach: three stages

| Stage | Condition | Loss allowance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | No significant increase in credit risk since initial recognition | 12-month ECL |
| Stage 2 | Significant increase in credit risk | Lifetime ECL |
| Stage 3 | Credit-impaired | Lifetime ECL; interest on net carrying amount |

Banks use the general approach with models for probability of default (PD), loss given default (LGD) and exposure at default (EAD):

~~~text
ECL = PD × LGD × EAD (discounted, weighted across scenarios)
~~~

## The simplified approach for trade receivables

Most corporates use the **simplified approach** for trade receivables without a significant financing component: always recognise lifetime ECL, often with a **provision matrix**.

| Ageing bucket | Balance | Loss rate | ECL |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Current | 800,000 | 0.5% | 4,000 |
| 1–30 days overdue | 150,000 | 2% | 3,000 |
| 31–90 days overdue | 40,000 | 10% | 4,000 |
| Over 90 days | 10,000 | 50% | 5,000 |
| **Total** | **1,000,000** | | **16,000** |

Loss rates come from historical data, adjusted for **forward-looking information** such as an economic slowdown in a key market.

## In the model

Forecast the allowance as a percentage of receivables by bucket, and show the movement as an impairment expense in operating costs.

lessons.title: DCF valuation: free cash flow, WACC and terminal value
lessons.content:
## Free cash flow to the firm

~~~text
FCFF = EBIT × (1 − tax rate)
     + depreciation and amortisation
     − capital expenditure
     − increase in net working capital
~~~

Forecast FCFF for an explicit period, usually five to ten years, until the business reaches a steady state.

## Weighted average cost of capital

~~~text
WACC = E/(D+E) × Ke + D/(D+E) × Kd × (1 − t)
Ke   = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium (+ country risk premium)
~~~

Use market values for debt and equity, a long-dated government bond yield in the cash flow currency for the risk-free rate, and an unlevered beta from peers relevered at the target capital structure. For emerging markets, add a **country risk premium** or use the cash flow currency consistently.

## Terminal value

Two methods:

- **Gordon growth**: TV = FCFF(n+1) ÷ (WACC − g), with g at or below long-run nominal GDP growth.
- **Exit multiple**: TV = EBITDA in final year × peer EV/EBITDA multiple.

Terminal value often represents 60 to 80 percent of enterprise value, so test it carefully.

## From enterprise value to equity value

~~~text
Equity value = enterprise value
             − net debt (including lease liabilities if EBITDA is post-IFRS 16)
             − minority interests
             + non-operating assets
Value per share = equity value ÷ diluted shares
~~~

## Sensitivity tables

Present value across a grid of WACC and terminal growth using Excel's **Data Table** feature (What-If Analysis). A table spanning WACC of 8 to 11 percent and growth of 1.5 to 3 percent shows how much the conclusion depends on two assumptions.

## Sense checks

Compare the implied EV/EBITDA multiple with peers and recent transactions. If the DCF implies 25 times EBITDA in a sector trading at 9 times, revisit the assumptions.

lessons.title: Budgeting, forecasting and scenario analysis
lessons.content:
## Budget versus forecast

- The **budget** is the annual plan approved by the board. It sets targets and resource allocations.
- A **forecast** is the current best estimate of the outcome, updated regularly.
- A **rolling forecast** always looks a fixed period ahead, such as 12 or 18 months, updated monthly or quarterly.

Many international groups now pair a lighter annual budget with quarterly rolling forecasts, so plans stay useful when markets change.

## Approaches to budgeting

| Approach | Description | When it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Incremental | Last year plus or minus a percentage | Stable cost bases |
| Zero-based | Every cost justified from zero | Cost reset programmes |
| Driver-based | Built from operational drivers | Most modern FP&A teams |
| Activity-based | Costs linked to activities | Shared services, manufacturing |

## Variance analysis

Explain variances between actual and budget by cause:

~~~text
Price variance  = (actual price − budget price) × actual volume
Volume variance = (actual volume − budget volume) × budget price
~~~

Present variances with a short commentary: what happened, why, and whether it will continue.

## Scenarios and sensitivities

- **Sensitivity analysis** changes one input at a time, such as price or FX rate.
- **Scenario analysis** changes a coherent set of inputs: base, upside and downside cases.
- **Monte Carlo simulation** runs thousands of random combinations to produce a distribution of outcomes.

Build a **scenario selector** on the inputs sheet, using CHOOSE or INDEX to pick the active case, so every output updates from one switch.

## Communicating

Show management a bridge chart from budget to forecast, the three scenarios side by side and the key decision each one implies, such as delaying hiring in the downside case.

lessons.content: This final assessment covers the whole course. You need 70 percent to earn your certificate.

courses.title: UX design with Figma
courses.subtitle: Research users, design accessible interfaces in Figma and hand off work that engineers can build.
courses.description:
Good UX design starts with understanding people and ends with an interface that engineers can build without guessing. This course covers the whole path: research, information architecture, wireframes, high-fidelity design in Figma, prototyping, accessibility, usability testing and developer handoff.

You will learn Figma the way product teams use it, with auto layout, components, variants, variables and Dev Mode, and you will apply WCAG 2.2 from the first wireframe rather than as an afterthought. The final lesson shows how to turn your work into a portfolio case study that international hiring managers want to read.

**Who this is for**

- Graphic and visual designers moving into product design
- Developers and product managers who want strong design skills
- Graduates building a first UX portfolio
outcomes: Plan and run user interviews and usability tests, and synthesise findings into insights.
Structure information with user flows, card sorting and wireframes.
Build responsive layouts in Figma with frames, auto layout and constraints.
Create a small design system with components, variants and variables.
Design to WCAG 2.2 AA for contrast, focus, target size and text alternatives.
Prepare prototypes and Dev Mode handoff, and present the work as a case study.

lessons.title: The design process
lessons.content:
## The double diamond

The UK Design Council's **double diamond** describes design as two cycles of opening up and narrowing down:

1. **Discover**: research to understand the problem space.
2. **Define**: synthesise findings into a clear problem statement.
3. **Develop**: explore many possible solutions.
4. **Deliver**: test, refine and ship the best one.

Real projects loop back often. A usability test in Deliver may reveal that you defined the wrong problem.

## Problem statements

A good problem statement is specific, human and free of a built-in solution:

~~~text
Candidates applying for jobs abroad cannot tell which of their skills
employers will accept, so they apply widely, receive few replies and lose confidence.
~~~

Turn it into **How might we** questions to open up ideas: "How might we show candidates exactly what an employer needs before they apply?"

## UX, UI and product design

| Discipline | Focus |
| --- | --- |
| UX design | Whether the product is useful and usable: flows, structure, behaviour |
| UI design | Visual layer: typography, colour, spacing, components |
| Product design | Both, plus business goals and metrics, usually inside a product team |

## Usability heuristics

Jakob Nielsen's **10 usability heuristics** are a quick lens for reviewing any interface. Four you will use daily:

- **Visibility of system status**: show progress and feedback, such as "Saved".
- **Match between system and the real world**: use the user's language, not internal jargon.
- **Error prevention**: disable impossible actions and confirm destructive ones.
- **Recognition rather than recall**: show options instead of asking people to remember them.

lessons.title: User research methods
lessons.content:
## Choosing a method

Pick research methods by what you need to learn and how confident you need to be.

| Method | Type | Answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User interviews | Qualitative, attitudinal | Why people behave as they do |
| Contextual inquiry | Qualitative, behavioural | How work happens in its real setting |
| Usability testing | Qualitative, behavioural | Where people struggle with a design |
| Surveys | Quantitative, attitudinal | How common an attitude or need is |
| Analytics | Quantitative, behavioural | What people do at scale |
| Card sorting | Mixed | How people group content |

## Running interviews

- Recruit five to eight participants per segment, for example recruiters in the UK and recruiters in the UAE.
- Write a discussion guide with open questions, but follow the conversation.
- Ask about real past events, not hypothetical futures.
- Record with consent, and handle personal data in line with the GDPR or local law.

## Synthesis

1. Write one observation per sticky note in FigJam: a quote, behaviour or pain point.
2. **Affinity map**: cluster notes into themes.
3. Write **insights** that explain a pattern and its cause: "Recruiters distrust self-reported skill levels because they cannot verify them."
4. Prioritise insights by frequency and impact.

## How many users?

Nielsen Norman Group research suggests that testing with **five users** uncovers most usability problems in a single round for one user group. Run several small rounds rather than one large one, and test each distinct user group separately.

## Ethics

Pay participants fairly, explain how data will be used, never test on people without consent and anonymise quotes in shared reports.

lessons.title: Personas, journeys and user flows
lessons.content:
## Personas grounded in research

A **persona** is a short, research-based description of a user group. Keep it practical:

- Goals and the job they are trying to get done
- Context: device, environment, constraints such as language or bandwidth
- Pain points and current workarounds
- A quote from real research

Avoid invented details such as hobbies that do not affect design decisions.

## Journey maps

A **customer journey map** shows the end-to-end experience across stages, channels and emotions. For an international job seeker the stages might be: discover role, check fit, close skill gap, apply, interview, relocate. Rows capture actions, thoughts, emotions, touchpoints and opportunities. Journey maps help teams see problems that cross departments, such as a certificate that the recruiter never sees.

## User flows

A **user flow** is a diagram of the steps a user takes to complete one task inside the product, including decisions and error states.

~~~text
Job page → [Meets mandatory skills?]
   ├─ Yes → Apply form → Review → Submitted
   └─ No  → Skill gap panel → Start course → Lessons → Quiz
              → [Passed?] ─ Yes → Certificate → Back to job → Apply form
                          └─ No  → Retry quiz
~~~

Design every branch, including the unhappy paths: empty states, errors, timeouts and permissions. These often decide whether a product feels finished.

## Task analysis

For complex tasks, list each step with the information the user needs and the decision they make. This reveals where to show defaults, hints or validation.

lessons.title: Information architecture and wireframes
lessons.content:
## Information architecture

Information architecture (IA) is the structure and labelling of content. Good IA helps people find things and understand where they are.

## Card sorting and tree testing

- **Open card sort**: participants group content cards and name the groups. Use it to discover mental models.
- **Closed card sort**: participants place cards into predefined categories. Use it to validate a proposed structure.
- **Tree testing**: participants find items in a text-only version of the navigation. It measures findability before any visual design exists.

Tools such as Optimal Workshop or Maze run these remotely with participants in different countries.

## Navigation patterns

| Pattern | Good for |
| --- | --- |
| Top navigation | Few top-level sections on desktop |
| Side navigation | Many sections, dashboards and admin tools |
| Bottom tab bar | Three to five key destinations on mobile |
| Breadcrumbs | Deep hierarchies such as course, module, lesson |

## Wireframes

Wireframes show layout, hierarchy and content without visual styling.

- Start with **low fidelity** sketches to explore several layouts quickly.
- Move to **mid fidelity** in Figma with real content, not lorem ipsum, so you see how long labels and translations behave.
- Annotate behaviour: what happens on click, empty and error states, and responsive changes.

## Designing for real content

International products must handle long German compound words, right-to-left Arabic, names with diacritics and currencies with different formats. Test layouts with the longest realistic strings early. A button labelled "Apply now" in English may become "Jetzt bewerben" in German, which is longer.

lessons.title: Frames, auto layout and constraints
lessons.content:
## Frames and layout grids

In Figma, **frames** are containers, similar to HTML elements. Use frame presets for devices (for example 360 × 800 for a small Android phone, 1440 × 1024 for desktop) and add **layout grids**: a 4-column grid on mobile with 16 px margins, and a 12-column grid on desktop.

## Auto layout

Auto layout makes frames behave like CSS flexbox:

| Figma setting | CSS equivalent |
| --- | --- |
| Direction: horizontal or vertical | flex-direction: row or column |
| Gap between items | gap |
| Padding | padding |
| Alignment | justify-content and align-items |
| Wrap | flex-wrap: wrap |
| Hug contents / Fill container / Fixed | width: fit-content / flex: 1 / fixed width |

Build every component and screen with nested auto layout. When text changes length, everything reflows, just as it will in code.

## Constraints and resizing

For layers inside frames without auto layout, **constraints** (left, right, left and right, centre, scale) define how they respond when the frame resizes. Inside auto layout, use **min and max width** to stop cards from becoming too narrow or too wide.

## A responsive card in practice

1. Create a vertical auto layout frame with 16 px padding and 8 px gap.
2. Add the company logo and job title in a horizontal auto layout row.
3. Set the card to **Fill container** and give it a min width of 280 px.
4. Place cards in a horizontal auto layout with **wrap** enabled.

Resize the parent frame from 360 px to 1440 px to check behaviour.

## Keyboard shortcuts worth learning

- Shift + A: add auto layout
- Ctrl or Cmd + Alt + K: create component
- Ctrl or Cmd + D: duplicate
- Shift + 1: zoom to fit

lessons.title: Components, variants and variables
lessons.content:
## Components

A **main component** defines an element; **instances** inherit its changes. Instances can override text, swap nested instances and toggle properties without detaching.

## Component properties

Figma supports four property types:

- **Variant**: a set of related versions, such as Type = Primary, Secondary or Ghost and State = Default, Hover, Disabled.
- **Boolean**: show or hide a layer, such as a leading icon.
- **Instance swap**: choose which icon or nested component appears.
- **Text**: expose editable text, such as the button label.

Name variants as Property=Value pairs, which Figma uses to build the properties panel. Keep variant matrices small; a button with 3 types × 3 sizes × 4 states already has 36 variants.

## Variables

**Variables** store reusable values: colours, numbers, strings and booleans. Organise them in **collections** with **modes**:

| Collection | Modes | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Primitives | One | brand/700 = #2F5D50 |
| Semantic colour | Light, Dark | color/text/primary → primitives |
| Spacing | Compact, Comfortable | space/sm = 8, space/md = 16 |

Semantic variables reference primitives, so switching a frame to Dark mode recolours the whole design. Variables map neatly to CSS custom properties, which makes handoff much easier.

## Libraries

Publish components, styles and variables as a **team library** so every file uses the same source. Use branching for large changes to the library, and write release notes when you publish an update.

## Naming

Use slash naming for structure, such as Button/Primary or Icon/Arrow right, and match names with the codebase wherever possible. Shared naming removes a large class of handoff questions.

lessons.title: Prototyping and Dev Mode
lessons.content:
## Interactive prototypes

Prototypes let you test flows before code exists. In the Prototype tab:

- Draw **connections** from a layer to a destination frame.
- Choose a trigger: on click, on hover, while pressing, after delay, key or gamepad.
- Choose an action: navigate to, open overlay, swap overlay, scroll to, back.
- Use **Smart animate** to animate layers with matching names between frames.

## Interactive components and variables in prototypes

Add interactions to variants, for example Default → Hover on hover, so every instance behaves correctly without wiring each screen. Prototype **variables** and **conditionals** let you simulate state, such as a basket count, or show a success screen only when a form field is filled.

## Testing prototypes

Share a prototype link with view access, choose the starting frame and device, and run moderated or unmoderated tests with tools such as Maze or Lookback.

## Dev Mode

**Dev Mode** is the developer view of a Figma file:

- Inspect spacing, sizes, typography and variables, shown with their names rather than raw values.
- Copy code snippets for CSS, iOS (SwiftUI) or Android (Compose).
- See **Ready for dev** status on sections, so engineers know what is final.
- Use **Code Connect** to show real component code from the design system repository instead of generated snippets.

## A handoff checklist

| Item | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| States | Default, hover, focus, disabled, loading, error, empty |
| Breakpoints | Mobile, tablet and desktop frames |
| Content rules | Truncation, maximum lengths, translations |
| Accessibility notes | Focus order, labels, landmarks |
| Assets | Icons as components, images exportable |

lessons.title: Accessibility with WCAG 2.2
lessons.content:
## Why it matters

Around one in six people worldwide live with a significant disability. Accessibility is also a legal requirement in many markets: the **European Accessibility Act** applies to many digital products and services from June 2025, and public sector bodies in the EU and UK must meet WCAG-based standards.

## WCAG 2.2 principles

WCAG is organised around four principles, often remembered as **POUR**: perceivable, operable, understandable and robust. Most organisations target **level AA**.

## Criteria designers own

| Criterion | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold) |
| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | 3:1 for UI component boundaries and meaningful graphics |
| 1.4.1 Use of colour | Colour is never the only way to convey information |
| 2.4.7 Focus visible | Keyboard focus is always visible |
| 2.5.8 Target size (minimum) | Targets at least 24 × 24 CSS pixels, or enough spacing |
| 3.3.2 Labels or instructions | Inputs have visible labels |
| 1.4.10 Reflow | Content works at 320 CSS pixels wide without horizontal scrolling |

## Practical habits in Figma

- Check contrast with a plugin or the built-in colour contrast tools while choosing colours.
- Design a **focus state** for every interactive component variant.
- Never use placeholder text as the only label.
- Add error messages that say what went wrong and how to fix it, not just a red border.
- Annotate headings, landmarks, reading order and alternative text for engineers.

## Testing beyond the file

Designers should try the built product with a keyboard only, with a screen reader such as NVDA, VoiceOver or TalkBack, and at 200 percent zoom. Automated checkers find only part of the issues; manual checks find the rest.

lessons.title: Usability testing and iteration
lessons.content:
## Plan the test

1. **Goals**: what decisions will the test inform?
2. **Participants**: five per user group, recruited from the real audience.
3. **Tasks**: realistic scenarios without hints in the wording, such as "You want to work in Dubai as a finance analyst. Find a role you qualify for and find out what you would need to apply."
4. **Measures**: task success, time on task, errors and a post-test questionnaire such as the **System Usability Scale (SUS)**.

## Moderating

- Ask participants to **think aloud**.
- Stay neutral; answer questions with questions: "What would you expect to happen?"
- Do not rescue participants too quickly. Struggle is data.
- Note behaviour, not just quotes: hesitations, back-tracking and repeated clicks.

## Severity rating

Rate each issue so the team can prioritise:

| Severity | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Critical | Users cannot complete the task |
| Serious | Users complete it with significant difficulty or errors |
| Minor | Small delays or irritation |
| Suggestion | Opportunity rather than a problem |

## SUS scores

SUS gives a score from 0 to 100. Around 68 is average across many studies; scores above 80 are considered excellent. Use it to compare versions over time rather than as an absolute judgement.

## Iterate

Share the top findings within 48 hours, fix critical issues first, and retest. A cycle of small tests every two weeks keeps design decisions grounded in evidence.

lessons.title: Building a portfolio case study
lessons.content:
## What hiring managers look for

Product design leads typically spend a few minutes on a portfolio before deciding whether to interview. They look for **process, judgement and impact**, not only polished screens.

## A case study structure

1. **Overview**: product, your role, team, timeline and the outcome in one or two sentences.
2. **Problem**: who was affected, the evidence and why it mattered to the business.
3. **Research**: methods used and the key insights, with one or two artefacts.
4. **Exploration**: options you considered and why you rejected some of them.
5. **Solution**: final designs with annotations explaining decisions.
6. **Validation**: usability results, metrics after launch or feedback.
7. **Reflection**: what you would do differently.

## Show your thinking

- Use captions on every image to explain the decision it shows.
- Show constraints honestly: deadlines, technical limits and compromises.
- Quantify impact where possible: "Task success rose from 55 percent to 90 percent across two test rounds."

## International applications

- Write in clear English and avoid local slang.
- Respect confidentiality agreements: anonymise client names and blur sensitive data.
- Make the portfolio accessible itself: good contrast, alternative text and fast loading on mobile networks.
- Link your Figma prototypes with view-only access, and keep a PDF version for applicant tracking systems that cannot open links.

## Quantity

Three strong case studies beat ten thin ones. Include at least one project that shows research leading to a change in direction.

courses.title: German for professionals (A1 to B1)
courses.subtitle: Learn the German you need to work, interview and settle in Germany, Austria or Switzerland, from A1 to B1.
courses.description:
Germany is one of the largest job markets for international engineers, IT specialists, nurses and finance professionals, and German opens doors in Austria and Switzerland too. Even when the working language is English, German makes interviews, onboarding, paperwork and team life far easier.

This course follows the **Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR)** from A1 to B1. Each lesson teaches real phrases with English translations, the grammar behind them and the cultural rules that matter at work, such as when to use Sie or du. The final module prepares you to write a Lebenslauf and Anschreiben and to answer common interview questions in German.

**Who this is for**

- Professionals planning to work in Germany, Austria or Switzerland
- Candidates applying for roles where German is listed as a required or preferred skill
- Anyone preparing for Goethe-Zertifikat or telc exams at A2 or B1
outcomes: Greet colleagues, introduce yourself and choose correctly between Sie and du.
Handle numbers, dates, times and appointments in spoken and written German.
Build correct main and subordinate clauses with the right verb position.
Use nominative, accusative and dative cases and talk about the past with the Perfekt.
Write workplace emails, make phone calls and take part in meetings politely.
Write a German CV and cover letter and answer standard interview questions at B1 level.

lessons.title: Greetings, introductions and Sie or du
lessons.content:
## Greetings through the day

| German | English | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Guten Morgen | Good morning | Until about 10 or 11 am |
| Guten Tag | Hello, good day | During the day, formal |
| Guten Abend | Good evening | From about 6 pm |
| Hallo | Hi | Informal, very common at work |
| Moin | Hi | Northern Germany, any time of day |
| Grüß Gott / Servus | Hello | Bavaria and Austria |
| Auf Wiedersehen | Goodbye | Formal |
| Tschüss | Bye | Informal |
| Schönen Feierabend | Have a good evening (after work) | Leaving the office |

## Introducing yourself

- **Ich heiße Priya Sharma.** My name is Priya Sharma.
- **Ich komme aus Indien und wohne jetzt in München.** I come from India and now live in Munich.
- **Ich arbeite als Softwareentwicklerin bei Northwind.** I work as a software developer at Northwind.
- **Freut mich.** Nice to meet you.

Note that German leaves out the article before jobs: *Ich bin Ingenieur*, not *Ich bin ein Ingenieur*. Many job titles have a feminine form ending in -in: Ingenieurin, Entwicklerin, Beraterin.

## Sie or du

German has two words for "you":

- **Sie** (always capitalised) is formal. Use it with customers, senior colleagues and anyone you do not know, together with Herr or Frau and the surname: *Guten Tag, Frau Becker. Wie geht es Ihnen?*
- **du** is informal. It is used with friends and, increasingly, with colleagues in start-ups and many technology companies.

The more senior or older person usually offers du: *Wollen wir uns duzen?* (Shall we use du?) Until that happens, stay with Sie. In Austria and Switzerland, titles such as Doktor or Magister are used even more often in formal settings.

## The verb sein (to be)

~~~text
ich bin        wir sind
du bist        ihr seid
er/sie/es ist  sie/Sie sind
~~~

*Sind Sie neu hier? – Ja, ich bin seit Montag im Team.* Are you new here? Yes, I have been in the team since Monday.

lessons.title: Numbers, dates, times and appointments
lessons.content:
## Numbers

From 21 to 99, German says the unit first: **einundzwanzig** (one-and-twenty), **fünfundvierzig** (45), **achtundneunzig** (98). Hundreds and thousands follow: **dreihundertzwölf** (312), **zweitausendsechsundzwanzig** (2026).

German formatting differs from English:

| English | German |
| --- | --- |
| 3.5 percent | 3,5 Prozent |
| 1,500 euros | 1.500 Euro |
| 22/10/2026 or 10/22/2026 | 22.10.2026 |

## Dates

Ordinal numbers end in -te up to 19 and -ste from 20: **der dritte Oktober**, **der zwanzigste Mai**. With am: *Das Meeting ist am dritten Oktober.* The meeting is on the third of October.

Days: Montag, Dienstag, Mittwoch, Donnerstag, Freitag, Samstag (Sonnabend in parts of the north), Sonntag.

## Telling the time

In business, the 24-hour clock is standard: **14:30 Uhr** is read *vierzehn Uhr dreißig*. In conversation people say:

- **Viertel nach drei**: quarter past three (3:15)
- **Viertel vor vier**: quarter to four (3:45)
- **halb vier**: half past **three** (3:30), literally "half to four"

*Halb* causes many missed meetings, so confirm with the 24-hour time when in doubt.

## Making an appointment

- **Haben Sie am Dienstag um 10 Uhr Zeit?** Do you have time on Tuesday at 10?
- **Der Termin passt mir gut.** The appointment suits me.
- **Leider kann ich am Donnerstag nicht. Wie wäre es mit Freitag?** Unfortunately I cannot do Thursday. How about Friday?
- **Ich schicke Ihnen eine Einladung.** I will send you an invitation.

## Punctuality

Being on time matters in German-speaking workplaces. If you will be even five minutes late, send a short message: *Ich verspäte mich um etwa zehn Minuten.* I am running about ten minutes late.

lessons.title: Verb position and the present tense
lessons.content:
## Regular present tense

Most verbs take these endings on the stem. Example: **arbeiten** (to work), stem arbeit-.

~~~text
ich arbeite         wir arbeiten
du arbeitest        ihr arbeitet
er/sie/es arbeitet  sie/Sie arbeiten
~~~

Stems ending in -t or -d add an extra e (du arbeitest, er arbeitet). Some strong verbs change their vowel in the du and er forms: *sprechen → du sprichst, er spricht*; *fahren → du fährst, er fährt*.

## The verb-second rule

In a German main clause, the conjugated verb is always the **second element**. Anything can come first, but then the subject moves after the verb.

- **Ich arbeite heute im Büro.** I am working in the office today.
- **Heute arbeite ich im Büro.** Today I am working in the office.
- **Im Büro arbeite ich heute.** In the office I am working today.

## Questions

- W-questions keep the verb second: **Wann beginnt das Meeting?** When does the meeting start?
- Yes or no questions put the verb first: **Haben Sie einen Moment Zeit?** Do you have a moment?

## Separable verbs

Verbs such as **anrufen** (to call), **teilnehmen** (to take part) and **vorbereiten** (to prepare) split in main clauses. The prefix goes to the end:

- **Ich rufe Sie morgen an.** I will call you tomorrow.
- **Wir bereiten die Präsentation vor.** We are preparing the presentation.

## Subordinate clauses: verb at the end

After conjunctions such as **weil** (because), **dass** (that), **wenn** (if, when) and **ob** (whether), the conjugated verb moves to the end:

- **Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin arbeiten möchte.** I am learning German because I would like to work in Berlin.
- **Ich glaube, dass der Kunde morgen anruft.** I think that the customer will call tomorrow.

Notice that the separable verb joins up again at the end: *anruft*.

lessons.title: Cases: nominative, accusative and dative
lessons.content:
## Why cases matter

German shows the role of a noun with the **article**. The three cases you need first are:

- **Nominative**: the subject, who does the action.
- **Accusative**: the direct object, what the action affects.
- **Dative**: the indirect object, usually the receiver.

## Definite articles

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nominative | der | die | das | die |
| Accusative | **den** | die | das | die |
| Dative | **dem** | **der** | **dem** | **den** (+ n) |

## Indefinite articles

| Case | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nominative | ein | eine | ein |
| Accusative | **einen** | eine | ein |
| Dative | **einem** | **einer** | **einem** |

Only the masculine changes in the accusative. That is a useful shortcut.

## Examples from the office

- **Der Kunde ruft an.** The customer is calling. (nominative)
- **Ich schreibe den Bericht.** I am writing the report. (accusative, der Bericht)
- **Ich gebe dem Kollegen die Unterlagen.** I am giving the documents to the colleague. (dative and accusative)
- **Wir helfen den Kunden.** We help the customers. (helfen always takes the dative)

## Prepositions decide the case

- Always accusative: **für, ohne, gegen, durch, um** — *Das ist für den Chef.*
- Always dative: **mit, nach, bei, seit, von, zu, aus** — *Ich fahre mit dem Zug zur Arbeit.* (zur = zu der)
- Two-way prepositions (**in, an, auf, über, unter, vor, hinter, neben, zwischen**) take the accusative for movement towards a place and the dative for location:
  - *Ich gehe ins Büro.* I am going into the office. (ins = in das, accusative)
  - *Ich bin im Büro.* I am in the office. (im = in dem, dative)

## Learning tip

Always learn nouns with their article and plural: **der Vertrag, die Verträge** (contract), **die Rechnung, die Rechnungen** (invoice), **das Projekt, die Projekte** (project).

lessons.title: The Perfekt: talking about what you did
lessons.content:
## Form

The Perfekt is the main past tense in spoken German. It has two parts:

~~~text
haben or sein (conjugated, position 2)  ...  past participle (end)
~~~

- **Ich habe die E-Mail geschickt.** I sent the email.
- **Wir haben gestern mit dem Team gesprochen.** We spoke with the team yesterday.
- **Sie ist nach Frankfurt geflogen.** She flew to Frankfurt.

## haben or sein

Most verbs use **haben**. Use **sein** with verbs of movement from one place to another (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen) and changes of state (werden, aufstehen), plus **sein** and **bleiben** themselves.

## Forming the participle

| Verb type | Pattern | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regular | ge- + stem + -t | machen → gemacht, arbeiten → gearbeitet |
| Irregular | ge- + stem (often changed) + -en | schreiben → geschrieben, sprechen → gesprochen |
| Separable | prefix + ge + stem + t/en | anrufen → angerufen, teilnehmen → teilgenommen |
| Inseparable prefix (be-, er-, ver-, ent-) | no ge- | besprechen → besprochen, verkaufen → verkauft |
| Ending in -ieren | no ge- | telefonieren → telefoniert, präsentieren → präsentiert |

## Präteritum for a few common verbs

For **sein**, **haben** and the modal verbs, Germans usually use the simple past (Präteritum), even in speech:

- **Ich war letzte Woche in Hamburg.** I was in Hamburg last week.
- **Wir hatten ein gutes Gespräch.** We had a good conversation.
- **Ich konnte gestern nicht kommen.** I could not come yesterday.

## Reporting at work

Use these patterns in stand-ups and status updates:

- **Ich habe das Ticket abgeschlossen.** I have closed the ticket.
- **Wir haben den Fehler gefunden und behoben.** We found and fixed the bug.
- **Der Kunde hat die Rechnung noch nicht bezahlt.** The customer has not paid the invoice yet.

modules.title: German in the workplace (A2 to B1)

lessons.title: Emails and phone calls
lessons.content:
## Opening a formal email

- **Sehr geehrte Frau Becker,** Dear Ms Becker,
- **Sehr geehrter Herr Wagner,** Dear Mr Wagner,
- **Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,** Dear Sir or Madam,
- Less formal: **Liebe Frau Becker,** or **Hallo Jonas,**

After the comma, the first sentence starts with a **lower-case** letter (unless it begins with a noun or Sie): *vielen Dank für Ihre Nachricht.*

## Useful sentences

| German | English |
| --- | --- |
| Vielen Dank für Ihre schnelle Antwort. | Thank you for your quick reply. |
| Anbei sende ich Ihnen das Angebot. | Please find the quotation attached. |
| Könnten Sie mir bitte die Unterlagen bis Freitag schicken? | Could you please send me the documents by Friday? |
| Ich melde mich bis Mittwoch bei Ihnen. | I will get back to you by Wednesday. |
| Bei Fragen stehe ich Ihnen gern zur Verfügung. | I am happy to help if you have any questions. |

## Closing

- **Mit freundlichen Grüßen** — formal, standard in applications and with clients
- **Viele Grüße** or **Beste Grüße** — friendly, common between colleagues

## On the phone

- **Guten Tag, hier spricht Priya Sharma von Walnut.** Hello, this is Priya Sharma from Walnut.
- **Ich rufe wegen Ihrer Bewerbung an.** I am calling about your application.
- **Könnte ich bitte mit Frau Becker sprechen?** Could I speak to Ms Becker, please?
- **Könnten Sie bitte etwas langsamer sprechen?** Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
- **Können Sie das bitte buchstabieren?** Could you spell that, please?
- **Kann ich eine Nachricht hinterlassen?** Can I leave a message?

## Spelling names

Germans spell with a phonetic alphabet. The traditional version uses names (A wie Anton, B wie Berta); the updated DIN 5009 standard from 2022 uses city names (A wie Aachen, B wie Berlin). Either will be understood: *Sharma: S wie Salzwedel, H wie Hamburg, A wie Aachen, R wie Rostock, M wie München, A wie Aachen.*

lessons.title: Meetings and small talk
lessons.content:
## Running and joining a meeting

| German | English |
| --- | --- |
| Lassen Sie uns anfangen. | Let us begin. |
| Auf der Tagesordnung stehen heute drei Punkte. | There are three items on the agenda today. |
| Darf ich kurz etwas ergänzen? | May I add something briefly? |
| Ich bin der Meinung, dass wir mehr Zeit brauchen. | I think that we need more time. |
| Da stimme ich Ihnen zu. | I agree with you there. |
| Das sehe ich etwas anders. | I see that a little differently. |
| Könnten Sie das bitte genauer erklären? | Could you explain that in more detail, please? |
| Wer übernimmt das, und bis wann? | Who will take this on, and by when? |
| Halten wir fest: … | Let us note that … |

*Das sehe ich etwas anders* is a polite way to disagree. German workplace culture values direct, factual discussion; disagreeing with an argument is not seen as a personal attack.

## Small talk

Small talk is shorter than in many English-speaking or Gulf workplaces, but it exists:

- **Wie war Ihr Wochenende?** How was your weekend?
- **Haben Sie gut hergefunden?** Did you find your way here easily?
- **Mahlzeit**: a common greeting around lunchtime in many offices.
- **Schönen Feierabend**: have a good evening, said when leaving work.

Safe topics are travel, the city, food, sport and holidays. Avoid asking about salary, religion or politics with new colleagues.

## Workplace culture in brief

- Meetings start on time and follow the agenda.
- Decisions are documented; people expect written follow-up.
- Working hours and **Feierabend** are respected; messages after hours are less common.
- In many companies, colleagues bring cake on their own birthday.

lessons.title: Modal verbs and polite requests
lessons.content:
## Modal verbs

Modal verbs express ability, obligation, permission and wishes. The modal is in position two and the infinitive goes to the end.

| | können (can) | müssen (must) | dürfen (may) | möchten (would like) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ich | kann | muss | darf | möchte |
| du | kannst | musst | darfst | möchtest |
| er/sie/es | kann | muss | darf | möchte |
| wir | können | müssen | dürfen | möchten |
| ihr | könnt | müsst | dürft | möchtet |
| sie/Sie | können | müssen | dürfen | möchten |

Also learn **sollen** (should, be supposed to) and **wollen** (want to).

- **Ich muss den Bericht heute fertigstellen.** I have to finish the report today.
- **Darf ich das Fenster öffnen?** May I open the window?
- **Sie sollen die Rechnung bis Montag schicken.** You are supposed to send the invoice by Monday.

Careful: **nicht müssen** means "do not have to", not "must not". *Sie müssen nicht kommen* means "You do not have to come". "You must not" is **nicht dürfen**: *Sie dürfen hier nicht parken.*

## Konjunktiv II for politeness

The Konjunktiv II makes requests softer, which is expected in professional German.

- **Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?** Could you help me, please?
- **Würden Sie mir die Datei schicken?** Would you send me the file?
- **Ich hätte gern einen Termin nächste Woche.** I would like an appointment next week.
- **Es wäre gut, wenn wir den Termin verschieben könnten.** It would be good if we could move the appointment.

## Hypothetical situations (B1)

- **Wenn ich mehr Zeit hätte, würde ich einen Deutschkurs am Abend besuchen.** If I had more time, I would attend an evening German course.
- **An Ihrer Stelle würde ich zuerst mit dem Kunden sprechen.** In your position, I would speak to the customer first.

lessons.title: Lebenslauf and Anschreiben
lessons.content:
## The Lebenslauf

The German CV is a **tabellarischer Lebenslauf**: a clear, reverse-chronological table, usually one or two pages.

- **Persönliche Daten**: name, address, phone number, email. Date of birth and nationality are optional. A photo is common but not legally required; the General Equal Treatment Act (AGG) protects applicants from discrimination.
- **Berufserfahrung**: month and year, job title, employer, city, and three or four bullet points with results.
- **Ausbildung**: degrees with institution and dates. Many applicants note whether a foreign degree is recognised (anerkannt), which can be checked in the anabin database.
- **Kenntnisse**: IT skills, certificates and **Sprachkenntnisse** with CEFR levels, for example *Deutsch: B1 (Goethe-Zertifikat), Englisch: C1*.

## The Anschreiben

The cover letter is one page and follows the DIN 5008 layout: sender, recipient, place and date, subject line, greeting, body, closing, signature and attachments.

~~~text
Berlin, 22. Oktober 2026

Bewerbung als SAP FICO Berater (m/w/d) – Kennziffer 4711

Sehr geehrte Frau Becker,

mit großem Interesse habe ich Ihre Stellenanzeige auf Walnut Jobs gelesen.
Als SAP-Berater mit fünf Jahren Erfahrung in S/4HANA-Projekten möchte ich
Ihr Team in Frankfurt unterstützen.

In meiner aktuellen Position bei Northwind habe ich die Einführung von
S/4HANA Finance in drei Ländern begleitet und den Monatsabschluss um zwei
Tage verkürzt. Ich arbeite gern im internationalen Team und spreche
Deutsch auf B1-Niveau.

Ich kann die Stelle nach einer Kündigungsfrist von drei Monaten antreten.
Meine Gehaltsvorstellung liegt bei 75.000 Euro brutto im Jahr.

Über eine Einladung zu einem persönlichen Gespräch freue ich mich sehr.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen
Arjun Patel

Anlagen: Lebenslauf, Zeugnisse
~~~

## Notes on vocabulary

- **(m/w/d)** stands for männlich, weiblich, divers. Job adverts include it to show the role is open to all genders.
- **Kündigungsfrist**: notice period. **Gehaltsvorstellung**: salary expectation, given as a gross annual figure.
- **Zeugnisse**: certificates and employer references. German employers write formal **Arbeitszeugnisse**, and applicants usually attach them.

lessons.title: Job interview phrases
lessons.content:
## Typical questions and model answers

**Erzählen Sie etwas über sich.** Tell me about yourself.
*Ich bin Datenanalystin und habe fünf Jahre Erfahrung im Bankwesen. Zurzeit arbeite ich in Dubai und analysiere Kreditrisiken mit Python und SQL.*
I am a data analyst with five years of banking experience. I currently work in Dubai analysing credit risk with Python and SQL.

**Warum möchten Sie bei uns arbeiten?** Why do you want to work for us?
*Ihr Unternehmen ist in Europa führend, und mich interessiert besonders Ihr Projekt zur Digitalisierung.*
Your company is a leader in Europe, and I am especially interested in your digitalisation project.

**Was sind Ihre Stärken?** What are your strengths?
*Ich arbeite strukturiert und kann komplexe Themen einfach erklären.*
I work in a structured way and can explain complex topics simply.

**Wo sehen Sie sich in fünf Jahren?** Where do you see yourself in five years?
*Ich möchte mich fachlich weiterentwickeln und später ein kleines Team leiten.*
I would like to develop professionally and later lead a small team.

**Wann könnten Sie anfangen?** When could you start?
*Ich habe eine Kündigungsfrist von drei Monaten, also ab dem ersten Februar.*
I have a three-month notice period, so from the first of February.

## Questions to ask the employer

- **Wie sieht ein typischer Arbeitstag aus?** What does a typical working day look like?
- **Wie ist das Team aufgebaut?** How is the team structured?
- **Gibt es die Möglichkeit, teilweise im Homeoffice zu arbeiten?** Is it possible to work from home part of the time?
- **Wie geht es nach dem Gespräch weiter?** What are the next steps after this interview?

## Words you will hear

| German | English |
| --- | --- |
| die Probezeit | probation period, usually up to six months |
| brutto / netto | gross / net |
| der Urlaubsanspruch | annual leave entitlement |
| der Arbeitsvertrag | employment contract |

## Why B1 matters

B1 is the level at which you can handle familiar topics at work independently. It is also the language level required for German naturalisation and helps EU Blue Card holders qualify for a settlement permit sooner. Goethe-Institut and telc certificates are widely recognised.

courses.title: Business English for global teams
courses.subtitle: Write, speak and present in clear, confident English with colleagues and clients around the world.
courses.description:
English is the working language of most multinational teams, yet most people using it at work are not native speakers. Clear, plain English is therefore a professional skill, not a matter of accent or vocabulary size. This course teaches you to write emails people act on, run and join meetings, disagree politely, present data and adapt to colleagues from different cultures.

Every lesson contains real phrases and before-and-after examples. You will also learn where British and American English differ, so your writing stays consistent, and how to work well with colleagues from high-context and low-context cultures.

**Who this is for**

- Professionals working in or applying to international teams
- Non-native speakers at B1 to B2 level who want to sound clear and confident
- Native speakers who want to communicate better with global colleagues
outcomes: Write short, structured emails that lead with the main point and a clear request.
Run and take part in meetings and video calls with confident, polite language.
Disagree, negotiate and give feedback diplomatically.
Present data and trends accurately using the right vocabulary.
Adapt communication to high-context and low-context cultures.
Choose British or American conventions and apply them consistently.

lessons.title: Plain English for emails
lessons.content:
## Why plain English

Plain English is easier to read for everyone, especially colleagues reading in a second language or through translation tools. It also reduces mistakes and follow-up questions.

## Six rules

1. **Prefer short sentences**: aim for an average of 15 to 20 words.
2. **Use the active voice**: "The finance team approved the budget", not "The budget was approved by the finance team".
3. **Choose everyday words**: *use* not *utilise*, *start* not *commence*, *help* not *facilitate*.
4. **Avoid idioms and sports metaphors**: "touch base", "ballpark figure" and "hit it out of the park" confuse many readers.
5. **Put actions and dates in clear sentences**: "Please send the signed contract by Friday 24 October."
6. **Write numbers and dates unambiguously**: 03/04 means 3 April in the UK and 4 March in the US; write "3 April 2026".

## Before and after

~~~text
Before:
Further to our previous discussions, I wanted to reach out in order to
ascertain whether it might be feasible for your team to provide the
requisite documentation at your earliest convenience.

After:
Could your team send the signed documents by Thursday 23 October?
We need them to finish onboarding.
~~~

## Subject lines

Make the subject line do work. Include the topic and, if needed, the action and date:

- *Action needed: approve Q4 hiring plan by 30 Oct*
- *Decision: we will launch in Germany on 12 January*
- *FYI: new travel policy from 1 November*

## Tone

Be warm but brief. "Thanks for the quick reply" and "Happy to help" sound friendly in every English-speaking region. Avoid writing in capital letters, which reads as shouting, and use exclamation marks sparingly in professional email.

lessons.title: Structuring messages: bottom line up front
lessons.content:
## Lead with the point

Busy readers decide in a few seconds whether to act. **Bottom line up front (BLUF)** puts the conclusion or request in the first sentence, then the supporting detail.

~~~text
Subject: Request: approve 2 extra days for the SAP data migration test

Hi Maria,

Could you approve two extra days for the data migration test? Without
them we risk migrating incorrect opening balances.

Background:
- The third test cycle found 46 mismatched vendor balances.
- The fix is ready, but we need one more full cycle to confirm it.
- Go-live on 1 December is not affected.

If you approve by Wednesday, we start the cycle on Thursday.

Thanks,
Ahmed
~~~

## The pyramid principle

Barbara Minto's **pyramid principle** structures longer documents:

- Start with the **governing thought**: the answer or recommendation.
- Support it with three to five **key arguments**.
- Support each argument with **data and examples**.

Each group should be **mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive** (MECE), so points do not overlap and nothing important is missing.

## Formatting for scanning

- Short paragraphs of two or three sentences
- Bullets for lists of three or more items
- **Bold** for the one thing the reader must not miss
- Numbered steps for instructions

## Replying well

- Answer every question asked, in the order asked.
- Quote or restate the question if the thread is long.
- Close with the next step: who does what, by when.

## Chat tools

On Slack or Microsoft Teams, write the whole message before sending rather than "Hi" followed by a pause. Colleagues in other time zones can then answer when they start work.

lessons.title: Running and joining meetings
lessons.content:
## Opening

- "Thanks for joining. The aim today is to agree the launch date for Germany."
- "We have 30 minutes and three items on the agenda."
- "Sara, could you take notes, please?"

## Managing the discussion

| Purpose | Phrase |
| --- | --- |
| Inviting input | "Daniel, what is your view on this?" |
| Keeping time | "We have five minutes left on this item." |
| Parking a topic | "Let us take that offline and come back to it on Friday." |
| Interrupting politely | "Sorry to interrupt, could I add one point?" |
| Clarifying | "Just to check I understand, you mean…?" |
| Returning to the agenda | "Let us get back to the launch date." |

## Closing

- "To summarise, we have agreed three things…"
- "Mei will send the revised plan by Wednesday."
- "Is there anything we have missed?"

Always send written follow-up with decisions, owners and dates. Colleagues who missed the call, or whose English is weaker, rely on it.

## Video calls

- Turn on live captions in Teams or Zoom if anyone finds accents hard to follow.
- Pause after asking a question; silence on a call often means people are thinking or translating.
- Use names when passing the turn, because body language is hard to read on video.
- Share the screen with the document you are discussing, and say which page or slide you are on.

## Speaking clearly

Native speakers often speak too fast and use contractions and idioms. Slow down slightly, finish your sentences, and check understanding with open questions: "What questions do you have?" works better than "Does that make sense?", which people tend to answer with "yes" even when it does not.

lessons.title: Disagreeing politely and negotiating
lessons.content:
## Softening disagreement

Direct disagreement can sound rude in English, especially British English. Use softeners:

| Direct | Softened |
| --- | --- |
| That is wrong. | I am not sure that is quite right. |
| I disagree. | I see it slightly differently. |
| That will not work. | I have some concerns about whether that will work. |
| No. | That might be difficult, because… |
| You are late with the report. | It looks like the report is a few days behind schedule. |

Combine agreement and disagreement: "I agree that speed matters, but I am worried about data quality."

## Giving feedback

Use **situation, behaviour, impact (SBI)**:

~~~text
In yesterday's client call (situation), you presented the budget figures
without the currency breakdown (behaviour). The client was confused about
the EUR and AED amounts and asked for a second meeting (impact).
Could we add a breakdown slide next time?
~~~

## Negotiation language

- Exploring: "What is most important to you in this agreement?"
- Proposing: "We could offer a 10 percent discount if you commit to two years."
- Conditional trading: "If you can pay in 30 days, we can deliver in November."
- Holding firm: "I understand, but that is the lowest price we can offer."
- Closing: "So, to confirm, we have agreed…"

## Principled negotiation

Fisher and Ury's *Getting to Yes* recommends:

- Separate the **people** from the problem.
- Focus on **interests**, not positions.
- Invent **options** for mutual gain.
- Use **objective criteria**, such as market rates.
- Know your **BATNA**: your best alternative to a negotiated agreement.

Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away, and it gives you confidence in every negotiation, including salary discussions.
