lessons.title: Presentations that land
lessons.content:
## Structure

A simple structure works in every culture:

1. **Opening**: who you are, the purpose and what the audience will get.
2. **Main points**: three is ideal; signpost each one.
3. **Close**: summary, recommendation and next steps.
4. **Questions**.

## Signposting language

| Purpose | Phrase |
| --- | --- |
| Starting | "Today I would like to show you why we recommend launching in Germany first." |
| Outlining | "I will cover three points: the market, the costs and the timeline." |
| Moving on | "That brings me to my second point." |
| Referring to a slide | "As you can see on this chart…" |
| Emphasising | "The key point here is…" |
| Summarising | "To sum up…" |
| Inviting questions | "I am happy to take any questions." |

## Slides

- One message per slide, written as a full sentence in the title: "Germany offers the largest market for SAP talent."
- Few words; let the speaker explain.
- Readable fonts at 24 points or larger and high colour contrast.
- Label charts directly instead of relying on a legend.

## Handling questions

- Thank the person and repeat or rephrase the question so everyone hears it.
- If you do not know: "That is a good question. I do not have the figure with me, but I will send it by tomorrow."
- If the question is off topic: "That is an important point. Could we discuss it after the session?"

## Delivery for global audiences

Speak more slowly than in conversation, pause between points, avoid jokes that rely on wordplay, and send the slides in advance so colleagues can read along in their own time.

lessons.title: Describing data and trends
lessons.content:
## Verbs of movement

| Upward | Downward | Stable |
| --- | --- | --- |
| rise, increase, grow | fall, decrease, decline | remain stable, stay flat |
| climb, go up | drop, go down | level off, plateau |
| jump, soar (large and fast) | plunge, slump (large and fast) | fluctuate (move up and down) |

## Adjectives and adverbs of degree

- Large: **sharp(ly), significant(ly), dramatic(ally)**
- Medium: **steady (steadily), moderate(ly)**
- Small: **slight(ly), gradual(ly), marginal(ly)**

Examples:

- "Applications **rose sharply** in March, by 35 percent."
- "There was a **slight decline** in cost per hire in the second quarter."
- "Revenue **levelled off** at around 2 million euros."

## Prepositions matter

- **rose by** 10 percent (the change)
- **rose to** 1,200 (the new level)
- **rose from** 1,000 **to** 1,200
- **a rise of** 20 percent
- **at a peak of** 1,500

## Percentages and percentage points

If an interview rate moves from 10 percent to 12 percent, it has risen by **2 percentage points**, which is a **20 percent** increase. Mixing these up is a common and costly mistake in reports.

## Approximation and comparison

- **roughly, approximately, just under, just over, nearly**: "just over a third of candidates"
- **twice as many as, half as much as, three times higher than**
- **compared with** last year, **year on year**, **quarter on quarter**

## A model paragraph

~~~text
Between January and June, qualified applications rose steadily from 820
to 1,240, an increase of just over 50 percent. Growth was strongest in the
UAE, where applications almost doubled. In contrast, the UK remained flat.
We expect the trend to continue in the third quarter.
~~~

lessons.title: High-context and low-context cultures
lessons.content:
## Edward Hall's distinction

Anthropologist Edward T. Hall described cultures on a spectrum:

- **Low-context** cultures expect messages to be explicit and literal. Good communication is precise and simple. The United States, Germany, the Netherlands and Australia are often placed here.
- **High-context** cultures rely more on shared understanding, relationships and what is implied. Good communication is layered and nuanced. Japan, Korea, China, India, the Gulf states and much of Southeast Asia are often placed here.

These are tendencies, not rules for individuals. Industry, generation and company culture also matter.

## The Culture Map

Erin Meyer's *The Culture Map* compares cultures on eight scales:

| Scale | From | To |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Communicating | Low-context | High-context |
| Evaluating | Direct negative feedback | Indirect negative feedback |
| Persuading | Principles first | Applications first |
| Leading | Egalitarian | Hierarchical |
| Deciding | Consensual | Top-down |
| Trusting | Task-based | Relationship-based |
| Disagreeing | Confrontational | Avoids confrontation |
| Scheduling | Linear time | Flexible time |

## What this means in practice

- With **high-context** colleagues, listen for what is not said. "That may be difficult" can mean no. Build relationships before business, and do not push for an immediate decision in a group meeting.
- With **low-context** colleagues, be explicit. Spell out decisions, owners and dates. Directness is usually meant as efficiency, not rudeness.
- In **hierarchical** cultures, involve senior people early and address them formally until invited otherwise.
- In **relationship-based** cultures, such as much of the Middle East and Latin America, time spent over coffee or a meal is part of the work.

## A useful habit

When something feels wrong, describe it, interpret it in more than one way, and evaluate only after checking: "I noticed you did not comment on the plan. Would you like more time to review it?"

lessons.title: British, American and international English
lessons.content:
## Pick one standard and be consistent

Global companies usually choose British or American English for documents. Mixing them looks careless. Most Commonwealth countries, the EU institutions, India and the Gulf tend to use British spelling; the US, and many tech companies, use American.

## Spelling

| British | American |
| --- | --- |
| organisation, prioritise | organization, prioritize |
| colour, behaviour | color, behavior |
| centre, metre | center, meter |
| travelled, cancelled | traveled, canceled |
| licence (noun), license (verb) | license (noun and verb) |
| programme (plan), program (software) | program |
| catalogue | catalog |

## Vocabulary

| British | American |
| --- | --- |
| CV | résumé (for most jobs) |
| holiday, annual leave | vacation, PTO |
| mobile | cell phone |
| first floor (one above ground) | second floor |
| fortnight | two weeks |

## Dates, numbers and times

- UK: 22 October 2026; US: October 22, 2026. ISO 8601 (2026-10-22) is unambiguous in data and file names.
- "Billion" now means one thousand million in both.
- Many countries use a comma as the decimal separator; check numbers in documents translated from German, French or Spanish.

## International English

When writing for a global audience:

- Avoid phrasal verbs with many meanings when a single verb is clearer: *postpone* rather than *put off*.
- Spell out abbreviations the first time.
- Use time zones explicitly: "15:00 CET / 18:00 GST / 19:30 IST".
- Prefer "please" and "thank you" in written requests; direct imperatives can read as harsh when translated.

courses.title: Global job readiness: CV, interviews and relocation

Applying for jobs in another country means learning new rules. A CV that works in Bengaluru may be rejected in Berlin; a salary that sounds generous in Dubai may not cover rent in London; and a work permit can take longer than the interview process. This free course gives you the practical playbook.

You will learn country-specific CV formats, how applicant tracking systems read your application, how to answer behavioural questions with the STAR method, how to negotiate pay in different markets and what to organise before and after you relocate. It ends with a plan for your first 90 days in a new role.

**Who this is for**

- Candidates applying for roles outside their home country
- Graduates starting an international career
- Professionals who have received an offer abroad and are planning the move
outcomes: Adapt your CV to the conventions of the US, UK, EU, Gulf and Asian markets.
Structure your CV so applicant tracking systems parse it correctly.
Answer behavioural interview questions with the STAR method.
Compare offers across countries using gross, net and total compensation.
Build a relocation checklist covering visas, documents, banking and housing.
Plan your first 90 days in a new international role.

lessons.title: CV formats by country
lessons.content:
## One CV does not fit every market

Recruiters expect different formats in different countries. Adapting your CV is a quick win.

| Market | Name and length | Photo | Personal details | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| United States, Canada | Resume, one page (two if senior) | No | No age, marital status or photo, because of anti-discrimination law | Achievement bullets with numbers |
| United Kingdom, Ireland | CV, two pages | No | No date of birth or photo | Short personal profile at the top |
| Germany, Austria, Switzerland | Lebenslauf, one to two pages | Common but optional | Date of birth optional | Reverse-chronological table, certificates attached |
| EU (general) | Europass accepted, often two pages | Optional | Optional | Europass is well known in public sector and academia |
| UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar | CV, two to three pages | Common | Nationality and visa status often included | Mention notice period and availability |
| India | Resume, two pages | Rarely | Often includes current and expected CTC in the application form | Projects and certifications matter |
| Japan | Rirekisho (standard form) plus shokumu keirekisho (work history) | Yes, on rirekisho | Yes | Foreign firms in Japan often accept English CVs |

## Europass

**Europass** is the EU's free CV builder. It is useful for EU public bodies, research roles and when an employer asks for it. Many private employers prefer a concise, tailored CV, so use Europass as a starting point rather than a default.

## Universal rules

- Reverse chronological order: most recent role first.
- Start bullets with an action verb and include a result: "Reduced month-end close from 8 to 5 days by automating bank reconciliation in SAP."
- Name the tools and standards recruiters search for: SAP S/4HANA, IFRS 16, Python, ISO 27001.
- List language skills with **CEFR levels** (A1 to C2) rather than "fluent" or "basic".
- Use a professional email address and include your LinkedIn URL.
- Save as PDF unless the employer asks for Word, and name the file clearly: Priya-Sharma-CV-SAP-Consultant.pdf.

lessons.title: Beating applicant tracking systems
lessons.content:
## What an ATS does

Most multinational employers use an **applicant tracking system (ATS)** such as Workday, SAP SuccessFactors, Oracle Taleo, Greenhouse or Lever. The ATS parses your CV into fields, stores it and lets recruiters search and filter candidates. Many CVs are never seen by a human because they parse badly or do not match the search.

## Format so the parser can read it

- Use a **single-column** layout. Two-column templates often scramble the reading order.
- Use standard headings: **Experience, Education, Skills, Certifications, Languages**.
- Avoid text in headers, footers, text boxes, tables and images.
- Use common fonts such as Arial, Calibri or Garamond.
- Write dates consistently: "Mar 2022 – Present" or "03/2022 – present".
- Do not put skills in charts or rating bars; the ATS cannot read them.

## Match the keywords honestly

Recruiters search the ATS with words from the job advert. Mirror the exact terms where they are true for you:

~~~text
Job advert: "Experience with SAP S/4HANA Finance, IFRS 16 and month-end close"

Weak:  Worked on ERP finance projects and closing activities.
Strong: Configured SAP S/4HANA Finance asset accounting and led
        IFRS 16 lease accounting in the month-end close for 4 entities.
~~~

Include both the abbreviation and the full term once: "applicant tracking system (ATS)", "Customer relationship management (CRM)".

## Check before you send

- Paste your CV into a plain text editor. If the order still makes sense, the ATS will probably read it well.
- Compare the job advert and your CV side by side and highlight the matching skills.
- Never hide keywords in white text. Recruiters see them in the parsed text and reject the application.

## Certificates help

Verified certificates, such as those from Walnut courses, give recruiters evidence beyond self-reported skills. List them under **Certifications** with the issuer, date and verification link.

lessons.title: The STAR method
lessons.content:
## Behavioural interviews

Most multinational employers use **behavioural questions** that begin with "Tell me about a time when…". The idea is that past behaviour predicts future performance. The **STAR** method keeps your answer focused.

| Part | What to say | Share of the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Situation** | Context in one or two sentences | About 10 percent |
| **Task** | Your responsibility or goal | About 10 percent |
| **Action** | What **you** did, step by step | About 60 percent |
| **Result** | The outcome, with numbers, and what you learnt | About 20 percent |

## A model answer

*Question: Tell me about a time you handled a difficult stakeholder.*

~~~text
Situation: During an SAP rollout in Saudi Arabia, the regional finance
director rejected our new approval workflow two weeks before go-live.

Task: As the finance lead, I had to get agreement without delaying go-live.

Action: I met him the same day to understand his concern, which was losing
visibility of large payments. I proposed adding a threshold alert for
payments above SAR 500,000, tested it with his team and shared a
one-page summary with the steering committee.

Result: He approved the workflow, we went live on time, and the alert
became standard in two other countries. I learnt to ask about the
concern behind an objection before defending the design.
~~~

## Prepare a story bank

Write six to eight STAR stories covering common themes:

- Leadership or influence without authority
- Conflict or a difficult stakeholder
- Failure and what you learnt
- A tight deadline
- Working across cultures or time zones
- Improving a process with measurable results

Most questions can be answered by adapting one of these stories.

## Common mistakes

- Saying "we" throughout; interviewers need to know what **you** did.
- Spending too long on the situation.
- Forgetting the result or giving a vague one.

lessons.title: Video, panel and case interviews
lessons.content:
## Video interviews

Remote first rounds are now standard for international roles.

- Test the platform (Teams, Zoom, Google Meet or HireVue) the day before.
- Use a wired connection or sit close to the router; have a phone hotspot as backup.
- Place the camera at eye level, light your face from the front and choose a quiet, neutral background.
- Confirm the **time zone** in writing: "Confirming Tuesday 4 November at 10:00 GMT, 14:00 GST."
- In **one-way video interviews**, you record answers to preset questions with a time limit. Practise with a timer.

## Panel interviews

Panels are common in the public sector, banks and Gulf organisations. Address your answer to the person who asked, then include the others with eye contact. Note each panellist's name and role at the start.

## Case and technical interviews

- **Case interviews** (consulting, strategy and product roles): think aloud, structure the problem before calculating, state assumptions and summarise a recommendation.
- **Technical interviews**: clarify requirements, explain your approach, then solve; talk through trade-offs.
- **Assessment centres** (graduate roles in the UK and Europe): group exercises, presentations and in-tray tasks. Assessors watch collaboration as much as answers.

## Cultural expectations

| Region | What tends to impress |
| --- | --- |
| United States | Confidence, clear achievements, enthusiasm |
| United Kingdom | Concise evidence, modesty with substance |
| Germany, Netherlands | Facts, precision, directness, punctuality |
| Japan | Humility, respect for hierarchy, preparation |
| Gulf states | Relationship building, respect, formality at first |

## Closing the interview

Ask two or three thoughtful questions, such as "What would success look like in the first six months?", and send a short thank-you email within 24 hours.

lessons.title: Comparing offers across countries
lessons.content:
## Gross, net and total compensation

A salary number means little without context. Compare offers on three levels:

- **Gross salary**: before tax and social contributions.
- **Net salary**: what reaches your bank account.
- **Total compensation**: salary plus bonus, allowances, equity, pension contributions and benefits such as health insurance.

## How pay is quoted around the world

| Country | Common convention |
| --- | --- |
| United States | Annual gross base salary; bonus and equity stated separately |
| United Kingdom | Annual gross; pension and benefits listed |
| Germany | Annual gross, sometimes paid in 12 or 13 instalments |
| Netherlands | Annual gross plus 8 percent holiday allowance (vakantiegeld) |
| UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar | Monthly package: basic salary plus housing and transport allowances |
| India | Annual cost to company (CTC), including employer contributions and variable pay |

## Gulf packages

In the UAE there is no personal income tax, so gross and net are close. Packages usually split into **basic salary** and **allowances**. End-of-service gratuity is calculated on basic salary only, so a higher basic share is worth more in the long run. Check whether the employer pays for family visas, medical insurance, school fees and annual flights home.

## Cost of living

Use purchasing power, not exchange rates alone. Rent in central London, Zurich or Singapore can take 30 to 50 percent of a net salary. Compare monthly rent, school fees, transport and health insurance with sources such as Numbeo, Expatistan or official statistics.

## Other terms that matter

- **Notice period** and **probation** length
- **Relocation package**: flights, shipping, temporary housing, visa costs
- **Repayment clauses** if you leave within a year or two
- **Annual leave**: for example at least 20 working days in Germany for a five-day week by law, 28 days including bank holidays in the UK, and 30 calendar days in the UAE after one year of service

lessons.title: Negotiating your salary
lessons.content:
## Prepare with data

Before negotiating, research the range for the role, level and city. Sources include company salary bands published under pay transparency laws (for example in several US states and, from 2026, in the EU under the Pay Transparency Directive), salary surveys from recruitment firms, and platforms such as Glassdoor and Levels.fyi.

Know three numbers:

- Your **target**: what you will ask for, near the top of the realistic range.
- Your **acceptable** figure.
- Your **walk-away** point, informed by your best alternative.

## When asked for your expectations

- Early in the process: "Based on my research, roles like this in Amsterdam pay between 70,000 and 80,000 euros. I am looking for a package in that range, depending on the full offer."
- Give a range whose bottom is a number you would accept.
- In some places, including several US states, employers may not ask about your salary history. You can politely decline: "I would prefer to focus on the value I can bring to this role."

## Negotiating the offer

1. Thank them and express enthusiasm.
2. Ask for time: 24 to 48 hours is normal.
3. Make one clear, justified counter-offer: "Given my S/4HANA migration experience and the cost of housing in Dubai, I would like to ask for a basic salary of AED 32,000 per month."
4. If salary is fixed, negotiate other items: sign-on bonus, start date, relocation, remote days, training budget, title.
5. Get the final offer in writing before resigning from your current job.

## Cultural differences

- In the US and UK, negotiation is expected and rarely offends.
- In Germany and the Netherlands, factual arguments carry weight; overstated claims do not.
- In Japan, negotiation is more limited and usually handled through recruiters.
- In the Gulf, negotiation is common, and allowances often have more flexibility than basic salary.

lessons.title: Visas and the relocation checklist
lessons.content:
## Common work visa routes

Rules change frequently, so always check the official government website before you rely on any detail.

| Country | Common route for skilled professionals |
| --- | --- |
| Germany | EU Blue Card or skilled worker visa; Chancenkarte (Opportunity Card) for job search |
| United Kingdom | Skilled Worker visa, sponsored by a licensed employer |
| Netherlands | Highly skilled migrant permit through a recognised sponsor |
| United States | H-1B (annual cap and lottery), L-1 for intra-company transfers, O-1 for extraordinary ability |
| Canada | Express Entry for permanent residence; employer-specific work permits |
| UAE | Employer-sponsored employment visa and Emirates ID; Golden Visa for eligible professionals |
| Singapore | Employment Pass, assessed with the COMPASS points framework |

Official sources: make-it-in-germany.com, gov.uk, ind.nl, uscis.gov, canada.ca, u.ae and mom.gov.sg.

## Documents to prepare early

- Passport valid for at least the length of your contract plus six months
- Degree certificates and transcripts, often with **attestation** or an **apostille** (the Gulf states typically require attestation through the issuing country and the embassy)
- Recognition of qualifications where needed, for example through anabin or ZAB in Germany
- Police clearance certificate
- Employment reference letters
- Birth and marriage certificates for family visas, translated and legalised

## The relocation checklist

| When | Task |
| --- | --- |
| 8–12 weeks before | Visa application, document attestation, notice period, school places |
| 4–6 weeks before | Temporary housing, shipping quotes, international driving permit, health insurance |
| 1–2 weeks before | Cancel or transfer contracts, tell your bank, carry documents in hand luggage |
| First week | Register address (Anmeldung in Germany), collect residence permit or ID, open a bank account, get a local SIM |
| First month | Tax number, social security registration, find permanent housing, register with a doctor |

## Money

Keep enough savings for two to three months of costs. Many landlords ask for a deposit of up to three months' rent, and the first salary may arrive later than expected.

lessons.title: Your first 90 days
lessons.content:
## The 30-60-90 plan

Michael Watkins' *The First 90 Days* argues that new leaders succeed by learning fast and securing early wins. A simple plan works for any level.

| Phase | Focus | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1–30 | Learn | Meet your manager and team one-to-one, understand goals, systems and unwritten rules |
| Days 31–60 | Contribute | Take ownership of a defined piece of work, propose one or two improvements |
| Days 61–90 | Deliver | Show a measurable early win, agree goals for the rest of the year |

## Questions to ask in your first weeks

- "What does success look like for me in six months?"
- "Who are the people I should meet early?"
- "How do you prefer to receive updates, and how often?"
- "What has been tried before that did not work?"

## Learning the culture

Watch how decisions are really made, how people disagree, how formal emails are, and whether people leave on time. Ask a colleague you trust: "Is there anything about how things work here that I should know?"

## Building relationships across distance

- Introduce yourself to key contacts with a short message and a 20-minute call.
- Learn names correctly, including pronunciation.
- Be reliable in small things: deadlines, meeting preparation and follow-up notes.

## Looking after yourself

Relocation is demanding. Expect a dip in mood a few weeks after arrival, often called culture shock. Join a language class, a sports club or an expatriate group, keep in touch with home, and use your employer's assistance programme if one is available.

## Probation review

Before the end of probation, ask your manager for a review against the goals you agreed. Bring evidence of results so the conversation is concrete.

courses.title: SAP S/4HANA finance for energy operations at Falcon Gulf
courses.subtitle: Run joint venture accounting, plant assets, UAE tax and the month-end close in S/4HANA the way Falcon Gulf's finance team does.
courses.description:
Falcon Gulf Energy is a UAE energy group with upstream concessions, a gas processing plant, power generation assets and a trading arm. Its finance team runs on SAP S/4HANA, and new joiners need to be productive in their first month. Walnut's course studio designed this course with Falcon Gulf's finance leadership to close the gaps they see most often in candidates.

The course focuses on four areas that general SAP training rarely covers in depth: joint venture accounting with partners, asset accounting for large plants, UAE VAT and corporate tax, and a disciplined month-end close. Each lesson connects IFRS requirements to the S/4HANA configuration and Fiori apps you will use.

**Who this is for**

- Candidates applying for finance, SAP FICO and controlling roles at Falcon Gulf
- SAP FICO consultants moving into the oil, gas and power sector in the Gulf
- Accountants in energy companies who want to understand the S/4HANA side of their work
outcomes: Describe how an energy group's legal entities, ledgers and currencies map to S/4HANA.
Explain joint venture accounting: ventures, equity groups, cash calls, cutback and partner billing.
Account for plant assets from capital project to depreciation, componentisation and decommissioning.
Apply UAE VAT rules, including zero-rating for crude oil and natural gas, in S/4HANA tax codes.
Explain the basics of UAE corporate tax, including the extractive business exemption and Pillar Two top-up tax.
Run a month-end close checklist using standard S/4HANA transactions and Fiori apps.

lessons.title: Group structure, ledgers and currencies
lessons.content:
## How an energy group maps to S/4HANA

Energy groups in the Gulf usually combine several legal entities with very different businesses. A typical structure, similar to Falcon Gulf's, looks like this:

| Entity | Business | Company code | Local currency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Holding company, Abu Dhabi | Group functions, treasury | FG10 | AED |
| Upstream operations | Concession interests with partners | FG20 | AED (USD functional) |
| Gas processing | Plant operations | FG30 | AED |
| Power generation | Independent power plant | FG40 | AED |
| Trading, ADGM or DIFC | Crude and product trading | FG50 | USD |

## Functional currency

Under **IAS 21**, an entity's functional currency is the currency of its primary economic environment. Oil and gas are priced in US dollars, so upstream and trading entities often have **USD** as their functional currency even when their registered office is in the UAE. In S/4HANA this is handled with the company code currency and additional currencies in the Universal Journal. The UAE dirham has been pegged to the US dollar at about 3.6725 AED per USD since 1997, which reduces but does not remove translation work.

## Ledgers

- **0L**, the leading ledger, follows **IFRS**, which is mandatory for UAE financial reporting.
- A **non-leading ledger** may hold tax-specific valuations, for example for corporate tax adjustments.
- **Group currency** is usually USD, so consolidated reporting is consistent across entities.

## Controlling

All operating company codes share one **controlling area** with a common operating chart of accounts. Plants are modelled with **cost centres** for each operating unit (for example Ruwais gas processing, maintenance, laboratory), **WBS elements** for capital projects and **maintenance orders** from plant maintenance (PM) for repairs.

## Why this matters for your role

Most posting questions at Falcon Gulf start with: which company code, which currency and which cost object? Knowing the structure lets you answer quickly and spot misposted entries during review.

lessons.title: Fiori apps for daily finance work
lessons.content:
## Your launchpad

Falcon Gulf's finance users work in the **SAP Fiori launchpad**, with spaces assigned by business role. The apps below cover most daily tasks.

| Task | Fiori app |
| --- | --- |
| Post manual journals | Post General Journal Entries |
| Upload many journals | Upload General Journal Entries (from a spreadsheet template) |
| Review and reverse journals | Manage Journal Entries |
| Investigate balances | Display Line Items in General Ledger, Trial Balance |
| Supplier invoices without a PO | Create Supplier Invoice |
| Supplier payments | Manage Automatic Payments |
| Bank reconciliation | Manage Bank Statements, Reprocess Bank Statement Items |
| Fixed assets | Manage Fixed Assets, Asset Balances |
| Cost centre reporting | Cost Centres – Actuals |
| Projects | Project Cost Report, Monitor Projects |

## Approval workflows

Manual journals above an approval threshold go through **workflow for journal entry verification** in many S/4HANA systems. The preparer submits the entry, an approver reviews it in the **My Inbox** app, and only then is it posted. This supports segregation of duties, which external auditors test every year.

## Working smarter

- Save **variants** with your usual company codes and ledgers in analytical apps.
- Use **Jump to** links to move from a trial balance line to the journal entries behind it.
- Export to spreadsheet only for analysis; the system remains the record.
- Add an **attachment** (invoice, approval email, calculation) to every manual journal so reviewers and auditors can see the evidence without asking.

## Classic transactions you will still meet

Support teams often refer to transaction codes: **FB03** (display document), **FAGLL03H** (G/L line items), **FBL1H** and **FBL5H** (supplier and customer line items), **AW01N** (asset explorer) and **CJI3** (project actual line items). Many are available as tiles in the launchpad.

lessons.title: Ventures, equity groups and IFRS 11
lessons.content:
## Why joint ventures are everywhere in energy

Upstream concessions and large plants are usually shared between partners to spread cost and risk. One partner, the **operator**, runs operations and pays the bills; the **non-operators** fund their share. The joint operating agreement (JOA) sets out the shares, budgets, billing and audit rights.

## IFRS 11 in brief

IFRS 11 classifies joint arrangements as:

- **Joint operation**: the parties have rights to the assets and obligations for the liabilities. Each party recognises **its share** of assets, liabilities, revenue and expenses. Most unincorporated oil and gas concessions are joint operations.
- **Joint venture**: the parties have rights to the **net assets**, usually through a separate legal entity. Each party uses the **equity method** under IAS 28.

## SAP Joint Venture Accounting (JVA)

S/4HANA includes **Joint Venture Accounting**, which records costs at 100 percent and then splits them to partners. Key master data:

| Object | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Venture | The joint operation, for example Block 7 Offshore |
| Equity type | The phase or purpose, such as exploration or production |
| Equity group | The partners and their percentage shares for that venture and equity type |
| Partner | A business partner who funds a share |
| Recovery indicator | Says whether a cost is billable to partners (shared) or borne only by the operator |

Cost objects such as cost centres, WBS elements and orders carry the venture and equity group, so every posting knows how it will be shared.

## A simple example

Falcon Gulf operates Block 7 with a 60 percent interest; Partner A holds 25 percent and Partner B 15 percent. A maintenance invoice of USD 1,000,000 is posted at 100 percent. JVA allocates USD 600,000 to Falcon Gulf and bills USD 250,000 to Partner A and USD 150,000 to Partner B.

## Controls

- Equity shares must match the signed agreements; changes need an effective date.
- Recovery indicators must be reviewed, because non-billable costs, such as certain penalties, should never reach partners.

lessons.title: Cash calls, cutback and partner billing
lessons.content:
## The monthly JVA cycle

1. **Cash calls**: before the month, the operator requests each partner's share of forecast spending, based on the approved work programme and budget.
2. **Operational postings**: during the month, invoices, payroll, inventory issues and allocations post at 100 percent to venture cost objects.
3. **Overhead calculation**: the operator charges overhead to the venture as allowed in the JOA, often a percentage that decreases as spending rises.
4. **Cutback**: at period end, JVA splits the venture's costs by equity group. The operator's share stays in its books; partner shares move to partner receivables.
5. **Billing**: the system produces **joint interest billing (JIB)** statements for each partner, net of the cash already called.
6. **Settlement**: partners pay the difference, or the operator refunds overcalls.

## Cutback in accounting terms

Before cutback, the operator's books show the full cost. After cutback:

~~~text
Before cutback (100%)
  Dr Maintenance expense – Block 7       1,000,000
  Cr Supplier                            1,000,000

Cutback (partner shares 40%)
  Dr Partner receivable – Partner A        250,000
  Dr Partner receivable – Partner B        150,000
  Cr Maintenance expense – Block 7         400,000

Cash call applied
  Dr Partner cash call clearing            400,000
  Cr Partner receivables                   400,000
~~~

The operator's income statement then shows only its 60 percent share, which matches IFRS 11 for a joint operation.

## Common issues at month end

| Symptom | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Costs not cut back | Cost object missing venture or equity group |
| Partner billed for a non-billable cost | Wrong recovery indicator |
| Cash call imbalance | Budget revised but cash call not updated |
| Partner disputes a statement | Missing supporting documents for large items |

## Audit rights

JOAs give non-operators the right to audit the operator's charges, typically within a set period after year end. Keep documentation for every billed item, and use JVA reports by venture, partner and cost category to answer audit queries quickly.

lessons.title: Capital projects and assets under construction
lessons.content:
## From project to asset

Large plant investments, such as a new gas compression train, are managed as **investment projects** in the Project System (PS):

1. **WBS elements** are created for the project and flagged as investment measures. An **investment profile** creates an **asset under construction (AuC)** automatically.
2. Costs post to the WBS elements: supplier invoices, internal engineering hours, materials and capitalised borrowing costs.
3. At period end, **settlement** (transaction **CJ88**, or the Fiori settlement app) moves the costs from WBS elements to the AuC.
4. When the asset is ready for use, a **final settlement** moves the AuC balance to the final fixed assets, using a settlement rule with one or more asset receivers.

## What can be capitalised

Under **IAS 16**, cost includes the purchase price, directly attributable costs to bring the asset to working condition, and the initial estimate of decommissioning costs. Under **IAS 23**, borrowing costs on qualifying assets that take a substantial time to build must be capitalised.

Not capitalised: general administration, training staff, and costs incurred after the asset is ready for use, such as start-up losses.

## Depreciation starts at "ready for use"

Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use, not when the project is formally closed. A delayed final settlement understates depreciation and overstates profit, which auditors look for.

## Units of production

Upstream assets are often depreciated using the **units-of-production** method, based on production as a share of proved (and sometimes probable) reserves. In S/4HANA this is configured with a depreciation key that uses units of production and periodic entry of actual and estimated total units.

~~~text
Depreciation = carrying amount at start of period × (production in period ÷ reserves at start of period)
Example: 900 million × (4 million bbl ÷ 60 million bbl) = 60 million
~~~

## Useful reports

- **AW01N** asset explorer: values by depreciation area
- **CJI3**: project actual cost line items
- **Asset Balances** and **Asset History Sheet** apps for the IAS 16 movements note

lessons.title: Componentisation, decommissioning and impairment
lessons.content:
## Componentisation

IAS 16 requires each **significant part** of an asset with a different useful life to be depreciated separately. A gas turbine might be split into:

| Component | Useful life |
| --- | --- |
| Turbine core | 25 years |
| Major overhaul | 4 years, until the next overhaul |
| Control system | 10 years |

In S/4HANA, components are usually separate **asset sub-numbers** under a main asset, each with its own useful life. When a major overhaul is performed, the new overhaul cost is capitalised and the remaining carrying amount of the previous overhaul is derecognised.

## Decommissioning provisions

Plants and wells must be dismantled and sites restored at the end of their life. Under **IAS 37**, a provision is recognised at the **present value** of the expected cost, and the same amount is added to the cost of the asset.

~~~text
Initial recognition
  Dr Plant and equipment (decommissioning asset)   45,000,000
  Cr Decommissioning provision                     45,000,000

Each year (unwinding of the discount)
  Dr Finance cost                                   2,250,000   (5% × 45,000,000)
  Cr Decommissioning provision                      2,250,000
~~~

Changes in the estimate (cost, timing or discount rate) adjust both the provision and the asset under **IFRIC 1**, and the revised asset is depreciated prospectively.

## Impairment

Under **IAS 36**, assets are tested for impairment when there is an indicator, such as a sustained fall in oil and gas prices, lower reserves or higher costs. The test compares the carrying amount of the **cash-generating unit (CGU)** with its **recoverable amount**, the higher of value in use and fair value less costs of disposal.

Typical CGUs at an energy group are a field, a plant or a power station. An impairment loss is posted against the assets of the CGU; in S/4HANA it is recorded as unplanned depreciation in the asset (transaction ABAA or the corresponding Fiori posting).

## Climate and energy transition

Auditors and regulators increasingly ask how energy transition assumptions, such as long-term prices and carbon costs, affect useful lives, decommissioning timing and impairment. Document these assumptions in the year-end memo.

lessons.title: UAE VAT in S/4HANA
lessons.content:
## The rules

UAE VAT was introduced on **1 January 2018** under Federal Decree-Law No. 8 of 2017 at a standard rate of **5 percent**. It is administered by the **Federal Tax Authority (FTA)** through the EmaraTax portal.

| Treatment | Examples relevant to energy groups |
| --- | --- |
| Standard rated, 5% | Most local services, equipment, office rent for commercial property |
| Zero rated, 0% | Exports of goods and services outside the GCC implementing states, international transport, **crude oil and natural gas** |
| Exempt | Residential property leases, bare land, certain financial services |
| Out of scope | Supplies with no UAE place of supply, certain transactions within a VAT group |

Zero-rated supplies allow input VAT recovery; exempt supplies do not, so the distinction matters for refining and trading entities.

## Registration and returns

- Mandatory registration when taxable supplies exceed **AED 375,000** in 12 months; voluntary from AED 187,500.
- Related UAE entities can form a **tax group**, which files one return.
- Returns are usually **quarterly**, due by the 28th day after the end of the tax period.
- **Reverse charge** applies to imported services and to certain goods, such as imports declared through customs.

## Configuration in S/4HANA

VAT is configured through the country's **tax procedure** with input and output **tax codes**, maintained in **FTXP**, and G/L accounts for each code in **OB40**. A simplified tax code set might look like this:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| V5 | Input VAT 5%, recoverable |
| V0 | Input, zero rated |
| VR | Reverse charge on imported services (input and output 5%) |
| A5 | Output VAT 5% |
| A0 | Output, zero rated (exports, crude oil and natural gas) |
| AX | Output, exempt |

The VAT return is prepared from the tax line items, typically with the **Advanced Compliance Reporting** framework, and reconciled to the VAT G/L accounts before submission.

## E-invoicing

The UAE has announced a phased e-invoicing mandate using a Peppol-based exchange model, starting with large businesses. Check the latest Ministry of Finance timeline and make sure master data (TRNs, addresses) is clean well ahead of go-live.

lessons.title: UAE corporate tax basics
lessons.content:
## The regime

The UAE introduced federal **corporate tax** under **Federal Decree-Law No. 47 of 2022**, effective for financial years starting on or after **1 June 2023**.

| Taxable income | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| Up to AED 375,000 | 0% |
| Above AED 375,000 | 9% |
| Qualifying income of a Qualifying Free Zone Person | 0% |

Taxable income starts from accounting profit under IFRS, adjusted for items such as exempt dividends, disallowed entertainment costs (only 50 percent deductible) and interest limitation (net interest above 30 percent of tax EBITDA, with a de minimis of AED 12 million).

## Extractive businesses

**Extractive businesses**, which hold a UAE right or concession to explore or extract natural resources, can be **exempt** from federal corporate tax when they are subject to emirate-level taxation and meet the conditions in the law, including notifying the Ministry of Finance. Non-extractive natural resource businesses, such as certain processing activities, can qualify under similar rules. Other group activities, such as trading or power generation, may still be taxable.

## Pillar Two: Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax

From financial years starting on or after **1 January 2025**, the UAE applies a **Domestic Minimum Top-up Tax (DMTT)** of 15 percent to constituent entities of multinational groups with consolidated revenue of at least **EUR 750 million** in at least two of the four preceding years. Finance teams must calculate jurisdictional effective tax rates and keep the data to support Global Anti-Base Erosion (GloBE) calculations.

## Compliance

- Registration and returns through **EmaraTax**; returns are due within **nine months** of the financial year end.
- **Transfer pricing**: related-party transactions must be at arm's length, documented in line with OECD guidelines, with a disclosure form and, above thresholds, master and local files.
- **Tax groups** are possible for UAE resident companies with at least 95 percent common ownership.

## In S/4HANA

Tax-relevant data needs to be captured at posting: correct G/L accounts for non-deductible items, trading partner fields for related-party transactions and profit centres by entity. A separate tax ledger or account-based adjustments support the computation, and deferred tax under IAS 12 is calculated at the 9 percent rate on temporary differences.

lessons.title: The month-end close at Falcon Gulf
lessons.content:
## A five-day close calendar

| Day | Activities | Key transactions and apps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day minus 2 | Remind cost centre owners, check open purchase orders and goods receipts | Manage Purchase Orders, GR/IR monitor |
| Day 1 | Final supplier invoices, accruals, recurring entries, payroll posting | Post General Journal Entries, F.14 |
| Day 2 | Depreciation run, project settlement to AuC, maintenance order settlement | AFAB, CJ88, KO8G |
| Day 3 | JVA overhead, cutback and partner billing; foreign currency valuation; GR/IR regrouping | JVA period-end, FAGL_FCV |
| Day 4 | Intercompany matching, VAT reconciliation, balance sheet reconciliations, provisions review | Intercompany Reconciliation, tax reports |
| Day 5 | Trial balance review, management pack, close period | Trial Balance, OB52 |

## Order matters

Sequence is not arbitrary. For example:

- Settle projects **before** the cutback, so partners receive their share of capitalised costs where the JOA allows.
- Run depreciation **after** final settlements from AuC, so new assets depreciate in the right period.
- Run foreign currency valuation **after** the last partner billing, so USD receivables are revalued at the closing rate.

## Reconciliations Falcon Gulf expects

- Bank accounts to statements, with every unreconciled item explained
- Partner receivables and cash call balances by venture
- Asset sub-ledger to balance sheet accounts
- VAT control accounts to the tax report
- Intercompany balances agreed with counterparties

## Close orchestration

Falcon Gulf runs the close as a task list in the **Financial Closing cockpit**, with owners, dependencies and background jobs. Each task records who executed it and when, which supports internal control testing and the external audit.

## Continuous improvement

After every close, hold a 30-minute retrospective: which tasks ran late, which journals were corrected, and which manual steps could be automated. Small changes, such as a validation that blocks postings without a venture on JVA cost centres, remove recurring errors.
